tice Greenbaum's order, though it had

CHICAGO, March 7.--Western rail-
roads have practically decided to make
wholesale reductions in all class rates
from the eastern seaboard to Missouri
river territory. These will be followed
by similar reductions in rates between
Chicago and the Missouri and Missis-
slppi rivers and the entire valley dis
trict.


A proposition to this effect was pre-
sented at the meeting of the western
executive officials held here today and
a conference has been called for next
Tuesday between the railroad officials
and the Missouri river jobbing inter-
ests to perfect the plans.


The reduction plan was advanced by
the ST. Paul road and seconded by the
Burlington. The reasons assigned are
that rates are too high since the abo-
lition of preferential rates and rebates;
that there has not been a readjust-
ment in rates for the last fifteen years,
and that the traffic between the east
ern seaboard and the Missouri river
has increased enormously.


The proposed reduction will cost the
railroads many millions annually in
revenue, and doubtless will be fol-
lowed by similar reductions in rates
from New York to Chicago. Many of
the western traffic men believe that 1t
is the part of wisdom to make reduc-
tions before the shippers take their
case before the interstate commerce
commission.

OMAHA, Dec. 12.-Several hundred
able-bodied colored men gathered at
the Union station this morning to take
the overland limited train for San
Francisco to help rebuild the city.
They were going to have their fare
paid, their meals provided on the way
and they were to receive high wages
when they reached their. destination,
and they were in high fettle. The we'll
dressed stranger who had hired them
and told them to report at the station
at train time, however. did not appear.
The negroes stood around patiently
waiting for their guide, philosopher
and friend until the train had gone
and then they returned up town, &C
cepting In none too amiable frame of
mind the station masters explanation
that they were the victims of a prac-
teal joker.

Those who put off buying their turkeys
for the Thanksgiving day dinner were able
to purchase them last night and this morn
ing at much lower rate than has existed
for ten days or two weeks.


1t is stated that yesterday morning the
retail dealers were asking from twenty
three to twentyseven cents per pound for
turkeys, but purchasers, scared by these
prices, turned away from the benches and
bought something else. Other purchasers
made arrangements to use something else
as the main dish of the feast today and
they passed through the market without
looking at the poultry benches. The con-
sequence was yesterday afternoon prices
began to drop and last night prime tur-
keys, it is said, could be bought as low as
eighteen and twenty cents per pound, and
many sold even lower. These prices were
asked this morning, but many of the deal
ers will be left with large stocks of turkeys
ON their hands to carry over until next
week.

The plain girl must not be Ill tempered
If she has plain features she need not
have an ugly disposition. She must be
SO sunny in her expression that she makes
those who lock at her forget how plain
she u.s.


The unattractive girl can always have
attractive hands. She can take great care
of her nails, and can polish them until they
are as pink as rose leaves and as glossy
as marble. She can put soothing and
identifying creams upon them to make
them white and massage them until they
are plump.


The plain girl can learn to walk well.
There Is no reason why she should not
hold her shoulders erect and walk grace
fully. She can also have good figure, and
she can dress well. The ugly girl can
speak prettily, and in this way add charm
to her personality. She can be graceful,
too. The fact that nature did not give her
a naturally pretty face need not keep her
from being graceful.


The ugly girl should have virtues of
heart, says Womans Life. She should
cultivate a kind heart. A good heart
shines through the eyes. You can tell
1t the minute you look at a person, and
how one loves person with kind heart
instinctively and with gush of tender
gratitude!

preaching train.

said he was running about six miles an
hour when the accident occurred. He said

happened had it not been for the fact that
steam and smoke from a nearby furnace
almost entirely enveloped the crossing.

are attracting much attention at the
war department.


The models are about twenty feet
long and show not only the exterior of
the ship, but also the interior. One
model represents the transport cut in
half and shows the relative positions

and machinery rooms.

the beds for the men are reproduced
on small scale and the freight is
represented by miniature barrels and
boxes.

ing. checked the Merrimacs conQuering

perhaps. enough credit for his perform

water supply of the city was polluted.

not been pure. The ice companies also

The two-masted schooner Alethea, about
five months ago. arrived here with cargo
of lumber. and after discharging was an
chored in the harbor for several weeks.
Then she was taken to a pier to load street
sweepings for Norfolk. The craft sprang
a leak, and a tugboat was kept alongside
her the greater part of one night to keep
her from sinking in the dock. She was then
lowed to the flats, about half way between
this city and Alexandria, and was there
anchored. The night she was left there
she went to the bottom, but the water was
shoal, and she was quickly raised. She was
then brought back to this city, and while
lying in the mouth of the Eastern branch
she again filled and sank.


In a water-logged condition, the schooner
was left there for several months, but about
week ago the cargo aboard her was
moved and the craft was again foated.
Some repairs were made here, and Monday
she started down the river, bound for the
Rappahannock, 1t was stated, to load
cargo of lumber for this city: but she had
hardly left the harbor when she was struck
by the heavy northwest wind. Her foresai,
was carried away and the jib split by the
wind and under one sail the schooner went
down to Alexandria and anchored. Repairs
were made to the damaged jib, and yeSter-
day afternoon the vessel got under way, but
she had not got out of sight of Alexandria
when it is stated, she ran ashore, and at
latest accounts was still hard and fast.

them from their overhead fastenings. Some
excitement was occasioned among the

damage, but nobody received injury.

pairing the damage. The accident occurred
shortly after o'clock and 1t was not until

San Francisco, Nov 2S.-Ths grand Jury has
worked steadily this week and has found several
Indictments against gratters IN municipal office.
Probably more important than the indictments
for bribery and extortion is the indictment of
petty official for perjury In connection with his
testimony before the jury. This indicted man Is
Peter Duffy, former elevator man of the Hall
Of Justice. who did thriving business serving
warrants and engaging shyster lawyers to defend
criminals. Duffy denied under oath that he
knew about Supervisor Nicholas receiving a
rake off" furniture purchased for the city
officials. but three four reputable business
men testified directly against him. His fate has
spread terror among the small grafters and has
done more than anything else to make the way
clear for the conviction Of the men who have
fallen in office.


On the original indictments Mayor Schmitz
and Boss Ruef be easily convicted, the
prosecutors think. since these indictments
were found much stronger evidence OF plain
blackmau has been secured. Ruef has relied
throughout upon his position attorney TO free
him from all criminal taint- But he reckoned
without the damaging testimony Of several
French restaurant proprietors who now out
Of business, and therefore free TO tell the whole
truth Several Of these men have testified that
they never would have dreamed of paying Ruef
the sums that they gave him merely to act as
their counsel. They paid for police protection
and because they knew he was the boss who
could secure the cancelling Of their liquor license
whenever he pleased. They declared they paid
this blackmail only when threatened with police
persecution and loss of their licenses.

Mrs. Annie Sanderson was murdered

Sanderson was president of the Cali

When Olive Carson, the maid who

noon off yesterday she found Mrs. San
derson in the little downstairs con-
servatory soaked in her own blood
Her throat had been cut from ear to
ear by her husband and the room was
spattered with her blood.


The struggle and subsequent crime
occurred in Mrs. Sanderson's room up
stairs. Chairs and writing desk were
overturned and Mrs. Sanderson's room
was also covered with blood.


Terrible Struggle for Life

woman was an awful look of terror
which death itself was not strong
enough to efface. Sanderson is be-

expectedly, seized her, thrown her to
the floor, pinioned her arms with his
knees and then deliberately taken the
throat

frenzied man went back to his owr
room whence he had emerged to
kill his wife, and after prostrating him.
self upon a leather divan oalmost sew.

single sweep of the razor.

the one in which he killed his wife
The leather couch was literally soaked
with blood and the clothing worn by
the murderer reeked with gore.


The most terrible and ghastly fea-
ture of the murder was that Mrs. San
derson was not killed Immediately, but
lived long enough to rise from the
prone position in which she had been
when her throat was cut and to cross
the room and hall and jump from the
balcony, on the second story to the con-

recorded; 1924 in the third, and 1920 in

nary fuel was used. This reduced the speed
for that hour and brought the average
down correspondingly.

NEW YORK, December 5.-Awakened
by the sound of a stealthy footstep in his
home in East 63d street near 5th avenue
early today, Elias Asiel, broker, found
himself confronted with two revolvers
held only few inches from his face
We'll shoot if you make a squeak" said
voice as the men behind the guns began
to draw slowly away toward the door of
the room. Mr.. Asiel did not heed the
warning, but, raising himself on his elbow,
shouted for help. In an instant the two
men were upon him, raining blows upon
his head, and when servant, who had
heard the cries, rushed into the room the
broker was lying helpless, on the verge of
insensibility, his pillow soaked with blood.
The robbers had escaped.


Invest cation showed that the burglars
gained entrance to the house by saving an
inch-thick iron bar, which held gate
guarding the basement door, and then cut
ting out the glass panel of the door. A
large amount of gold and silver plate in
the dining room had been gathered and
tied UP in two compact bundles, but in
their flight from the house the men did
not have slime to take their booty with
them.


So far as can be learned the only reward
they gained for their desperate act was
few silver knives forks and spoons which
were probably thrust into their pockets
while footing the dining room, and dozen
pearl and sapphire stick pins, which are
missing from Mr.. Asiel's bed room.

Perfect sanitation and cleanliness are
proving fatal to the West Indian negroes
employed on the Panama canal. Although
Col. Gorgas and his assistants have ban
ished yellow fever and other tropical fe-

burying ground for the French canal build
ers, they have found that sanitary pre-
cautions taken In the quarters occupied by
workmen make the jamaican negroes es-
pecially susceptible to pneumonia and other
throat and lung troubles. West Indians
are not accustomed to an abundance of
fresh air and well ventilated, Clearly quar-
tiers. Living for generations in small huts
where large families crowd in rooms tightly
closed against the night air. the negroes
from Jamaica and other tropical islands
have developed lungs with cramped capaC-
ity and are especially susceptible to changes
of temperature.


The officers in charge have found that the
West Indian laborers cannot be induced
to eat sufficient wholesome food to keep
them In good health, even when supplies
are furnished to them at cost prices and
meals are made attractive at great expense

WARSAW, Ind, Nov. 29.-An old fashioned
wolf hunt was pulled off in this county to-

on the outskirts Of the line.


At Q O'Clock this morning people from
all parts Of the county gathered at Leesburg.

when the line was complete the hounds
were placed inside the circle and the march
began.

we're sent after him. He escaped into a
thicket of short underbrush and was lost
sight of for a while, but when he appeared
again two timber wolves were with him
Two other timber wolves were seen a little

made their escape through the lane and
only the gray wolf was killed. The sport
lasted for five hours. The wolves nave been

apart, and the Rockaway towed the schoon.

Santiago de Cuba Oct, 1.-The arrival here
this afternoon of the American cruiser Des
Moines relieved a serious situation Fully four
thousand armed revolutionists were encircling
the city within three miles. They were undisci-
plined. badly organized, without shelter and
hungry. There had been constant rains. discon-
tent was rife, and they were threatening to raid
the city The government forces concentrated
inside Santiago were not sufficient TO drive the
besiegers away.


All official Cuban flags had been lowered when
the Des Moines entered the harbor. Commander
Culver says he has no instructions to change the
present government. and that his mission here Is
solely for the preservation Of order. Demetrio
Castillo is expected here tonight He will
begin at once the work OF dissrming the revolu-
tionists With the exception Of taking cattle,
horses and provisions there has been no out
lawry. Commander Culver will not land his
marines unless such action becomes necessary

PEKING, April 4--The Russo-China
negotiations appear to have reached a
deadlock, At any rate they are drag
ging along slowly. M. Pokotiloff, the
Russian minister to China, and Tong,
the Chinese commissioner appointed to
negotiate an agreement with Russia
regarding northern Manchuria, have
conferred only two or three times dur
ing the past month.


Russia has the upper hand because
she holds nearly all the provisions she
contends for, while demanding that
China officially grant them.


The Chinese, on the contrary, are
also determined to Withstand all for
eign encroachments.


Both parties to the conference are
trying to keep the details as secret
as was the case with the Chinese
Japanese treaty.


One bone of contention is believed to
be the mining and other concessions
which the Tartar generals in Manchuria
gave to Russian corporations and which
Russia wants the Chinese government
to ratify


The Chinese insist that their govern
mert never sanctioned these conces-
sions and that therefore they are in
valid.

From the Cork County Eagle


Two remarkable angling stories come from


Durrus, in Cork county, the one relating


to the attempt made to land a police con-


stable by means of a salmon fishing rod


and the other to the strange experience


which befell DIR. Orr, a Huddersfield


surgeon, in the same place.


DIR. Lewis. the medical officer of Durrus,


undertook to land any swimmer in the


river in fifteen minutes, and Constable Ken


nedy, a noted swimming champion, con-


scented to act the fish A belt was fasten-


ed across the constable's shoulders and to


this was attached a strong salmon hook


Lakewood rod and the ordinary salmon


fishing line were used. The human fish took


the water at high tide and with bold


stroke swan out ten yards At this dis


lance DR.. Lewis checked the constable's


progress. and then the fish dived and turned
on his back. but without avail.


For two minutes it was an even contest
between angler and fish, then the con-
stable swan away for twenty yards when
| he was again brought up. He dived and
wriggled like an eel but not another inch
could he add to his advantage. After eleven
| minutes struggle the angler was gaining
ground; but Constable Kennedy gathered
strength, and diving. made away with a
powerful stroke. At the fourteenth minute
! when only one minute remained the salmon
! line snapped and the fish was declared the
victor.
| More remarkable still was the incident


which followed. DIR. Orr of Huddersfield
! was fyfishing in the river when the pony
which brought him from Dunbeacon broke
| loose from where 1t was tied and fell into
| deep water with the trap attached. The
pony make frantic efforts to swim ashore
| but was hampered by the weight of the
| trap.


DR.. Orr, the narrative goes on, was fish
ing at the opposite side of the stream and
he threw his line toward the pony. By a
fortunate chance the fishing hook caught
the pony i'm the ear and held fast. The
angler pulled his line and the pony re-
spOnded, with the result that both pony and
trap were safely landed on the store.

only Few hundred yards distance to get

of the reform legislation enumerated by
the governor in his official call was enacted
with the exception of civil service for the
state officers. Three bills have already
been signed, and the remainder Will be
acted upon within the next thirty days.
Among the important bills passed were the
following:


Consolidating the cities of Pittsburg-
Allegheny City to Greater Pittsburg; per-
sonal registration for cities; abolishing the
fees of the secretary of the commonwealth:
abolishing the fees of the insurance COM
missioner and designating the number and
ance department; establishing uniform
system of primary elections to be held
twice a year; establishing civil service and
regulations for the municipal employees OF
Philadelphia; prescribing the purposes for
which candidates and campaign commit tees
may expend money, and repeating the
Philadelphia ripper" which takes away
from the mayor and places with the city
councils the appointment of directors OF
public safety and public works.


The session also authorized legislative
inquiry into the affairs of the Philadelphia
and Reading Railroad Company and its
constituent companies; directed the attor-
ney general to inquire by what authority
certain railroad companies In the state
are engaged In the anthracite coal mining
business, and to make an investigation OF

entrance to tho national park by a lone highway
man. who obtained a considerable amount of
money and jewelry. The conveyances were
halted in succession at a curve in the road near
Ahwahnee. at the identical spot where a bandit
year ago robbed several wealthy tourists of their
vauabes

apart to avoid each others dust, and when the
first vehicle reached the turn In the road the
highwaymany whose features were hidden by
duster thrown over his head stepped out, pointed
gun at the driver and commanded him to halt
Some of the women passengers screamed while
others began wildly to hide their valuables.


The highwayman directed all passengers to
throw out their money and jewelry. and when
they had complied directed the driver to move
on The second stage arrived within few min
utes after the first. and the driver and passen-
gers went through a similar experience The
process was repeated until all five coaches had

saved in the attack against Moro outlaws

range by shell fire.


The attack was delayed six months while
Governor Scott was endeavoring to persuade the
outlaws to surrender. All overtures were scorned
and the defiant attitude of the leaders of the out
laws and the Arab priests persuaded their fol-
lowers that the government would be unable to
dislodge them from their fortress within two
years


Leading Moros, in their desire for the extermi-
nation Of the outlaws aided the troops in the
fight. Two hundred Moros under the direction
Of dattOs carried water to the troops.


The reports Of company and troop comman-
ders TO Major General Wood show that every
effort was made to save women and children.
After the fight was over the general ordered
supplies and assistance for the women and chill
dren remaining alive in the crater.

LONG BEACH, May 25.-The woman,
who was the companion of Thomas
Blake, recently arrested in this city by
Los Angeles detectives, charged with
the theft of $4,000 worth Of stocks from
his Boston employers, left this city a
few days ago, stating that she was
going to her home in Boston. The
proprietor of the hotel where Blake
and the woman registered under the
names of Mr.. and Mrs. Richards, pitied
the woman after Blake's arrest and
has kept her location secret until this
morning.


The woman told nothing about her
family, but said that her maiden name
was Smith. She said that she and
Blake were married three weeks before
they came to Long Beach. According
to her story, the wedding was an elope-
ment and took place after she had
broken her engagement with another
man, and Blake, likewise, had forsaken
another woman to whom he was be-
trothed. She said that she knew Blake
had a quantity of stocks in his pos
session, but that she supposed he had
inherited them from his father, who
left considerable estate.


Blake and the woman came to this
city in a Pullman drawing room car
and he lavished money upon her in
various ways. After his arrest she sent
to friends in Boston for money, which
was soon Forthcoming For several
days following the Arrest she is said
to have appeared to be almost frantic.

slipped into the water and sank.

gon and called on the woman they
| both admired.


In few hours afterwards the two
men put off in canoe, ostensibly tc
rejoin the surveyors, but they were soo1
afterward seen astride their overturned
canoe fighting with all their strength
A fisherman and his daughter on the
shore, half a mile away, were the only

After sleeping twenty days, Miss
Florence Parker awakened yesterday
morning and remained awake. Miss
Parker has been under the care of the
best nerve specialists that Southern
California afforded for nearly two
weeks at the Sisters hospital and
though the doctors have brought the
girl out of the comatose state they still
remain mystlfed concerning her case.


Miss Parker was brought to Los An
geles some time ago by her father, Col.
l.. G. Parker, wealthy mining man of
Tucson, Ariz. The young woman was
suffering from peculiar nervous dis
ease that baffled the efforts of Arizona
doctors. AS last resort the young
woman was removed to this city


Until Miss Parker left Deer Lodge,
Mont, her former home, last summer
to join her father in Tucson, she en-
joyed perfect health. Some weeks after
arriving in the Arizona town it was
noticed that she was suffering from
peculiar disease-a nerve disease.


After doctoring with specialists in
Arizona, 1t was advised that the young
woman have change of climate. To-
gether with her parents, Miss Parker
came to Los Angeles, but after a short
time she went north not having found
any relief here. EARLY in the fall the
young woman returned to Tucson


Gradually the young woman became
worse. Just twenty days ago she went
to sleep in a hospital in Tucson. The
physicians who had been attending the
woman tried to relieve her but were
unable to do anything.


Medical Skill BaffIed


AS last resort, Col Parker brought
his daughter to Los Angeles January
90 and sent her to the Sisters hospital.
The best physicians and nerve spe-
cialists of the city were called in to
investigate the case, but they could find
no parallel in medical history. Neither
could they decipher the case of Miss
Parker.


Though the young woman slept calm
ly, there were times when she was in
a conscious condition. She did not open
her eyes, but when the conscious mo-
ments came she would respond with
mods.


Mrs. Parker arrived nine days ago
and Immediately her daughter gradual
ly became better. The periods of con-
seriousness grew longer and at last it
was thought that Miss Parker would
waken. Yesterday morning Miss Parker
gradually opened her eyes and re-
mained awake all day.


All doubt that the young woman will
fully recover has past. She will remain
awake, the specialists say, and grad
ually recover from her ailment.

quiet In the furnace strike situation here
today. The Shenanago valley steel plant and
the Raney and Mckinley furnaces are still
in partial operation, but the Rosena and
Red Jacket closed during the night. This
morning the entire night city police force
was detailed to guard the plants from to
6 o'clock, while the day-turn men went to
the works. The police found the plants
picketed, but the groups Of strikers were
easily dispersed and there was no outbreak.


The steel plant and two furnaces yet
operating are running under reduced forces
many of the employees not having been able
to enter the works last night. A report
last night that one Of the three strikers shot
yesterday had died caused much excitement
among the strikers. and mob Of fully 400
gathered on Raney street at the approach
to the steel plant, and became very threat
ening. The city police were again called
and additional Carnegie police were brought
here in the night from Youngstown and
Sharon. The strikers now demand a wage
increase of Is cents daily. The three
wounded strikers are doing well today and
all have a chance for recovery. General
Superintendent John Oursler today said
there Is no possibility Of the strikers de-
mands being granted while the trouble is
on.

and George Spaulding quickly got their
boat out and pulled over to the Vesuvius.
which was seen drifting with the tide. They
found the boat deserted and after searching
around for some time were picked up by
the revenue tug Calumet. in charge OF Capt

The Calumet also took the Vesuvius In

TRONDHJEM, June liking Haa-
kon VII, his Queen and his son rest
tonight in the ancient capital of Haa-
kon the Good, where Norway was first
created a nation. They came at $50
o'clock this evening in the gunboat
Heimdal. amid scenes of picturesque
ness betting the occasion. The elab-
crate preparations for their reception
had hardly been completed before
crowds began to congregate along the
route of the procession from the pier
to the Palace, on the breakwater and
bluffs marking the entrance on the
hills trimming the harbor.


Expectation had made the ordinarily
grave Norwegians Persians In their
gayety. On the pier was built a great
pavilion in old Morse form, decorated
with green and the nations colors and
fianked by tribunes. Around the pa
vilfon were gathered members of the
diplomatic corps from Christiania. Of
ficers of the army and navy and mu-
nicipal officials. All save the latter
were brilliantly uniformed. A con-
spicuous figure was Baron Won Wedel
Jarlsberg. who played a prominent part
in the selection of Haakon as King and
who is called by the Norwegians


arW1ck the Enigma ker.


At 6:05 o'clock the guns of the Dan
ish warship Hekla, booming the royal
salute, gave the crowds the announce
ment that the Kings yacht was ap-
preaching. The full salute was fired
and the granite walls of the Fjord
had not ceased echoing it before the
HeimdaIe rounded the promontory. The
crowds waited silently until the yacht
entered the slip, when they broke into
the short, sharp hurrahs that express
Norwegian enthusiasm.


The first figure discernible on the
deck was the little Crown Prince Olaf
in white sailor suit, held high above
the rail by his nurse and showing a
precocious interest in the scene. The
King soon joined the Prince, and the
crowd barked out another cheer which
was renewed when Queen Maud ap-
peared.


speedily landed and shook hands with
the members of the diplomatic corps.
the municipal officials and army and
navy officers. The King conversed
briefly with several of the diplomats
and told the German Minister, DIR.
Steubel, that he was delighted with the
prospective visit of Emperor William
The municipality presented an address
of welcome. for which King Haakon
returned his thanks. Then, taking
Crown. Prince Olaf in his arms, the
King, accompanied by Queen Maud en-
tered a carriage and, escorted by a
troop of cavalry, drove to the Palace
through cheering crowds. Throngs of
people surrounded the Palace for hours
and cheered the King and Queen when
they appeared at a window.


Although Norway is regarded as
safely outside the bombthrowing belt
of Europe and country free from
violent political animosities the Nor
wegian police are taking precautions
to protect King Haakon and the visit
ing Princes and other notable person
ages. Detectives watch all trains and
steamers, hover about the Palace, and
will accompany the King throughout
the coronation ceremonies. King Haa-
kon. who is exceedingly democratic
insists on going among the people and
scouts the idea that any one can be
desirous of injuring him.

One of the most dastardly and most
horribly atrocious crimes ever COM
mitted in Los Angeles occurred last
evening about Q o'clock when Sam Can
MALTA of S07 Castelar, street shot his
wife, Mary Cannalla, twice through the
abdomen, fatally wounding the woman
and instantly killing her unborn child.


For more than a year, according to
Antonio Gallo, ather-in-law of the
murderer and father of the murdered
woman, Cannalla abused his wife and
many times beat her. For the past few
months while the woman has bee: in
a delicate condition the husband has
been especially cruel and quarrels be-
tween the two were frequent.


The climax to the marital trouble
Game last evening, when the husband,
without the excuse of intoXication nor
the slight palliation which jealousy
would give to the crime, deliberately
walked up to the bed upon which his
sick wife was reclining, jerked her half
way across the room and fired two
shots into her body He then fired
twice at Antonio Gallo, the father-n-
law, and then turned the weapon upon
himself. infiicting a slight wound in
his own neck. The bullet which Can
MALTA fired into his neck passed through
his mouth and after knocking out two
teeth cut open his lower lip. The
monster was arrested and placed in the
city Jail.


Perform Difficult Operation


The woman did not die Immediately
but was taken from the house to the
city receiving hospital. The caesar
otomy was performed in the hope of
saving the chld's life, as it was not
known positively that the bullets PEN
etrated the childs body. Doctors c..
w. Cook, Quint, Bonynge, Freedman,
Tanner and Sexton assisted in per-
forming the operation, which is one of
the most difficult as we'll as one of the
most unusual known to surgery.


The incision was made in the caes-
arean section and the babe removed.
Then n was found that the first bullet
of the murderer passed through the
chld's head and back.


The second bullet lodged higher up
in the woman's abdomen.


Mrs. Cannala lived about an hour
after the operation and then died.


All the time the operation was in
progress and until the news was given
out that the woman was dead. Mr.. and
Mrs. Gallo. father and mother of Mrs.
Cannalla. paced up and down the cor
ridor of the dingy Jail waiting for the
result of the operation.


Then when a surgeon went to the
door of the Jail and told the stricken
parents that their daughter was dead
both of the old people broke down ut
terly, and sitting upon bench walled
over their irreparable loss.


Father Witnesses Awful Deed


The murderer was seen to commit
the foul crime only by the father-in-
law, at whom Cannalla shot when the
old man cried for help.


The bullet holes in the walls of the
cottage at S07 Casterar street were mute
witnesses against the murderer, for
they told of the terrible tragedy which
had been enacted so recently.


In the wall near the door leading TO
the street were the two holes made by
the bullets which Cannalla fired at his
father in law, while near the bed from
which the murdered woman was drag
ged to her death was a pool of blood
from which the terrified Italians who
thronged the house drew back in hor-
ror.


Cannalla's wound in his neck, which
he inflicted upon himself, was dressed
by the police surgeon and then he was
imprisoned in the tanks. He denied
vehemently that he had committed the
crime and stated that his father-in-
law at whom he fired shots was the
real murderer.


When asked to explain how he had
received the wound in the neck, he
asserted that it had been inflicted upon
him by Gallo, but the powder burn S
which are deep in his neck belle his
statement


In addition to the evidence of the
father of the woman which was TO the
effect that he had seen Cannalla com
nit the crime, Mrs. Cannalla after be-
ing told that she was going to die,
said that her husband had shot her


A few minutes before she died Mrs.
Cannalla said my husband was a
Sicilian and that race kills" She knew
that her babe had been killed and
would say no word of forgiveness to
the murderer. While his wife was dy-
ing the murderer sat in the next
room and moaned, not because he
had killed his wife, but because his
head was sore from the self inflicted

catastrophe was at Horn island, where
Light Keeper Johnston with his wife
and daughter were swept into the gulf
with their light house and drowned.

storm two bodies were seen floating in

men were in the Klondike building on

them safely back to land.

cargo of lumber. and Norwegian bark
Anna, with $4,000 worth of lumber,
were blown up on Horn island and left
saved by tug boats which put out from
the main land.


The experience of the American bark
Florine, which was wrecked on Cat
island. shows the strength of the wind.
When the bark began to drift tug
made fast a line attempting to tow

wind dragged them both at tbs mercy

main property loss to the sound cities

lumber mills located there reported
many of their buildings and machinery
razed to the ground. Large quantities
of pine timber were virtually destroyed.

Seated at table in the dining room. their
hands clasped in what they expected would
be their farewell to earth, William Meth
nor and his wife Anna were found un-
conscious by neighbors in their home in
New York Wednesday. Between the lips of
each was a rubber tube. which connected
with two gas jets from the chandelier.
They sought death rather than see the
house in which they lived pass from their
hands, for yesterday the heavy mortgage
was to be foreclosed and their savings of
a lifetime thus swept away. The choice
lay between death and the poorhouse, and
they chose death. Methnor Is sfxty-three
years old. His wife Is ten years his junior.
They dined ON the last food the larder
contained and spent last evening in plac-
ing the house In order. Then, shortly after
midnight, they sat down and arranged their
death pact. AS soon as she could speak
the woman inquired anxiously for her hus-
band, and when she found he had not yet
been revived she wept bitterly. Methnor
was later restored to consciousness.

vey was practically complete. Fellows had

PHILADELPHIA, Feb. 4.--Rather
than marry a man she did not love
Jennie Graham, nineteen years old
swallowed laudanum in the presence of
her aunt and friends this morning. She
is now in the hospital and may recover.


Miss Graham was to have been mar
ried to Reuben Dean, 81 years old, at
her aunt's house this morning. All the
arrangements had been made for the
ceremony, and the guests were waiting
for the arrival of the bridegroom when
the girl attempted to end her life.


She had known Dean for many
months. but in the mean time she met
Charles Parfitt, with whom she fell in
love. Nevertheless, having engaged her
self to Dean, she determined to keep
her troth, but when the decisive mo-
ment came she weakened.

Half a century ago the crofters in the
West Highlands seldom saw money, and
never needed it. They erected for them
selves huts mostly built OF turf, fioored
with clay. and rooted with heather; they
kept a few cattle, goats and sheep which
grazed at will on the open hillside and pro-
yided them with milk and wool. They lived
a truly simple life. and their needs were
few. They grew oats for their own food
and potatoes, which formed their other
chief article of diet. Tea was an unknown
luxury-it was by no means uncommon to
find persons who had never tasted It.
Wheaton bread had never been seen in
those parts. Their clothes were made from
the feeces Of their own sheep, spun and
woven by the good wives during the long
winter nights and dyed from the simple
dyes made from the lichens which grew on
the stems Of trees or on the powders of
rock In the neighborhood. The whisky they
drank came from secret stills on the hill
side. and had never paid excise. The near
est parish church was often many miles
away; no school was there for the children
very few of them. indeed. could read or
write. Still fewer had ever heard a word
Of English spoken. Their spiritual needs,
however, were not neglected, for they re-
ceived constant visits from the Men," as
they We're called. who had constituted
themselves the spiritual guides of their
neighbOrhood.

I'm THE banks of the Little Big
u Horn river. in Montana, many
-, years ago.. lay encamped blood
thirsty hordes Of Indians, fresh from
pillage and murder, who were fleeing
from the white mans vengeance. A
few hours later on that eventful June
day was enacted bloody scene which
has gone down in history when Custer
and his gallant little band fell, fight
overpowered by the resistless savagery
hurled against them.


A few days ago the banks of this
little stream were again crowded with
Indian tepees; the smoke of q hun
bred campfres disentangled itself from
among the tentpoles and foated away
into the blue sky. Blanketed forms
glided hither and thither and the grim,
stoical image of the red man was to
be seen on every side, Their mission
was, however, peace, not war, this time,
and their welcome to the white man
friendly "ugh" instead of the fendish
warwhoop.


The occasion was the third annual
fair Of the Grow Indians, held on the
row agency on the line of the Bur-
ington; about seventy miles southeast


This fair is the most unique of it's
lind. probably the only fair in the


ntire United States conducted entirely
" Indians, without assistance or super
5ision of any kind whatsoever from


he whites.


indian policemen uphold the solemn


=; of the law, Indian Judges inspect


ne exhibits in the agricultural hall,
where only the Indians are allowed to
compete for the prizes; Indian chiefs
|,onduct the races, open to Indian horses
with Indian riders, and when the shades
Of evening fall, thousands of specta-
,ors from among the whites gather to
watch the ancient rites and dances
given by the Indians themselves IN
huge tents, where, amid savage pa,
geantry, are enacted the weird and
thrilling customs of the past.


National Event for Redskins.


This annual fair of the Crows might
almost be called national event for
The redskin race. Invitations are sent
to every reservation in the western
United States, and the descendants Of
savage tribes whose memory is syno-
nym for cruelty, and the sons and
daughters of noted Indian chiefs whose
names are known to every schoolboy,
gather at the call.


And here and there among the thou
sands assembled may be distinguish led
the bent forms and scanned faces of
the few among the warriors who, in the
early settlement of the country, resist
ed with gun and arrow the advance of
civilization. A mere remnant, await
ing the call to the happy hunting
grounds. = =

HORSES and dogs have perhaps exhibited
L more devotion and sagacity than most
other dumb animals. 1t would take volumes
to contain all the instances of courageous atfec-
ton and love which these animals have shown.
A few months ago, Old Charlie, bay horse
which draws the junk wagon of New Jersey
man, showed wonderful intelligence when he
saved the life of his masters daughter.


The little girl, who was four years old, was
PLAYING on the bank of canal which runs
through the field in the rear of her fathers
place, when she tumbed into the water.
Old Charlie was in the field. He saw his little
mistress disappear, and started a gallop
for the edge of the canal. When he reached
the bank he saw the little girl go down. With
out moments hesitation the faithful animal
plunged into the water, and when the child
came the surface seized her skirts in his teeth
and climbed the bank to safety He trotted
across the field to the house and set her down
on the doorstep, where the mother found her.


That night when the father returned and
was told of the incident, he ran to the barn
and broke his whip into pieces, declaring that
he would never again beat the faithful horse.

The women of the isthmus and Chiapas
are much better looking than those Of the
Aztec race in northern and central Mexico
and have much more cheerful dispositions.
The Aztecs are sad; you seldom see one
smile, but the women down here seem 10
be full of life and gayety and fond OF
amusement. Perhaps the bright colors or
THEN costumes make them look more cheer
full than they would appear if they wore
the black shawls that are common
among the women in the northern part or
the republic. A battle. or ball, is given on
every feast day and national holiday, and
such occasions occur with surprising ire
quency. One of the railway contractors
was complaining to me yesterday that the
feast days average about three week.
But whenever they come there is always
ball, and In the city of Tehuantepec the
people dance in the market house. Tne
benches are taken out. the pillars are dec
GRATED with mirrors and fancy calicoes, the
women put on their brightest costumes and
their chains of golden coins and dance
barefooted upon the stone floor. The men
wear leather sandals.


Every employer of experience testines
that the laboring people down here like all
Mexican poems, are very difficult to get
along with Notwithstanding their amiabe
dispositions. They are ''sot'' In their ways
They are extremely tenacious of their Gus
toms and every employer who undertakes
to introduce reforms or innovations may
expect trouble at once. They much
more difficult to handle than the'ignorant
negroes of our own southern states, and
only employers who have experience are
likely to get along without difficulty. That
is one of the reasons why so many planters
from the United States and other strangers
have failed at farming down here. They
have not been able to get the worth OF
their wages.

OAKLAND. Dec. 25.--Faithfully and
unerringly through the long years of
his service William Riordan watched
guard the trains that came and went
meath him. The lives OF the millions
of people who passed to and fro on the
Oakland pier during the many years
that he was stationed there were in
trusted to his care. A misplaced
switch would have meant frightful dis
aster, but never did the crippled man
falter. His eye was ever alert, his
hand ever steady. Trains whizzed back
and forth in bedlam of noise and a
lurching confusion, but never once was
one misdirected, nor was a passenger
or trainman hurt through fault of the
aged towerman.


This evening William Riordan, the
careful towerman, who had never fall
tered or erred at the most difficult post
on the whole Southern Pacific system,
making his way along that same Death
Curve, occupied with thoughts of the
Christmas joys awaiting him at home
after the days work and unmindful of
the Berkeley locals screeching blasts,
was struck down and killed instantly.


Riordan was an old Southern Pacific
Company employe, having lost both
legs in a railroad accident long years
ago. His form was mangled almost
beyond recognition.


He was 55 years of age and resided
at 1880 Seventh street. The Coroner
took charge of the remains.

PARIS, Oct. 14.-There were violent
public demonstrations at the Long
champs race course this afternoon in
consequence of an unsatisfactory start
in the Free handicap. The trouble cul-
minated in riots, pillage- and ineen-
diarism. Many persons were arrested.
The programme comprised six races,
and the first two passed off without
incident There were nine starters In
the Free handicap, the next event, and
four, including the favorite. were left
at the post. Amid terrific uproar a
complete outsider won.


The public Immediately became en-
ragged, broke down the barriers and in
vaded the track Crowds demanded
the return of their bets. They sur
rounded the bookmakers booths
chased out the cashiers and seized the
money. Attempts to restore order were
in vain, the small force of police pres
ent being Inadequate. The crowds an
ger increased and men began breaking
chairs and throwing them on the track
Then rougher element raided some
automobiles and seized some supplies
of petroleum, with which they sprin-
killed. the booths and other woodwork
and set them af1re.


The squad of firemen on duty were
helpless, as the water hose had been
cut. The authorities telephoned for
assistance to Mount valerian, and a
strong body Of troops was at once sent
upon the double quick. The soldiers
succeeded in eventually clearing the
inclosure by charging, but in the mean
time the betting structures had burned
to the ground. A large wooden build
ing belonging to the bookmakers also
was set on fire.


The last three races were postponed
Sixty arrests were made and a large
number of policemen and rioters were
injured


A large force of troops will remain
on duty throughout the night at the
Longchamps automobile course.

The engineers who for many months
have been trying to bring the Colorado
River again under control have finally
succeeded. They have turned the river
back into its own channel, and it now
flows in its usual course to the Gulf of
California instead of pouring into the
Salton Sink and wasting the lands that
had been reclaimed by irrigation. The
river, entirely abandoning its old chan
mel, had followed it's lawless course
northward, destroying much property
and threatening millions of dollars
worth of fruit, farm and grazing lands.


This arid region had been turned TO
good account by an irrigation system
supplied with water taken from the
Colorado River. Unfortunately, no o n
troll works had been built at the head of
the main canal that tapped the river, and
the latter d%eepened and wideped the en-
trance into the canal until the whole river
poured into it. The natural river chan
mel became dry, and as the irrigation
system could not carry of the entire
food flow, there was great damage to
the bitches and crops, and a large lake
was formed, covering about $50 square
miles at the lowest part Of the sink, some
260 feet below sea level.


Nearly 5000 people had settled in the
basin Of the Imperial Valley and were
raising excellent crops of barley and
alfalfa. They had opened many stock
farms and were raising the date palm;
and the shipments Of products from this
verdant oasis were said to exceed those
of any other town in southern California.
But prosperity was checked by the I'M
welcome floods and the pioneers have
awaited anxiously the abatement of the
evil.


They are now thoroughly convinced
that too much water il a nuisance, and
they will doubtless take good care in
future to keep this desirable commodity
duly harnessed and under control.

Mrs. Lucius Tuckerman died yesterday at
her country home. Ingleside, Stockbridge,
Mass. She closed her Washington resi-
dence early In May and enjoyed her usual
health throughout the summer until three
weeks ago, when she was attacked with the
illness which resulted in her death.


The deceased was about eighty-seven
years old. and was the widow of Lucius
Tuckerman of New York and later of this
city. She had lived in Washington for
many years and was prominently identified
with the social and phianthropic life of the
capital. She came Of New England stock
and was the granddaughter of Oliver VOL
colt. Secretary Of the Treasury under
Washington Her son-n-law and daugh-
ter, Mr.. and Mrs. James Lowndes, and her
daughter, Miss Emily Tuckerman, have
been spending the summer season with Mrs.
Tuckerman and were with her at the time
of her death.


In addition to her daughters. two sons,
Alfred Bayard Tuckerman and Paul Tuck
erman, survive her.


No news other than was contained in a
telegram announcing her death has been
received by her friends here. The family
homes are closed.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 1s.-The trop-
ical hurricane which swept over Cuba,
breaking cable communication and
passing on the southern and eastern
coast of Florida early today, cut off
communication south of Jacksonville
and flooded various places in it's
course. Tonight it is apparently safe
away from land and heading toward
the Bermuda islands and the ocean be-
yond.


The storm swept with terrific force,
but it's path was hardly more than
seventy miles in width. 1t ragged last
night in Havana, leveling the inland
wires in that neighborhood, passed
over the west end of Cuba, it's vortex,
crossing Sand Key and Key West with
winds blowing at least seventy-two
miles an hour, tipping the east coast
of the peninsula and sweeping on
toward the ocean.


The weather bureau announced that
the storm has evidently passed east
ward through the Florida straits and
is now over the Atlantic some distance
east of the Georgia coast.


So far as reports from the land
weather stations show there are no
dangerous winds tonight along the i'm
mediate coast and adjacent territory.
Storm warnings, however, are dis
played all along the Atlantic coast
from Florida to Cape Cod.

Heavily roned and handcuffed to

The two men do not look like they did
when they entered the county bastile
during August. 1904. At that time
Jacob, known as the big fellow. weighed
somewhere in the nelghborhood of 200
pounds, all of which was hard muscle.
Silas, the smaller one, weighed about
fifty pounds less, but both men were
as hard as iron from long years of hard
work on the ranges and before they
could be landed in Jail they put up
desperate fight against the arresting
officers.


But the Jail life has taken the fight
out Of the boys and today when
they leave and enjoy the fresh air for
the first time in two years they will be
so different from the boys who went in
the Jail that their own friends would
not recognize them.


Exercise in Small Tank


Both have relished the Jail food but
the constant worry and confinement
have made wrecks of them. Their only
exercise room has been the low iron
tank, midway between roof and cell
ing to the west side of the county Jail
and for a few hours each day they
have been allowed to pace up and down
| the hard floors and converse with their
companions.


To men who have spent their lives
in activity on cattle ranches and in the
mountains the change was fearful and
the boys broke under the strain.
But the officers will take no chances
Before when the Casteal brothers We're
taken into custody the officers made a
| mistake of putting but a single pair of
cuffs on them and simply cutting them
together with the result that the boys
put up desperate fight and nearly es-
| capped.


So today when the men start north
with the officers in charge both will
| wear the Oregon boot strapped TO their
legs and With the mass of sixteen
pounds it is not likely they will stand
any chance of escape. But. as an extra
precaution each man will be handcuffed
anC then handcuffed to an officer.
Yesterday the final papers i'm the case
arrived in department one of the SUI
peiior court and the trip north will be
the last chapter to the famous prosecu-
| tlon of the case.


Leave Trail of Crime


The Casteal boys are to serve SEN
tence for crimes committed during the
summer of 1904. At that time the two
brothers, who before that had been
good ranchmen. held up peddler on the
Capistrano road and took all his money
his goods and his horse and wagon.


Then while Deputy Sheriffs Len
Cleveland and Bert franklin went
scouting over the country for them the
two brothers worked their way TO the
| eXtre me southern section of California,
leaving behind them a trail of robheries
and burglaries at every village and
hamlet along the line.


Finally they arrived at their brother
in-laws ranch i'm the White Water cam
yon and there late ono evening i'm Aug
ust the local officers trailed them after
having spent six days and nights in
| the hunt


DurineSthe pursuit the only time the
officers caught the Casteal brothers off
their guard was while they We're at
supper that night and before either
man could draw weapon Cleveland
had stepped in one end Of the summer
house In which they were eating. while
Franklin showed up at the door of the
other end. The two desperadoes looked
up from their meal only TO find the
muzzes of the officers rifles glaring at
them.


They were handcuned and taken
about fifty yards down the road when
they turned and leaped on the officers
and before they were finally beaten into
submission they had managed to break

. half IN just enough boiling water to
coyer. Add salt when nearly done

"They are close by, Artie," she said; "but

And run they did, as fast as their little

now missing their footing and going ankle
deep into ditch, then up and on. as Peggy
afterward said, like scared rabbits"


II seemed such long way-would they

Peggy's feet ached, and she could scarcely
see, she was SO faint. Once she thought she
should certainly fall, and she murmured an
Involuntary prayer:


"Dear Heavenly Father, help us to reach
home, and don't let the Indians get granny
or Artie or me"


Breathlessy they ran on. There at last
was the road, and the row of apple trees,
and beyond rose the cabin. 1t was only a
few rods now.


Hot. tired, painting, Peggy sprang into the
dusty highway, and half dragging Artie, rush

face, the girl dashed through the doorway

toward the cabin.

are coming"

girl closed the heavy oaken door and barred
It. Two OF three tomahawks struck the
strong plank as she shot the wooden bolt into
it's place.


Grandmother Thompson looked up, very
much surprised, from her work over the hot
fire, frying doughnuts, at Peggy's alarming
information.


The girls sudden act convinced her that
danger was near at hand, too, and she i'm.
mediately dropped her turning-fork and hob
bled as fast as she could to one of the win
dows, to close the shutter. This she succeed
ed in accomplishing.


Peggy also hastened to window and drew
its shutter, after she closed the door. Then
she ran to another, and drew that


The shutter of the fourth window Grand
mother Thompson attempted to close, but the
Indians anticipated her, and breaking the
glass, stretched their brawny arms within,
and prevented the shutter being closed.


One of the braves even attempted to enter
by climbing up on his companions shoulders

DIES MONIES, IOWA.-The trial of Chief Of
Detectives Eli Hardin before the fire and police
commission on the charge of having kissed
women who came to see him in his private
office on official business is the sensation of tho
week in Des Moines. Six women have filed COM
plant that they were Rugged and kissed by the
police officer against their will.


Before crowded courtroom yesterday two
women told the commissioners their complaints.
He tickled me under the chin and then held
my hands down to my side and kissed me on
the mouth" said Mrs Charles Billings indig-
nantIy.


Mrs Billings was confused and uneasy when
she first took the witness stand but she gritted
her teeth and in few minutes regained her
self-control. She told her story quietly except
that she blushed deeply when compelled to admit
that she had been fondled and kissed. Accord
ing to her story, she went to the detective
department to intercede for her husband, who
had been arrested burglary charge. While
there she burst into tears and. under pretense
Of comforting her, she said Chief Hardin became
unnecessarily tender and solicitous.
Mrs. Minnie McGill, a brunette with flashing
eyes, detailed much the same experience. Mrs.
Jessie Fenner testified that the officer locked the
| door and insisted on kissing her.

Special Cable Despatch TO THE SUN.


PARIS, Oct. 1A-One Of the most extraor-
binary scenes probably ever witnessed
on a raoetrack occurred at Longchamps
in the Bots de Boulogne this afternoon.
A riot Of wild proportions turned the race
course into a pandemonium, and violence
reigned unrestrained for over an hour and
a half. Men and women were assaulted
and injured, shots were fired, and the mob
in the excess Of its fury resorted to incendi-
arism, joyfully burning the betting booths
and twice attempting TO set fire to the
grand stand.


The cause Of the rioting was the crowds
belief that there had been a false start.
when this belief spread, which it did like an
electric shock, the people seemed to &c
mad, but with a clear and definite purpose,
namely. to wreak vengeance on the man.
ayers Of the races and the operators of the
betting system, the pari mutueL


The trouble started at 3 o'clock, when the
third race was called. There were probably
100 900 persons present. Only three horses
got away. Those left at the post included
the fsvorite. The start was so patiently
false in public estimation that the people
supposed the horses would be recalled,
but this was not done, and as soon az the
spectators realized that there was to be no
recall those in the grand stand became
extremely excited, and those in the immense
field seemed to go wild. A. one man the
crowd cried Catch the robber!"


Those in the field made a rush for the
many betting booths, which form practically
one building in the field, demanding their
money. They contented themselves with
demanding only .~momentarily. Then they
stormed the booths, set them on fire and
assaulted their occupants. Men and women
we're knocked down and tumbled over
each other. The men about the booths
were seemingly crazy drunk and waved
over their heads great rolls Of bank notes,
which had been taken from the cashiers.


The sight made the crowd madden than
ever. They overpowered the booth keepers,
both tally men and cashiers. Bills and
gold and silver pieces flew in all directions.
The crowd fought and scrambled for the
money, and many were injured, Mean
while the fire was spreading.


Those in the grand stand were also fren-
zied but were somewhat less violent. They
demanded their money at their booths and
denounced the Soci6te encouragement
which controls all sport in France, threaten
ing legal proceedings.


Twice flames started in the cheaper part
of the grand stand, newspapers being used
10 encourage the flames, but the stand
was not burned. When the'lremen reached
the scene the Infatuated mob would not ct
them reach the burning booths. The mob
cut the harness of the horses attached to the
fire engines and the animals, which were
at high tension and. frightened by the
screams, galloped across the course. They
rushed uncontrolled into the dense crowd
bearing down many persons.


The police and gendarmes were power
less. They were treated by the crow
almost the same as the bet takers, and
several Of them were injured before rpen-
forcements arrived.


The police authorities ordered the races
stopped for the day, bu t the crowd refused
to go home. In the meantime aid was sum
moned from the city, NJ. Lepine, project
Of police, arrived and the crowd cheered
him, but even from him they demanded
that he refund their money. NJ. Lepine
restored order. His reenforcements slowly
and with difficulty forced the crowd from
the field, but not before the iron chairs had
been hurled even at the policemen.


Storm was The ~favorite in the bet ting.
Monsieur Perichon won. The mutuels
had begun TO pay bets at Il to l on Monsieur
Perichon when the rioters got the upper
hand.


The fire had destroyed every one Of the
seventy-lve booths and the tall tower
where the races are bulletined before it was
got under control. The damage amounts
to SO 900.


The pool sellers say that only $1,000 was
stolen by the rioters, but report places
the money thus lost as high as 100000.


1t was the worst outbreak hat ever
occurred on this the greatest racecourse
in France. There was a similar one at
Colombes sixteen years ago and one since
at Vincennes.

British steamer Arcs Castle yesterday after
a wedding trip which had extended over
1900 miles. The first and second officers.
with most of the members of the crew,

memorable one not only because the Arcs

est among the ships officers, and when the
news became known there was shining
of buttons and a sharpening of razors
which would have flattered the bride had
she known it. This feeling was intensified
when the day before the Arcs Castle sailed
Mrs Days piano was swung over the side
and her pet collie Jack Davis came TO take
possession of the vessel.

sea, was the life of the steamer from the
time her blonde head appeared over the
companionway until she bade the officers
goodbye yesterday.

fast express on the Norfolk & Western Railroad
ran into an open switch at Juniper Siding. ff-
teen miles from Norfolk. to-day. Seven persons
were injured in the wreck, and but for the Wig
ilance of Mark Noble. engineer of the train.
probably many passengers would have been
killed.


The train was running at the rate of seventy
five eighty miles an hour when Noble spied
the open switch thirty yards away. Imme-
diately he threw on his emergency brakes, reduc-
ing his speed TO about thirty miles by the time
the engine struck the switch.


The train jumped the track. then jumped an
adjoining ditch and ran headlong into the neigh
boring woods before it stopped Noble was
picked up twenty feet from the engine. with a
broken leg. The train careened but did not
turn over. No one was killed.


The switch which caused the wreck was wide
open, and one has yet accounted for the
cause. Noble had orders giving him free road
from Suffolk TO Norfolk 1t is said that the
switch left open after freight early in

likely to please his palate.


The sandwiches most often seen now on

cheese, through which chopped green pep

made and meet with such general favor

rassment unless at least four are allowed
to each guest. Cookies and simple indi-

SAN BERNARDINO, Cal, Dec. 13.-
A Southern Pacific passenger train from
Los Angeles to Riverside, due in the
latter city at $40 tonight, was wrecked
six miles west of Cotton by colliding
with freight train which had taken
the siding at Ailsa.


About three trainmen and several
passengers received injuries, but none
are said to be serious.


The freight had fifty five cars, While
the siding has a capacity for but fifty.
1t was bound east and had orders to
take the siding to permit the Riverside
train, also eastbound, to pass.


The freight took the siding, but be-
ing too long, ran into the head of the
train on the main line at the east end,
closing the switch at the west end and
turning. the tail lights to show a clear
track, and failed to put out any sig
nails to warn the passengers that the
line was blocked at the other end of
the switch


Engineer Tom Norton saw clear track
signals and let his engine out full
speed, but when half way up the
switch saw that the end of the freight
projected out on the main line and that
a collision was inevitable.


He slapped on the emergency and
slowed down greatly when the crash
came, the passenger engine being de-
molshed and sent into the ditch and
several freight cars smashed.


Engineer Norton and his fireman
jumped, both being badly injured.


Conductor Tom Mellen was also in
jured. as was also Mail Clerk Brasch
of Riverside.


Several passengers were injured, but
their names were unobtainable tonight.


The wrecker and two physicians We're
sent out from Cotton and the injured
win be brought in this morning.


A shoofiy Will clear the main line
this morning.

Carlos at Lisbon. The discipline aboard

were recently put in command. The men
resented this, and when shore leave was
refused them they seized a Lieutenant

Throw him overheard" Two warrant

taking an involuntary bath, hut the men
insisted that he be put ashore, which was
done.


Upon landing he informed Admiral
SCUBA, who accompanied him back to the
ship. The crew, however, refused 10 let
the Lieutenant aboard. They told the
Admiral that unless the Government prom
ised to pardon them and give them an
entirely new set Of officers they would sink
the ship. The Admiral promised to comply
with their demands il they would sur
render


The men showed him that they had pos
session of the ma gazine and that the guns
were loaded. They threatened to board
any warship that approached them, and
also to fire on the city If they were attacked
Admiral Anaral also conferred with the
men and promised them justice and free
dom from arrest. Eventually the men
yielded, and 4S5 of them went ashore. Their
fate has not beer reported.

the torpedo boat destroyer Teio. Naval
officers say that their prestige is gone, and
that it would have been better to have
sunk the Dom Carlos thar to have capitu-

hills, the Plum run mine was opened this

guard. They were greeted by fusillade

tement and gathered on the slopes above

l. The great navy search lights have been

PORTLAND, Ore, Sept. 1.-THE
county poor farm has, according to the
assertion of the inmates, the cleverest
COW in the state. The animal is an old
red Jersey that has been on the farm
for years. The matron at the farm last
summer discovered that the faucet on
the hydrant in the back yard was fire.
quently turned on, but constant watch
ing failed to disclose the miscreant.


The same trouble occurred again this
summer. The matron noticed the water
was turned on about the same time
every afternoon. While she watched
she saw the old red Jersey come leis-
urely up the road, into the back yard
and walk straight up to the hydrant.
The COW pushed the faucet with her
nose, but 1t did not seem to work. So
she tried her horns, and when that
method failed, opened her mouth, took
hold Of the faucet and turned it.


Mrs. Bossy then drank her fill of cold
water and turned away toward the
green fields. evidently pleased that she
did not have to go quarter of mile
to the river to satisfy her thirst.


The next day the COW seemed much
peared detected when after half an
hour of hard work she could not get
her drink. Then the matron had a
watering place made and the cold
water was allowed to run at all times.

BOSTON, December 22.-The o'clock
train from New York for Boston over the
Boston and Albany division of the New
York Central railroad was derailed near
the Allston station at 1920 last night.
With the exception of one locomotive, the
entire train left the rails, but no one was
killed Some passengers were severely
shaken, cut by flying glass and bruised,
but not seriously enough to necessitate the
immediate attention of physicians. One
of the brakemen had his arm broken.


The train. which consisted of eight cars,
drawn by two locomotives. was late reach
ing Allston and was going at high speed.
The driving rod on the second locomotive,
a big mogul, snapped and the whirling end
deraled the train, with the exception of
the forward locomotive. None Of the cars
was overturned, but humping over the ties
smashed the windows and threw some of
the passengers to the floor.


The train ran several hundred yards be-
fore it came to stop. Then the fright
ened passengers left the cars. All were
able to get out unassisted. One baggage
car was thrown thirty feet from it's tracks,
blocking the tracks for some time.

Judging from this, the book will he
one of the most artistic novels yet
placed upon the market.

the book are genuine high art photo
graphs of Spanish scenes about Capt.
strano. These are pasted on the upper
edges in tine book and were taken by
Harold A. Taylor of San Diego. Besides
the pages are elaborately decorated by

of old California Spanish songs. These
have been made use of by Mrs. Ryan
in manner never before introduced
to the book-reading public. Strains
from these old songs with the music
set to them appear on the pages where
the songs are used.

Chicago, where she will complete final
arrangements with her publishers. I'm
mediately after the publication of the
book she will come to Los Angeles and
will probably remain here for several
months.

had been triced up on board the whaler

water for ffty-eight days by Captain

affirmed tnat Captain VaTnum

under Section 1911 of the Revised
Statutes. which prohibits logging and
all other forms of corporal punishment

only legal punishment for offending
sailors at sea is Imprisonment on bread
and water TO such an extent as not to
ieopardize the health of the prisoners.

Quebec. Que, July 21.-The Ameri-
can automobile army, sixty-fve strong,
attacked Quebec by road this afternoon
and made a successful entry with but
few casualties. The most severe set
back was received before the first Grim
mage line, when Kirkham, driving
Maxwell, broke his front springs and
was compelled to drive the remainder
Of the distance using boards for springs.
Kirkham was clean-score man up to
the start today, but suffered many
points setback.


The racers were required to climb
many hard hills in the run here from
Three Rivers, distance of ninety-seven
miles. A half-stone road was also one
of the drawbacks, and many punctures
resulted, but there is still no rain. There
are nineteen cars with clean records,
and with but four actual runnings days
yet, the committee is trying to figure
out method of determining the win
ner.


The tourists remain here until Tues
day, and then return to their native
country, Jackman, Me-, being the first
nights stop, then Wooterville, Rough
ley Lakes, and the final destination
Britton Woods.

SALINAS, Oct. 7--Forest fires which
started in wild canyon, fourteen miles
south of Monterey City, eight days ago,
that have been raging along the Palo
Colorado, Garrapalos, Mill and Stoney
creeks. are still unchecked. Hundreds
of men are fighting the flames, but
aside from saving ranch horses they
are making no headway


l. N. Swetr am, whose ranch Is on
the Palo Colorado creek and who has
been burned out, said this morning
that the fire has passed Notlesjes land
ing, twenty-four miles down the coast,
reached the lime kilns and was working
toward Sargent's ranch on the Little
Sur.


All work has been suspended In the
district, the men being out trying to
save houses and cattle.


Last night an attempt was made to
stop the fire by clearing a space thirty
feet wide at Murray Ridge, but the
flames leaped the clearing.


The fire has reached the Santa Lucia
government reservation, known as the
Pines, and is sweeping toward Tassa-
jara Springs eastward and Arroyo
Seco southwark.


A strip of land twenty-four miles
long, ten miles wide and covering
nearly $4,000 acres has been burned
over. The losses will be very heavy.

were released, placing them on the list

During the same period the construc-
ton Of thirteen new battleships, eigh-
teen armored cruisers and four pro-
tected cruisers was commenced.

These meetings of the lovers con-

The blue suit OF the soldier was like

With all the dignity and wrath that

This warning did not seem to cause

shoot him.


AS Daniel was unarmed, and the

pleasing, he departed, but not hope
less.


The secret meetings of the lovers
soon were resumed, and their cup Of
happiness seemed filled to the brim.
But all was soon to end, as most good

hearts, the girl suddenly screamed and

man turned apprehensively and beheld

Daniels first impulse was to stand

as he was without even so much as
the better part of valor, and he dived
for the hole in the hedge. He was
about half way through when the old
man reached him and cold chills
triclxled uncomfortably down his back

him down the high embankment be.
low the hedge, he was thankful, ano

Although the lovers had clandestine

dom and brief, and the two were

Daniels grief was intense, and he

A few months ago Daniel was taken

BLAIR, Neb., Aug 31.-One thousand
men and teams have been working
night and day for forty-eight hours to
prevent the Missouri river from chang
ing it's course and leaving this town
five miles west of the channel, and also
to prevent the river from rendering
the big Northwestern railroad bridge
from becoming useless by spanning dry
land instead of the river.


The Northwestern bridge train came
at once and placed 200 men at work
making riprap and dumping stone and
sandbags in the way of the stream.
Friday night 500 yards of dixie was
carried away and Saturday morning
the force was increased to 1000 men and
teams.


There are several old channels in the
valley here where the Missouri ran
fifty years ago, and the stream has
taken a sudden notion to go back into
one of these dry beds. If it succeeds
the loss will be very great and the
Northwestern will be forced to build
new bridge.

BERKELEY, June 30.-By resolu-
ton passed this afternoon by the state
normal school board, which is meeting
here with the state board of education,
all normal schools in the state are
placed practically on high school
basis.


The resolution raises the standard
of normal school work by providing
that none but graduates of high schools
shall enter.


The length of the course is placed
at two years.


The Chico and San Diego normal
schools have been admitting ninth
grade pupils and this must now stop.


Governor Pardee presided this morn
ing and the action taken settles a
question that has been pending five
years.


The state board of education also
met today and Governor Pardee sue
ceeded in smoothing out the tangle into
which the board got yesterday over the
question of who should take the initi-
ative in purchasing state textbooks.
He counseled harmony between the
textbook committee and the board as
a whole.

SACRAMENTO, June 30.-Whie the
special train conveying fifty convicts
from Folsom prison to this city, en-
route to San Quentin, was passing
Twelfth and r streets early this MORN
Ing the engine struck a railroad tor
pedo, which exploded, causing a panic
among the prisoners. Warden Yell and
two guards were in the coach with the
prisoners, while at either end Of the
coach was a fiat car, each with three
armed guards.


When the torpedo exploded the con-
victs jumped to their feet in terror, be-
lieving the guards outside were prepar-
ing to shoot into the car. The warden
and his guards soon restored order and
the transfer was accomplished without
further incident.


Fifty able bodied men were turned
over to the San Quentin guards. War
den Yell said no notable convicts were
among the number, he having kept all
the desperate characters. Every pre-
caution was taken to'make the transfer
safely and it was accomplished without
incident other than that noted.


At O'Clock this morning a special
train was sent from this city to Fol-
som and at $50 the men were put
aboard. The train pulled into the
prison yard a short distance from the
main building and the trip to this city
was begun.


Arriving here at $50 the convicts
were turned over to the San Quentin
guards, who put them aboard the
steamer Caroline, which will take them
direct to San Quentin prison.

A HEARTBROKEN mother is


~ wandering up and down tho
n streets of San Francisco. crying


aloud for the safe return of her
daughter, her beautiful, fair-haired
May, the comfort of her life.


She is Mrs. c. L. Ross, and her home
is a little tent pitched at Devisadero
anc Lombard streets.


She is half crazed with her worry
ingS. Her daughter has been gone for
fifteen days, she knows not where. In
the vagaries of her mind she has
ciutched fiercely upon the idea that her
daughter was the Mrs. Harry Stevens
who committed suicide at 36 Parkside
avenue last Tuesday afternoon. She
cries that her daughter has met with
foul play. and she prays now and then
that the murderers may be found and
the murder avenged.


For the past two days Mrs. Ross has
been wandering about the city. She
read of Mrs. Harry Stevens suicide in
the papers, and she hurried the next
day to the hospital to prove that this
woman was her daughter. The body
had been removed. The next day she
called at the Morgue but by that time
the body was buried. She asked to see
the clothes, but they too had been
taken away. She carried her daugh-
ter's picture around with her. and, true
enough, the surgeons and nurses who
hao attended Mrs. Stevens were aston
ished at the resemblance of the two
women. They were not one and the
same women, however, was proved
by a description of the teeth. Yet Mrs.
Ross refuses to believe the evidence,
and she thinks that doctors and all are
trying to cover up a murder


The daughter May is Mrs. May l.
Jordan. She is 25 years old. fair haired
and blue eyed. She was employed by
r. D. Davis & Co. before the fire. She
left her mothers tent on August 2 to
seek work in Oakland. Mrs. Ross
waved good-by to her that morning and
has not seen her since. Mrs. Jordan
wore gray checked skirt and a white
silk waist when she left for Oakland.

A brutal assault upon Mrs. Lillian
Thurber, young matron living at 754
Crocker street, was attempted early
yesterday morning by an unidentified
negro who succeeded in making his
escape, although several armed men
followed close upon his trail for several
hours.


The attempted crime was rot re-
ported to the police until Saturday
afternoon. Several detectives were at
once detailed on the case to secure
cews if possible that would lead to the
arrest of the miscreant. Mr.. Thurber
was away from home at the time on a
business trip. Mrs. J. B. Rainey, liv-
Ing with her husband and child, in the
same house, volunteered to sleep with
Mrs. Thurber Saturday night, and to
this circumstance the young woman
practically owes her life.


Seized Sleeping Woman


The negro made his entrance about
o'clock by breaking through a wire
screen in Mrs. Thurber's sleeping apart
ment, and approaching the bed seized
the sleeping woman. She awoke to find
the brute's hand upon her throat,
stiffling her screams, but struggling
with all her power she kept the negro
at bay until her companion awoke.


Mrs. Rainey started to scream but
the negro reached over and muffled her
cries with his arm.


The little Rainey child was sleeping
beside its mother and she too was
nearly smothered by the ruffian.


Finally Mrs. Rainey managed to make
her escape, and rushing into the other
room where her husband was asleep
aroused him and in one tragic word told
the whole story.


Negro Escapes Through Window


Without thought of any danger to
himself, Rainey ran into the adjoining
room, but the negro, alarmed by the
escape of one of his victims. disap-
peared through the open window and
fled into the darkness.


Neighbors were quickly aroused and
several armed men followed the route
supposed to have been taken by the
negro.


They failed to find any trace of him,
and to make sure that he had not
doubled on his tracks they returned to
the house and searched it carefully.

The Years Work Nearly Done.--The
trees are beginning to blush and turn pale, and
there is the crackle of dead leaves on the side
walks, says an exchange. Though the air is
gentle and the sunlight lies softly among the
tinted leaves, there is somberness in the heart
and feeling that is almost like sorrow.
Beautiful Nature has done her years work,
has finished her flowers and her fruits, her
corn and her wheat; has brooded her birds
and sent them southwark has set the last
butterfly afloat and added legions to the homes
of the rabbits and the chipmunks.


The trickling brooks sound cold, the zephyr
hesitates to come out, there is a real chill in
the sunlight, and the sunset looks like there
will be snow tomorrow. One meets his neigh
Dor who is sure to say, "Cold night, Ell, last
night" and his metallic voice trembles into a
shiver. You sit between the open window and
the blazing hearth. and as the afternoon moves
by you pull down the window and draw closer
to the fire and watch the flames laugh and
dance as your heart fills up with tender regrets.
The great shadow of sunless sky is driving
the summer to its home in the tropics. Watch
the dawn and each morning you will see the
sun has gone step further south. He is TAX
ing the daylight with him. The nights grow
longer. Winter and night are sisters. They
are both natures sweet restorers. As one
arises refreshed from q nights sleep, so the
earth will awaken from its winters slumber.
