Oakland, Cal, April ia late re-
port confirms the dispatch which Gen
eral Funston sent to the War Depart
that the flames had crossed Van Ness
avenue, the dividing line between the
better residence district and the rest
of the city, and that the town was
doomed. Everything worth mention
ing except this residence district was
burned over by fire or on fire by yester-
day afternoon. The flames finished
with the business district, ran south
through what remained of the tene-
ment district, extended out through the
Mission, region of cheap residences,
and leaped to Mob hill, where stand the
great mansions of the early-day Cali
fornia millionaires. Before that time
the water supply had been wholly eX-
hausted. Even the sewers were sucked
dry. AT o'clock the firemen brought
to the volunteer helpers the news that
there was no more dynamite. 1t passed
from mouth to mouth.


mo more dynamitei" This cry was
the doom of San Francisco.


AS a last resort General Funston
emptied the artillery magazines of the
Presidion, and the troops and firemen
tried to make a last stand at Van
Ness avenue, west of which lie the
homes of the rich and well-to-do. Fun
ston's telegram at o'clock last night
showed that they had failed, and the
late news over the direct Western
Union wire confirmed this.

Irun, Spain, May 25.-King Alfonso
greeted his bride, Princess Ena of Bat:
tenberg, as she entered Spain in the
early hours Of the morning amidst an
enthusiastic popular welcome and the
homage of the Spanish minister.


The special train bearing the princess
reached the frontier shortly after sun
rise. The morning mists still hung over
the river Bibassoa, separating France
from Spain, as the train reached the
center Of the bridge and the Spanish
fortresses belched a welcoming salute
Of twenty,one guns from the heights Of
Pena De Aya, commanding THE frontier.
A. the same time regiments of carbi-
neers and ancient Sicilian guards were
massed on the footway of the pier, and
with trumpets and banners saluted the
bride IS entrance into the kingdom,
while the bands alternately played the
British and Spanish national hymns.


In the meantime, King Alfonso, in
the uniform of a field marshal, and sur
rounded by the ministers Of the brown,
the court chamberlains and the military
and civil authorities, awaited the prin-
cess at the raill<ad station, which was
sumptuously decorated with floral
arch carpeted with red velvet and hung
with the royal banners and other in
sigma.


Scores Of noble ladies Of San Sebas-
tian, with their little daughters daintily
costumed in white, bore bouquets and
garlands for the princess. Premier
Moret directed the governor general to
admit the public to the platform and
to give the people every facility to see
their future queen.

NEW YORK, December 24.-There was
actually little nothing In the news over
Sunday or in the occurrences of the day
which would account sufficiently for the
practical Generalization in which the stock
market was plunged during the first hour
Of business today. During that time there
took place in the various quarters of the
market declines running from fractional
limits to more than five points, and these
losses were incurred on tremendous deal
ngs..


For ten minutes there was great pressure
upon the high-priced stocks, and this had
the effect of frightening small traders to
such degree that selling orders were ex-
ecuted with little regard to value. But
there was. that mysterious buying power
on the floor which so many times has pre-
vented the market from being stampeded
by frightened traders on the long side. ably
assisted by the noisy bears


After the first fifteen minutes the market
steadied somewhat and some prices were as
good or better than the opening. Through
out the course of the business session, how
ever. the trading was characterized by
great fevershness and l. was evident that
confidence in the market situation has be-
come seriously undermined.


The only adequate explanation of the
course of affairs i'll the market WAS that the
genuine liquidation which become clearly
defined last week was resumed this morn
ing and il met with no counterbalanctng
degree of supporting orders, In fact such
buying of stocks as was observed seemed
to represent almost exclusively the covering
of short contracts and tentative purchases
by tire trading element of the floor who
were disposed to buy stocks solely on the
theory that the extent of the decline during
the past fortnight warranted more or less
extensive rally.


Perhaps the most striking feature which
was presented for consideration with the
opening of business was the contagious
rate charged at the fortnghtly settlement
In American stocks upon the London stock
exchange. The figures quoted ranged from
Hog to liz per cent. more exacting terms
than have been fixed within the present
generation


Notwithstanding these distressing re-
quirements, however, American stocks were
not notably weak in the London market,
and the operations here for foreign account
showed a, small preponderance OF pur-
chases


In the rather turbulent proceedings Of the
early part of the day there was little cr1ti-
cism upon the special movements in indl-
vdual stocks. Later there was some dis
cusson of the. impending strike on the
Southern Pacific lines in Texas and some
little attention was attracted to the ad-
vices from Minnesota to the effect that the
state authorities were contemplating
very large increase in the valuation for tax
ing purposes of the ore lands of the great
Northern Railway Company, which were
recently leased to the United States Steel
Corporation. ..
Great Northern preferred scored one of
the largest maximum declines which were
recorded during the day, but that was not
of itself remarkable, III view OF the market
level of the stock.

NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 29.-The suit
filed by Mrs. Coralie Amelia Bernier in
the New Orleans district court today
asking the formal annulment of her
marriage develops the remarkable fact
that, although she twice married the
same man, she was yet unwedded. Miss
Bernier married in 1902, in st. Bern
ards parish, man calling himself
Logs M. Lemoine. Some years after
the marriage she discovered that this
was an assumed name and that Lee
moine was Louis M. Thompson.


Fearing that the marriage under a
false name might invalidate their mar
riage, she insisted on a second mar
riage under the true name, and this
was solemnized in Vaudeville less than
two months ago. The publication of
the marriage brought out the fact that
Thompson had one wife already in
Helena, Ark, and the twice married
woman now asks that she be freed
from him.

NEW YORK. September 17.-Many Of the
t23 passengers On the steamer Massalia,
which arrived today from Marseilles,
Naples and Palermo, spent their time in
prayer and weeping while the steamer la
bored in terrific gale at sea on September
H. During the twelve hours in which the
gale continued the steamers decks were
continuously swept by heavy seas, and the
passengers were kept below decks. Cattle
pens, chicken coops, boat covers and al
most everything movable on deck were
smashed or swept overboard; yentilators
were battered, and the head of the main
mast broken off. Although the steamer
was run full speed ahead she was unable
10 make steerage way, SO heavy was the
wind and sea.

noon was crowded to its capacity.

patronized than yesterday. Men, wom-

Ventured in the breakers could not re-
sist the alluring swish Of the water.

Not only were the beaches popular,
but hundreds of families secured teams
and journeyed far into the mountain
canyons, where they selected cool,
shady places and spread good, old
fashioned picnic dinners.


Mount Lowe swarmed with tourists
from early morning until late in the
evening. Many remained on it's sum-
init to view Los Angeles during night
time, with its hundreds Of shimmering
electric lights that resembled a huge
mantel studded with gems and spread
from the mountains to the sea.

Lake Placid. n. Y. June 2s.-Dr. j. D. Mer-
is to-day recovering from the nervous strain of
a night spent alone the summit of Mount
Whiteface- In company with Miss ]. L. Warner,
OF Boston, with whom she has been trampng
through the mountains, DR.. Merrill went out
early Wednesday morning climb Mount
Nhiteface. planning TO descend the other side
and reach the village of Wilmington. The two
women had previously climbed Mount Marcy,
and believed that they could make the ascent of
Whiteface without a guide.


Halfway up the mountain the trail divides into
two branches. and there the women parted,
agreeing TO meet at the top. Miss Warner. be-
coming frightened after going a considerable
distance. shouted to her friend. and. getting no
reply made her way the boat landing the
foot of the mountain. where she found by
Morton Caster. of the late Congressman
Caster. who has a camp Lake Placid. He
took her in his launch back 10 the village. and
searching party started after DIR. Merrill


All last night the searchers secured the forests
on the mountainside without results and it was
not until to-day that the woman was found near
the summit. where she had climbed and waited
all night for her friend. She was suffering from
the intense nervous strain she had been under
and her face was terribly swollen from the bites
of black flies


The searchers assisted her back to the Lake
Side Inn. where there was an affecting scene be-
tween the two women. who had believed each
other lost.

New York to Shanghai with 300 drums
of naphtha and $50 cases of oil on board,

overheard and the fire was eventually
put out. The Indrani continued her
voyage.

flowed across the deck and the other
drums caught fire almost Immediately.

throwing the burning drums overheard,
clambered into lighters.

drani heaved the flaming drums into
the sea and managed to save the ship,
whose iron deck prevented a general
confagration.


Floating drums Of naphtha blazing
furiously drifted with the tide into
Singapore harbor and crossed the
man-of-war anchorage Shipping and
wfarves were damaged until the sea
tide carried the flaming drums to the
southwark, where they gradually
burnd out


This is the second fire that has oc-
Cured on the Indrani since she left
New York April 10 for Chinese ports.
A dispatch dated June 7 said that the
Indrani had been saved from destruc-
tion by fire by the throwing overheard
of $50 drums of naphtha.

deaths to the extent of $10O0 through

week.

| poison. and further investigation

CHICAGO, Oct. 1.-THE baseball sea-
son of both major leagues for 1906
ended today with games at Chicago,
st. Louis and Cincinnati.


For the first time since the two big
leagues were organized both cham
pionships have come to one city. The
Chicago National league team won first
honors In that organization easily.


Taking the lead early In June and
holding it to the end it established
new major league record for the num-
Der of games won. OF the one hundred
and fifty-three games played by the
team one hundred and fifteen were
victories, the previous best record in
this respect having been held by the
New York club in the same league.


In the American league the Chicago
team upset all calculations by winning
the pennant. The contest was not de-
cided until last week, the New York
team being within striking distance of
the leaders until October 8, when a
x-inning defeat at Philadelphia put
them out of the running.


| An equally hard struggle for the sec
ond place was not decided until two
days later, when Chicago defeated
OleNeldHu ana tOOk away lne ONO
clubs last chance to overhaul New
York.


The, fourth and fifth teams, Phila-
delphia and st. Louis, were within
hailing distance throughout the sea-
son; Philadelphia, in fact, leading the
league on three separate occasions, the
last time no later than August s.
Washington and Boston were tall
enders throughout.


In the National league, outside of
Chicago's work, the chief feature of
the season was the hard struggle for
the second place between New York
and Pittsburg. This lasted until the
first week in September, when the lat
ter team fell back.


The other five clubs In the league
occupied the same relative positions
most of the season, although Brooklyn
and Cincinnati finished with but one
game between them for fifth and sixth
places, respectively. st. Louis was
never a contender and the Boston
clubs record of one hundred and two
defeats was only exceeded by that of
the same club in the American league.


Tuesday the worlds, championship
series will begin here between the two
Chicago clubs.

SACRAMENTO, April To-day
brought revived hopes among all the
river residents who had passed a sleep
less night in dread of a recurrence of
the disastrous Edwards break of two
years ago.


Yesterday the swollen Sacramento
river was lashed into a surging sea by
a fierce north wind, which sent waves
breaking against the insecure levees
at various points down the river and
in some instances melted away their
front for distance of hundreds of feet
Today however, the north wind ceased
entirely and the river fell almost q
foot, thus relieving the high tension of
the past twenty-four hours.


The only points along the Sacramento
river where danger appeared were in
the vicinity of Freeport, where the
water either ran over the low parts of
the levees or percolated through
gopher holes which had escaped the
vigilance of the patrolmen.


Two large dredgers, one the property
of the Grand Island reclamation dis
trict. the other owned by the Sacra-
mentp Southern railway performed
splendid service throwing up new levees
at threatened points, and such was the
improvement in the situation at 1
o'clock today that it appeared the
crisis had been safely passed and that
the rich land along the river south of
this city will be saved from the slight
est danger.

The underground telegraph system con-

Scotland is now nearing completion. the
actual length of this line is 400.5 miles,
which may be shorter than some continent
tai underground telegraph lines, but the
total mileage of wire exceeds that of any
similar line Over 81, 700 miles of wire have
been laid down The route followed by the
cable is from London to Birmingham, then
through Stafford Warrington, Preston,
Kendel Carlisle. Beattock and Glasgow. The
pipe line consists of cast-iron pipes, each
nine feet long, not including the socket,
and having a nominal internal diameter OF
three inches. Great care was taken In Sc
lecting these pipes to see that no pipe was
less than three inches in diameter. The
average diameter is three and one-eighth
inches The line is divided into sections
about $50 yards long between Birmingham
and Carlisle and 220 yards between Carlisle
and Glasgow. The pipe is laid on an aver
age not more than fourteen inches below the
surface of a footway and not more than
two feet below the surface of roadway.
At intervals of five miles the cable conduc-
tors are led into connection boxes fitted In
pillar test boxes These boxes provide
facilities for making all ordinary electrical
tests, also for air-drying the cable In case
the Insulation becomes defective.


The cable line from London to Birming-
ham is III miles long and contains seventy
six conductors, each weighing 100 pounds
ner mile

The bark Andrew Welch, which ar
rived late yesterday afternoon from
Honolulu, brought the news of the loss
of the little American ship Great Ad-
miral She also brought fourteen men
and one woman. wife of the mate,
who had been rescued by a British
ship after clinging to the sea-washed
cook and steward of the Great Admiral
died of exposure. The Andrew welch
arrived too late to pass quarantine.


The Great Admiral, which was owned
by her master. Captain Sterling. was
bound from Mukflteo for San Pedro
with a cargo of lumber. She was
laden to her full capacity, and. as is
the custom with lumber carriers, the
center of gravity was raised to the
peril point by the high piled deck
load.


The Great Admiral left Mukilteo De-
cember 1, and all went well until De-
cember 6, when a heavy southeasterly
gale was encountered. The storm
broke suddenly. and. battered by wind
and wave, the topheavy ship keeled
and stayed there. In the hope that
she would right herself, Captain Ster-
ling ordered the masts cut away. This
was done, but too late. The cargo had
shifted to the starboard side, and
what had been a navigable ship was
nothing but helpless log at the mercy
of the troubled waters in which the
derelict laboriousIy rolled and creaked.
Seas swept the wreck and carried away
part of the house. Everybody man
aged to hang on, however. and for
three days, exposed to the pitiless wind
and pouring rain. they waited for help.


Before assistance came two members
of the crew, the cook and the steward,
succumbed to the exposure. Their
bodies were consigned to the deep.


The lookout on the British ship
Barcore, which left Puget Sound De-
cember 8 for Adelaide, sighted the
derelict and on December the four
teen exhausted men and the one brave
and wornout woman were taken off
the wreck and carried on board the
Barcore. There they were cared for
tenderly and stayed on the Barcore
until December "a. when the bark An
drew Welch, from Honolulu for San
Francisco, was sighted. Signals were
exchanged, both vessels hove to and
the shipwrecked company was trans
ferred to the Welch. which brought
the derelicts home in time to begin the
new year on that terra f1rma they had
neverA expected to see again

The Navy Department has decided to con-
centrate all the battleships in the navy on
the home stations, and to replace those on
the Asiatic station with armored cruisers.

ships Ohio and Wisconsin, which have been
In Chinese waters for several months past,
have left for the United States. The Ohio
sailed from Chefoo yesterday for Hamp-
ton Roads. She will stop at Cavite and
then sail across the Indian ocean through
the Suez canal and the Mediterranean sea.
Her place as flagship of the Asiatic station
has been taken by the auxiliary cruiser
Rainbow. When the Ohio has been over
hauled and repaired she will be added to
the battleship division of the Atlantic fleet.


The battleship Wisconsin is returning to
the United States by the Pacific route, and
will be added to the Pacific fleet for serv-
Ice on the western coast. She arrived at
Kobe, Japan, yesterday, and from there
will sail for Honolulu. She is bound for the
naval station in Puget sound for repairs
and cleaning.


The armored cruisers West Virginia, Col
orado Pennsylvania and Maryland will take
the places of the Ohio and the Wisconsin
on the Asiatic station They will sail from
New York in a few days. and will follow
the SueZ route.

westbound Los Angeles limited on the

eastbound was derailed near Evanston,
Wyo, and the engine turned over, but
no one was badly hurt in that accident.

double track and the line became
blocked for other trains.

Charles E. Barber, Los Angeles;
strain and bruise of back.


Mrs. K. L. Dodge, Long Beach, Cal.
bruised under left eye.


Isabelle Crosher, Los Angeles; neck
injured

shaken up and bruised but none of them
was seriously injured. Hans Bangs
the engineer, stuck to his post and was
not badly injured, although the loco
motive rolled thirty feet down an elm
bankment.


The accident, it is believed, was
caused by spreading of the rails.

SAN BERNA Jan. 15.-Clear-
ing up of the wreck of the Los Angeles
limited at Highland Junction is prog
ressing fast. The wrecking crew of the
Salt Lake arrived at noon. The line
is open for traffic. a shoony having
been built during the night, so that all
overland trains on both the Salt Lake
and Santa Fe got through this MORN
ing at $50.


The cars that went into the ditch
were the baggage car, the diner and
tourist car. The first Pullman ploughed
its way down deep in the earth, but
remained upright. Two other cars were
deraied, but remained near the track
and were soon gotten away from the
wreck. The wrecked cars are not bad
ly smashed up, though the trucks were
all torn loose.


The cause of the wreck was without
doubt the giving of the rails. In the
curve of the track, just as ii leaves the
junction, is a small Culvert on which
some work has been done the past
few days. AS the rain had consider
ably softened the track this culvert is
believed to have yielded as the heavy
engines passed over 1t, causing a rail
to spread. The tender to the engine
left the track while the mail car went
over all right. The baggage car
Jumped and headed for the ditch and
the three following cars followed it.
The two engines and mail car broke
away from the balance of the train
and ran several lengths, the derailed
tender tearing up the track all the
way. The track was torn for several
car lengths.


Not one of the half dozen employees
received anything worse than
scratch, nor did the passengers suffer.

The case of Nellie M. Schader against
the Los Angeles-Pacific Railway COM
pany was decided adversely to the
plaintiff in department eight Of the
superior court yesterday.


An interesting question was in point
the right of the defendant company to
charge a ten cent fare in the city limits
of Santa Monica. After the street rail-
chise agreeing to carry passengers
within the city limits for a five cent
fare, the city extended its limits and
the plaintiff, demanding that she be
carried from one point to another Of
the new city limits, rendered ten cents
for fare for herself and son.


The servant of the street railway
company refused to accept the amount
and elected plaintiff and her son from
the car, for which she sued, alleging
$4,000 damages.


The jury found that the railway com
pany was justified in charging a double
fare for any ride that involved greater
distance than that comprised within the
city limits established at the time the
franchise was granted.


The following instructions given by
judge Wilbur practically settled the
case.


THE court instructs the jury that
the changing of the boundary lines of
the city of Santa Monica subsequently
to the granting of the franchise offered
in evidence. did not have the effect to
take away the right of the defendant
to charge ten cents per passenger from
the place where the plaintiff, Nellie M.
Schader and her son boarded the car
to any point within the city limits"

of the Central High School where not only

friends, were feasted and entertained.


The two thousand or more hungry lunch

rarely equaled and which gave assurance

assistants, secured by volunteer contribu-
tons all the materials necessary, SO that
the proceeds are a clear gain.

! rarked by the emblematic colors worn, red





for the seniors, yellow for the juniors, pink
for the tender sophomores and invidious

butterflies; dolls, SNOWFALL and other badges

host Of pretty mattresses, and filled up to
the signing point with the best to be OBJ

sioners, members of the board of education,

booths and gayety of mattresses dlsap-
peared, but the managing committee, with
well-fllled boxes of coin in their hands.
hurried with satisfied faces, to a general
reckoning The luncheon had been sue
cess.

HUNTINGTON, Ind, May 22.-While
Henry Beauchamp, the regular Wabash
operator at Andrews, was temporarily
absent from the Office today Everett Kel-
lam took possession of the train dis
patcher's wire and began to give orders
to the various conductors along the line
regarding the running of trains. Kel-
lam was recently employed in the local
shops of the Erie road and was over
come by the heat and went insane. He
had been a telegraph operator, but
knew nothing about the Wabash system,
and when the operators received his or
ders the greatest confusion resulted.


Orders to hold a certain train were
followed by another to "Send her along
like hell" and in one or two instances
he stumbled on the right number of the
train and this made the mystery deeper.
The operator nearest Andrews finally
threw the wire open and after ground
ing ii got into communication with
train dispatchers along the line and it
was concluded the safest policy to hold
UP all trains till the trouble could be
investigated


When Beauchamp returned and saw
Kellam at his key he summoned assist
ance and the insane man was bound
after a struggle and sent to Jail. The
trouble was explained and the trains
were moved from the stations in which
they were being held.

Special Dispatch TO The Star.


LOS ANGELES, Cal, April I.-The fol-
lowing special is from Arthur Welshans,
the dramatic critic who was in the midst
of the disaster at San Francisco: 1.-The
flames have been conquered and the pail
of disaster is now lifting from the ruins
of the city. leaving bare to the gaze of
the world a specter of desolation such as
the people of the United States have never
before witnessed. The flames were checked
north of Telegraph Hill, the western boun-
dary being along Franklin street and Cali
fornia street southeast to Market street
The fremen checked the advance of flames
by dynamitfng the DR.. Milford and the
Notaling residences and then 2. firing. Many
times before had the firemen made such
an effort, but always previously had they
met defeat. But success at this hour means
little for San Francisco 1t stands for but
the conquering of flames after the battle
had been lost. Long ere the final struggle
came San Francisco had been lost its
greatness had been lowered, it's future ter
ribly blighted


The aInes are still burning ftfully about
the city, but the spread of fire has been
stopped. IT is the end of losses. but for
many days there will be smoke to carry its
message aloft into the skies. and for months
will be the ruins to bring their reminder of
holocaust


Oakland has become the nearest and the
logical place for refuge for the homeless
thousands who are leaving the doomed city
across the bay by every boat. Last night
5000 homeless ones found shelter and com
fort in churches. halls and private resi-
dences of the city.


The horrors of the scenes and the terri
BILE suffering occasioned by the lack of
water can perhaps be imagined by this
statement when small stream of dirty
water spurted up through the cobblestones
and formed q muddy pool at the corner of
Powell and Market streets, hundreds of men
and women, rich and poor, old and young,
knelt and drank to quench their terrible
thirst

OAKLAND, Aug. 14.--Ferris Hart
man, the comedian prevented panic
tonight at the Idora Park Theater when
he coolly and cleverly dismissed the
audience in the midst of the opera
"Girofle-Girofa" while fire was threat
ening the destruction of the playhouse.
Flames suddenly burst out in the rear
Of the stage shortly after 10 o'clock,
the woodwork having caught fire from
sparks from an electric lighting ma
chine used for stage effects. Stage
hands and members of the company
rushed TO fight the fire with the ap-
paratus in the theater.


Before the audience was fairly
aroused to the danger, Hartman, who
is the stage manager, quietly stepped
down to the footlights and without
alarm requested the audience to dis
perse His words of caution were so
moderate and undemonstrative that the
auditors filed out, quickly, but without
disorder. into the park. The fire was
extinguished without serious damage,
but the performance was not completed.

sweat shop district, and the tenements are
filled with employees in these places. When
they were aroused by the clang Of the

rying what few valuables they possessed.
Even when the fire was under control they
refused to return to their homes. and re-
manned shivering in the cold until the last
spark had been eXtinguished.


When the fire was discovered it had
spread through the entire lower part of
the factory building, and two watchmen
whose escape had been cut off by the
flames, were standing at upper window
wildly crying for help Gradually, as the
fire gained Roadway, the men were driven
upward until at last they We're forced to
seek refuge on the roof.


Ladder to the Rescue.


There they found temporary safety but
in few minutes the flames began to break
through the roof and close in around the
two men. The firemen We're helpless. Their
longest ladder would reach scarcely two
thirds the height of the burning building,
and the fire escapes were wrapped for half
their length in flames.


At almost the last moment, when the
blazing encircle had narrowed down until
the clothing of the helpless men had begun
to smoke from the intense heat, a great
new fire truck, with ladder which never
before had been called into service, dashed
through the frightened crowd in the street
Quickly the ladder was raised and almost
before its topmost round had touched the
coping q fireman appeared besiue the two
men. In another moment he had handed
them one after another to comrades who
had followed him and they were carried
to the ground.

ST. PETERSBURG, September 2O.-The
official report just issued gives but little
ground for expectation that the famine,
which has already a grip on many provinces
in Russia, will be less this winter. AL
though the winter wheat harvest was gen.
orally above the average, spring wheat
proved a disappointment. The rye and oat
crops also were unsatisfactory, especially
the latter. The Volga region. the most
fertile in Russia. was below the average in





the Battles made the best showing, all the
harvest being average.


The winter wheat harvest was generally
above the average and only poor in the
Volga region and less than average in the
eastern portion of the central agricultural
belt. Rye was less satisfactory and only
above the average In Poland and the six
southwestern provinces. Spring wheat was
below the average throughout Russia. In
the Volga region the harvest was bad and
in Ufa, Tambon and Ryazan, among the
largest provinces of the empire, unsatis-
factory. Oats also made a bad showing
and only nine OF the ten Polish provinces
came up to the average. Barley was some
what better. being good in all the Polish
provinces and fairly good in the Battles,
the southwestern provinces. portion of

noon. The bullet struck the fisherman

itself in his left lung, after passing
through the neck and seyering the Jug

Bay.

where recruits for the Marine corps are
given lessons in gunnery. 1t is believed
that a stray bullet went over the earth
mound and struck the unfortunate fish
erman. The spot is a particularly dan
gerous one for any one sailing in the
bay and several narrow escapes have
been reported recently.

leaves a wife and son. He has re-
sided in Vallejo for twenty years and
was highly esteemed among his coun-
trymen. His son conducts a large res
taurant here.

water tight. The supply Of available
field stoves has been exhausted. Others

colonists who arrived early in the fall

taking advantage of cheap round trip
excursion. The third class is known as
the wealthy class or the after-holiday
tourists. In February cheap eXcur-

the roads from the east to the west and
the people who come then make up
the fourth class

By Associated Press.


PASO REAL. Cuba, Sept. 9.-The gov
ernment troop train which left Havana
Friday jumped the track three miles
east of Consolation Del Sur.


The train was surrounded by several
hundred insurgents commanded by
Pine Guerra in person and sustained a
fire all Saturday night and until 9
o'clock this morning. The train would
have been captured but for the timely
arrival of Col. Avalos and 400 men,
who had fought their way through from
Consolation del Sur


When this force arrived the revolu-
tionists returned westward after having
destroyed the bridge over the Santa
Clara river and some culverts and
cutting wires near Herradura.


The revolutionists are camped to-
night at Arroyo Cruz, west of Con-
solacion del Sur.


Guerra's forces at Consolation del Sur
in that neighborhood number 1000 men
and those of the government 800.


The government forces suffered one
man killed and six wounded, including
Ravenna, who was slightly injured.


Previous to the lighting yesterday
Pine Guerra sent a note to Col Dlaz,
commanding the troops train. demand
ing his surrender. Diaz replied that he
would die first.


The engagement between Col. Avalos
and the insurgents near Colsolacion del
Sur lasted nearly an hour.


The troops will proceed westward to-
morrow.


Reports received by the government
at Havana say that 200 insurgents were
killed in the encounter near Conso-
lscion del Sur, but these figures are not
considered authentic.


A fight is reported to have taken
place at Guanajay, in Santa Clara
province. There were fierce machette
charges and the rebels retired. Several
Of them were wounded and five Were
captured.


News of the suspension Of hostilities
reached here this afternoon.

The two hundred and fifty young women

sylvania railroad from New York. The
party was in charge of President and Mrs.
Eshmann and Miss n. A. Moseley, the lat

several trains leaving at the hour when
the Radnor special pulled into the 9th street

confusion: but as soon the Radnor Col

A reporter of The Star. from his vantage

not less than the announced go passed the
station portals.


The entire party travels upon one rail-

the second largest ever sold out of Nash
vile, Tenn.


After leaving the station the party board

main in the city about twenty days.


Object Of the Trip.


1t is stated that the faculty of Radnor
recognizes Washington as the educational
center of the nation. and the trip is made
as means of acquiring knowledge. 1t is
declared that other colleges might profit
ably follow the example of this institution
in bringing students here for study and
recreation.


This small army Of attractive young wom-
en- will doubtless receive a hearty welcome
In this city. In return, 1t is said to be
within their power to do much toward the
building up Of Greater Washington, as
they can use their efforts to persuade rep
resentatives in Congress from their section
to deal more literally with the commercial
interests of Washington They can encour
age better commercial relations between
the business men of the capital and those
of their home sections, and it is said to be
the hope of the Radnor College faculty
that each of the young ladies when she
goes to her home will consider herself
personal representative of Greater Wash

text:
Over the long journey from the hin
terland, far away, where the snow flies
and the horse flies mingle in blizzardy
chill; from beyond the mountain ranges
that hedge about the icebound climes,
they came. Footsore and weary, their
turbans dropping and their tongues
hanging out, they clambered down the
steep slopes and made their weary way
across the trackless deserts. The burn
ing sands paTched their throats and the
dust choked them. Their feet were
scorched and their legs were sore with
much walking.


With them came their faithful camels,
humping themselves slowly and fear
somely. (They say a camel can go
eight days on one drlnk-but who the
h wants to be a camel?) The noble
beasts carried their heads afar front,
and their necks stretched, rubbering
all the journey through, and shifting
for the perfume of the flowers and the
scent of the salty sea.


And SO, over the scorching sands, the
caravan came, and into the Angelic
city oasis blew great bunch of good
fellows, each adorned with fez and full
evening clothes.


And here, in this oasis. meath the
shade of the sheltering palm, where the
ever-summer sea kisses the strands
gilded by the setting sun, where the
flowers never cease to bloom and the
air is heavy with the perfume of the
orange, the acacia, the magnolia and
the rose, they found rest for their
weary souls.


And Now Comes Cancels Milk


And, too, here their thirsty threats
were washed with cames milk and the
zem-zem wells were found to be ever
flowing and never dry, and The gushers
gushed and the sweet waters were wet
and the band played "a Hot Time"
and all went merry as a wedding bell
and then some.


1t was the annual initiation of AL
Malaikah temple, and they did it just
right. A class of $50 odd were sent the
route over the sand dunes and across
the valley of death. They were taught
to ride the camels-and the goat-to
take the awesome oath and to cock
the fez over the left optic; to give the
grip and the pass word. In the Spring
street armory an oasis was established
and there the work was done. 1t was
hard work and lively, and the initiates
will never regret that they went the
pace-though today they dive off the
mantelpiece and walk with that uncer-
tain tread which denotes great pertur-
baton.


But even the initiates were not so
incommoded that they could not take
their first trip beneath the fez to the
great feast meath the palm at the oasis
established under the rooftree of one
AL Levy, there to Al-LeVy-ate their
hunger-and thirst. And there, they
again quaffed the zem-zem and the
camePS milk and ate the dates and
figs, but now as full-hedged Shriners,
along with the host of their brethren
of the scimitar and the star.


The Great Feast


Oh, what a feast it was. And what
precursor of those greater doings when
the ShrinerS come in May!


All told, there were 1900 of them reg
istered-and all were there. Up on the
top floor, Levy threw several great
rooms together and thus made places
for the herd. Every place was taken
and the overflow stood outside and
hungered. For the brass band had led
a mighty host and the promise it gave
Of "a Hot Time" was more than veri-
fed. Marching up the steps it sounded
like the charge of mighty army and
seated about the table it looked as If
all Los Angeles had sent it's men folk
to dine at the same time.


1t was a sans ceremonie" throng. The
band played SHOW me how to get
home" and was hooted; it footed "Hot
Time" many times and everyone sang.
Then they applauded and then they
howled. Mott Flint walked about and
grinned like Cheshire cat and showed
the overflow downstairs to other rooms.
The army of walters could scarcely
navigate, but mighty cheers greeted
their every appearance. 1t was Levys
supreme test as a caterer = and he
met it.


OF course an utter lack of formality
prevailed al the function Everyone
knew everyone else and If he didn't
is was his ownsfault Everyone had
good time. save the pair of candidates
in chains. who looked on, but ate not
because that was not allowed to them.
And 1t was awful!

By Associated Press.


PORTLAND, Ore, April 1.-THE Hill
and Hartman construction gangs at
Carson, WASH, on the north bank of
the Columbia river, collided at noon
yesterday, when dynamite was freely
used to drive the Columbia Valley
Railroad companys graders off the
land belonging to the Hartman road.
One laborer was hit by flying rock,
but only slightly injured. A lighted
stick of dynamite was also thrown
among the Columbia Valley graders,
but the men took to their heels and
escaped injury. Finally a deputy
sheriff was summoned and warned the
Hill construction gang to desist from
further demonstrations.


The situation was serious last night
and further clashes are feared.


Deliberate Injury Charged


Members of the Columbia Valley
crew state that the blasts of dynamite
were deliberately laid with the inten-
tion of injuring their men, and were
not fired for the purpose of frightening
them merely. This, they say, is shown
by the fact that two mines of dyna-
mite were laid during the noon hour
upon the spot where the Columbia VAL
ley constructors were at work. When
they returned after dinner to resume
operations, the fuse to fire the blast
was quietly lighted without warning to
the Columbia Valley workers, who were
almost upon the spot before they
learned a blast was about to be fired.
The latter say these blasts were not
set upon the grade being established
by the Portland & Seattle railroad con-
tractors but upon the very spot where
the Columbia Valley crews would re-
sumo operations.


Warned by officer
The opposing factions then gathered
about the scene of the explosion and
long wrangle ensued over the rights
to the property. The Columbia VAL
lev men claimed ownership of the strip,
for which $500 had been paid. The
Portland & Seattle graders demanded
to see their papers. The Columbia Val
ley men resumed operations, but were
again scattered by a stick of dynamite
thrown in the crowd.


The dynamite throwing occurred
while the Columbia, Valley foreman
was turning in call for the sheriff
at Stevenson. Deputy Sheriff ]. w.
Imam soon reached the scene. and after
long parley warned the Portland &

While party Of three girls and two boys
were returning from Brightwood to Camp
Good VIII. along the Military road, shortly
after o'clock Friday evening, they were
attacked BY a bury colored man. He at
tempted to throw down one Of the girls,
but failed. succeeding. however, In dashins
another OF the party to the ground. The
latter was afterward carried in an uncon-
scious condition into the camp. The assail-
ant escaped, but the police are on his trail


camp Good WIN was greatly excited fol-
lowing the affair. and all day yesterday the
assault was the CHIEF topic of conversation.
The matter came to the attention of the
police yesterday afternoon, and Precinct
Detective Estes went at once to Camp Good
WIZ to learn the details OF the affair A
description OF the man was obtained and
has been sent throughout the city.


IN the party mentioned were Margaret
Waring, eighteen years old, an assistant In
the camp: Kate Meiklejohn. fourteen years
Old; Alice Meikiejohn thirteen years old;
Theodore Brice, thirteen years old, and AL
bert Crestile. twelve years old. They start
ed out about o'clock from the camp to 70
to Brightwood, distance of about three
quarters of a mile. 1t was early In the
evening and it was believed they could get
back before dark The walk to the village
was accomplished without incident, and





cream by Miss Warning.


little later the party started back along
Military road. Darkness was coming on
rapidly and haste was necessary.


Pursued by Colored Man.


All went well until they were approach
ing the bridge on Military road. which is
about 300 yards away from the camp There
they became aware that a colored man, ap-
parently drunk, was following them. The
children were frightened, but the older girl
cautioned them not to run away. as that
would show that they were afraid of the
pursuer. She thus tried to keep up their
courage.


They had not gone far when Miss Waring.
In glancing around. saw the colored man
start to run after them, the signs of drunk
enness disappearing. Miss Warning stood
her ground. hoping by show of courage to
prevent trouble, but the colored man at
tackled her. The girl struggled with the
powerful assailant and finally wrenched
herself free, with the help of Kate Meikie-
john, the older of the other two girls.


The colored assailant then turned upon
the smaller girl and grasped her about the
neck choking her. His grip was like iron,
but the little girl fought with all her frail
strength. The ruff1an threw her down on
the side OF the road with some violence.
The girl continued her struggle, and Miss
Warning bravely went to her aid 49, ,ai


Meanwhile the two small boys and the
smallest girl. Alice MeikIejohn, ran scream
ing toward the camp. The colored man evil
IDENTIFY became frightened at]the cutlery and
partially released his hold upon the child.
who jumped up, and started for the camp.
With her was. Miss. Maring.


Just as they neared the camp at the
top of the hill Kate Meiklejohn tainted from
fright and from the effects of the ordeal
which she had just been through. Miss
Waring and Alice Meiklejohn went at once
to her assistance. carrying her quickly into
the camp, where she was revived. She
was yesterday still suffering from the
shock --i.s-


Intellectual Search Made.


The cries Of the children and the bring
ing Of the unconscious girl into camp
caused a searching party to be sent out. but
no trace Of the assailant could be found
yesterday, and, as stated the affair was re.
ported to the police.


A peculiar incident following the occur
renee narrated occurred yesterday, when q
colored man went to the camp to do some
work for one Of the persons staying there
He resembled the assailant of the girls, II
was said, and when the children saw him
they became doubly frightened. and one
Of the little girls, Alice Meiklejohn, became
Ill as the result.


When Precinct Detective Estes of the
tenth precinct visited the camp yesterday
afternoon Kate Meiklejohn showed him sew
eral scratches and marks on her face and
neck, which, she stated, were inflicted by
the assailant. In giving description of the
colored ruffian the girls said he was ap-
parently about twenty-five or thirty years
old, feet 10 inches In height and weighed
about ITO pounds. He wore black trou.
sers, an old dirty shirt or jumper. and was
without hat They thought when they
first saw him that he was drunk, but they
say they did not notice the odor of liquor
when they were struggling with him. They
are not sure they could identify him.
Miss Waring has been at the camp the
greater part Of the summer, but the two
Meiklejohn girls have been there but 9
short time. They were sent out from theil
home in the city few days ago to enjoy
the fresh air and sunshine. But their pleas
ure from their stay in the country has beer
greatly marred by the unpleasant expe
rience Of last evening.


AS soon as the incident became known a.
police headquarters Lieut.. Peck dispatched

CHICAGO April 30.-Chicago's city hall
has settled to such an extent since the COM
pletion of the excavation for the adjoining
new county building that it was found nee
essary yesterday to rope in the entrances
to prevent pedestrians from being killed
by the falling sections of coping and cor
nces. At the south end of the building on
Washington street the foundations have
sunk several inches while the entire build
ing has assumed a list in the direction of
the hole which the building will cover.


The city hall and the county building
were Of the same massive construction, and
as IL was necessary to use giant powder to
wreck parts of the latter, there had been
no apprehension of the city's administra-
tive building coilapsing However, though
its foundation walls are many feet thick,
they do not rest on the rock which under
lies the city, but merely on the clay subsoil.


Yesterday omnious shivers ran through
the building. and with many snaps and
groans. cracks appeared in the board floors.
and desks assumed angles, the floor thing
tilted and dirt emerged from crevices
where It had lain undsturbed for years
Skylights doubled up and plaster fell from

brother and Queen Christina, the sill

service was begun. The ceremony was
performed with all the impressiveness

nitaries of the church. with scores OF

ly married couple and the chanting OF

Rover saved two children, William
Limeberry, who lives near Colombia,
across the Delaware river from here,

a decent burial and place tombstone
over the grave.


Rover is big shepherd dog that has
always been the companion and play

two years ago Daisy, then aged years,

drowned but for Rover barking and
whining till he had attracted Mr.. Lime

search was resumed, and when the
party came to the edge of the woods

to them. barking and whining.

The summer green has faded from the hills.


All dead and sere the stubbe fields stretch
wide,
The springtime music of the meadow rflls

The woodland foliage has thinner grown.
The red leaves twirl upon the maple stem,

Seek natures spacious LAP prepared for them

high,


Prepare to leave their summer home behind.
At dawn the husker strews the whitened shock


And piles his basket high with golden corn;
The scattered quail returning to the flock,


Take up their 'customed cleaning at the morn.
Now from the orchard sounds the pieker's song
And rears his slender ladder where on high
All red and gold, the scanty leaves among


Peer out the ''bush,'' the baldwin and the
"spy.''


And here's the entansled vineyard, autumn


Laden with fruit whose clusters seem to stand
As If Dame Nature meant that they alone
Should witness to the fulness of the land.
And this is autumn-aye. her sign is here;
Inc biood-red sumach standing on the hill,
The leadess alder swaying here and there
Told US in years agOne. and tell US still.
The gray squirrel scampers from his forest tree
To search the thousand golden leaves below,
The saucy jay in his untrammeled glee
Screams long and loud upon the topmost bough.
All this by day, and the round moon by night,
And silence, save perchanee some iperched
bird

Skips down the .leaf-strewn path, tho scarcely

IT'S now the coon peers from his dim abode

Now long the woodland brook in search of food

sky.


IT'S now the owl from some high pinnacle


Looks down into the woodlands deeper shade,
Or, muffed in the shadow of some dell,


His solemn moan re-echoes vale and glade.
Aye, this is autumn; this and more,


A joy that fills the heart-tho summer dies,
Her spirit still abides to hover DER

Japan has covenanted at our earnest re-
quest that she will not substitute certain
industries, for instance. tea export. Some
years ago she set apart an annual appro-
priation for the Japanese Japanese Tea
Guild. Subsidy Not at ALL said the jap
anese government, nothing In the way of
subsidy. 1t was merely to advertise Jap
anese teas, advertisement having been
made necessary by the serious and grow
ing competition of Ceylon and Assam teas.
1t is reported that about per cent of the
money was actually used for advertising
The rest went to pay the expenses of
branch tea houses opened in New York,
Boston Montreal Chicago and elsewhere
Why were these branch houses desired?
Because for years foreign firms, chiefly
American, had possessed the tea-exporting
trade of Japan, and the government was
determined to secure that trade for Jap
anese interests Foreign governments pro-
tested at Toxic. They wasted their time.
With that faultless politeness that is
one of the charming traits of the Japanese,
the government officials gave assurance of
their most distinguished consideration-and
renewed the appropriation. 1t lapsed while
the war was on, because Japan had need
elsewhere for all her funds; but now the
government has in hand an act that will


finish the work begun by the appropriation
and effectively put the foreign tea houses
out of business.

Suddenly Joe Elton-who was a little in
advance of the other two and doing his
best to guide them straight-stopped short
with cry of horror.


The grass above them was on fire, too!


Under the shadow of the rolling smoke,
the imperiled trio looked at each other IN
silent dismay. But before any one could
speak, Bob Barlow stumbled, dislodglng
an enormous stone, which went bounding
down the slope and vanished into the flame
tinged cloud below.


"Hurrah!" cried Joe. There's a chance
stones around. Roll 'em down on to the
fire, and mind you roll them all dead straight
in the same line"


Down went a second rock as he spoke,
crushing the still unkindled grass flat to the
earth, and tearing its way through the burn
light soil. Another and another followed,
each widening little more the narrow gap
in the blazing circle that hemmed them in.


Now, boys" shouted Joe. as the fire
neared them; ''let's make break through
that gap. Come aong!"


All that followed was like an ugly dream.
They were dimly conscious of punging
through tapping flames and flying sparks,
their pulses throbbing, their eyes aching,
rushing, roaring sound in their ears, and the
whole earth and sky seeming red-hot all
around them.


Then suddenly the fiery sea vanished, and
they were standing, spent and gasping, with
scorched feet and blistered faces, upon the
site slope came echoing the hearty cheer of
their friends from the hotel, who, alarmed
at the sight of the fire, had sailed forth in
search of them

Cape Henry, Va, Feb. 2S-In the face Of what
seemed like certain destruction. Captain Mere
dith Partridge OF the Norfolk towboat Jack
Twohy and his crew to-day effected a daring
rescue Of the crew Of the New-Hayen four
nasted schooner George N. Grant, which went
ashore here. Life savers from the Cape Henry
and Virginia Beach stations had repeatedly tried
to shoot line over the stranded schooner, but
without success on account of her distance from
shore. and had given up hope OF saving those on
board the battered vessel. because the sixty-mile
gale kept the water so rough that the launching
Of surfboat seemed suicidal


Suddenly the little towboat showed her nose
outside the capes and headed for the schooner
The Grant lay within eight hundred yards Of the
beach, with her midship rails awash and every
sea breaking over her with terrific force. The
schooner was pounding viciously and Captain
Partridge saw that the would soon be
swept of. So he pointed inshore, despite the
wind and waves. and came close TO the Grant on
the windward side. From this position he
dropped line with a float and it was carried to
the schooner by the current. Once made fast,
the tug veered seward and carefully passed to
leeward of the Grant Then, with each big sea
almost hiding her from view Of those on shore,
the Twohy slowly steamed bow on TO the Grant.


Two of the tugs crew stood in the peak of the
bow and when the tug touched the schooner's
side they reached out grabbed one of the ship
wrecked seamen and pulled him to safety On
the beach the lifesaving crews OF the Cape Henry
and Virginia Beach stations stood by their surf
boat ready TO brave almost certain death IN an
attempt to rescue should the tugs work fail
Each time the tugs bow hit the schooner
member of the latter's crew was dragged from
the deck of the wrecked craft. When the last
man had been taken aboard, the Twohy cut
loose and headed for Norfolk From the shore it
seemed that six men saved. The Grant
sank soon after the rescue

capped. The others were dead almost

hides.

BALLSTON, N. Y, July 3.-The Sara

New York, was wrecked in this village
early today, and although the train
was demolished not a passenger was
killed or injured.


The train left Saratoga at 7;4O with
twenty passengers and crew of seven
men.


At the north end of the village the
Schenectady Electric railway connects
with the steam railway, and when the
limited approached at the rate of fifty
miles an hour the switch tender made
a mistake and opened the switch,
thinking it was the local train to be
sidetracked.


The entire train leaped from the
track. The engine parted from the train
and landed in ditch on its side.


Engineer Crane and Fireman William
Falannery stuck to their posts and
were not injured.


The four palace cars followed the
track for a few feet and then over
turned and went into the ditch. The
fact that the engine parted from the
train and went to one side prevented
teescoping and probably saved a score
of lives.


Engineer Crane said that the signals
were set right for his train, It is be-
;ieved that the switch was turned just
before the train reached the junction.

refuge during the Spanish-American war

searched the records of the consulate
which is the oldest in continuous existence
dating back to 1890, and found that In the
vessels owned by Americans and flying the
American flag had entered and cleared at
the port. The vessels averaged from ITS
to 200 tons, and brought to Bordeaux cot
ton, sugar, tobacco. slaves, whale oil and
logwood. and carried back to the United
States cargoes of wine. brandy, dry goods,
wheat, fruit and hardware.

his own weapons.


Harry Draper of Spokane, one of the
pursuing posse, had his two blood
hounds In leash and they were leading
him through the woods on the trail of
the outlaw. The dogs led Draper
within three feet of the outlaw, who
was crouching behind log, before
Draper saw him.


"Are you Smith," demanded Draper.


Yes was the answer, and as Smith
made reply he attempted to draw his
revolver from the inside of his coat.


Draper was quicker with his own
weapon and sent bullet crashing
through Smiths temple.


Smith appeared in the village of
Candy early today and begged for
bread at a bakery. He left imme-
diately, but within a short time posse
of fifty men was organized and fol-
lowing his trail3 Draper with his
bloodhounds was of the posse.

But Yesterday was a sad day for the
doggies. For the past week they had
been chained to their benches like
galley slaves to their oars and the
heat and dust and excitment had
worked them into a frenzy.


And during the long hours of the
afternoon the dogs rested uneasily on
their straw pallets and growled at the
hundreds of visitors VINO came TO ad-
mire them.


The collies and st. Bernards were
the greatest sufferers and among the
collies a young riot was prectpitated

Two well-bred yellow dogs had been

dozen others, all from the same ken
nels The two yellow fellows had won
second prizes and evidently had been
having an argument as to which was
the best.


When argument failed the great
beasts leaped at one another's throats,
and for a few moments the dust and
straw flew through the air, while the
attendants leaped about trying to dash
in and part the dogs


But the flashing teeth and snarling
jaws as the collies rolled about kept
the trainers away until young man
from among the spectators caught one
of the dogs by the neck, pulling the
brute away from his teammate.


In the meanwhile all the other dogs
in the show had become greatly ex
cited and were barking their applause
The fox terriers, fairly frantic with
excitement and anxiety to get mixed
up in the fight, leaped about in their
stalls until their trainers quieted them

best behaved dogs in the show, and
all seemhed to be proud of the fact
that Joe of Holmby, a magnificent
collie, which took first prize in the
collie class, was among them.

for the express purpose of taking first
prize in the collie class.


The Let's dogs have won MANY
prizes and even in the present bench
show the southern bred dogs from the

nothing would satisfy Mr.. Let's but
that he win first for the best collie

proved himself amply good for that
purpose.

point between their farms lay.

HAVANA, Oct. 19.-The cyclone
which began here Wednesday afternoon
reached it's full fury on Thursday morn
ing. The greatest damage occurred IN
the harbor and along the docks. A
number of smaller craft and lighters
were sunk and some houses we're blown
down.


The total number Of deaths was
twenty, all Cubans of the poorer class.
There are number of sailors among
the dead. Several score of longshore-
men and sailors We're injured.


The torrential downpour of rain COM
pletely stopped the street car service,
and the wind and rain made 1t impossi-
BILE to get about the streets. Trees in
the parks and along the shaded avenues
were blown down In large numbers The
cyclone was con fined to the province Of
Havana and Pinar del Rio. Matanzas
City escaped. Ef.t3


All telegraphic' communica tion was
annihilated. Today the wind moderated
greatly and the city is fast resuming





Many farmers have lost their all and
are in great distress.


Save for the activity in all quarters
Of the city of gangs Of hundreds of
men of the public works department,
under the direction of Lieutenant Colo
mel William NJ. Black of the engineers,
United States army, in replacing up
rooted trees, Havana today resumed its
usual aspect.


Gay Crowds Promenade


Gay crowds are promenading the
streets and lounging in the cafes, OBJ
livious of the fearful experience through
which their city has just passed.


A great majority of the trees are be-
ing replaced, but owing TO the neces-
sity of looping off branches they will
be denuded Of foliage, and it will be
long ere the parks and the Prado are
restored to their former beauty.


No other traces of the hurricane are
visible excepting nasts of the wrecked
lighters protruding from the surface
of the harbor. These small vessels were
almost all driven by the force of the
wind against the harbor, where they
broke up and sank.


Street car traffic was fully resumed
this afternoon, but the electric light,
telegraph and telephone systems are
still badly crippled. The harbor has
been searched for dead and 1t is now
believed that all the bodies have been
recovered. All the stevedores and sail
ors who sustained injuries are tonight
reported doing well.


1t is estimated that the damage In
Havana province will reach fully ST.
100000! One hundred and fifty tobacco
farms In the Alquizar district have been
destroyed. The recently planted tobac-
co crop also has been seriously injured.
Enormous damage is reported from the
Guira section, the center of the banana
district. These crops are said to have
been practically totally destroyed.

Special Gable to The Herald.


PARIS, Sept. 8.-A drama could pc
made out of the story of a grocer's
marriage at Grenoble. He was seven
and twenty ambitious and pleasing.
He was introduced to rich trades
man with still buxom wife and a
pretty daughter of eighteen years. The
young grocer's game was obvious. The
sureSt way to win fair bride, ana
handsome fortune was to propitiate
his intended mother-in-law, and this
he did only too well.


She favored his suit, and was glad
to see him with sighs and long pres
sures of the hand, and it dawned upon
the terrified grocer that he had won,
not the daughter, but the mother. He
was twenty-seven, she was forty, and
woman of strong will, and he gave
in.


In the interval the husband died,
and the grocer grew more alarmed
than ever. Marriage with the mother,
not the daughter, now threatened him,
for the lady of forty was more and
more loving. He screwed up his
courage and told her that he loved her
no more. Tears and protestations did
not move him. The lady wept and
stormed still more when she found
him counting her daughter. AS sue
cessful with the daughter as with the
mother, he was accepted, and the
wedding day passed without a cloud.


But the discarded lady of forty was
nursing a horrible revenge. The bride
retired to change her dress, the mother
went with her and told her the whole
story, her mother had been her hus-
bands mistress. Tears and fury were
the result. In the uproar the bride was
forgotten. When the groom went to
find her she had flown, and the best

The close of the Alpine season has been
marred by the most terrible accident of
the year. Four tourists have been found
dead, roped together on the Plan-Neve
Glacier, at the foot of the Paschen Peak,
a mountain nearly 5000 feet high.


The unfortunate tourists, whose names
are not yet known, arrived on Saturday
afternoon at Les Plans. above Bex. From
their conversation, it was gathered that
they came over from Lausanne for the
weekend, and that they were students.
The hotelkeeper tried to persuade them
not to climb the peak. but they laughed
at mis- fears, and one said: do you think
we are rich Englishmen2" Another re-
marked that he had climbed the Swiss
mountains for years without guides.


They left the hotel about o'clock on
Sunday morning. and nothing more is
known Of their movements, When they
set out the guides warned them to be
careful. as much fresh snow had fallen.
and many places were exceedingly dan
geroUs.


When their bodies were found today by
two Swiss woOdcutters they were almost
unacceptable. Nearly every bone in
their bodies was broken, and the blood
they had lost was frozen to their clothing


From the traces they found in the snow
the woodcutters surmise that two of the
climbers were experienced. and the other
two novices. The rope is believed to have
broken at an awkward turning, after two
Of the men had slipped. who dragged the
others with them.


They must have fallen a great dis
lance. Three of the bodies lay few
yards apart. The fourth lay about fifty
yards away.

LONDON December 22-Dr. Green, sur
geon of the Bristol Hospital for Children,
describes in the Lancet remarkable case
of restoration of the heart action by means
of massage after apparent death. The pa
tlent. a boy of nine, suffered from a COM
plant which necessitated an operation.
Chloroform was administered and the oper-
alton commenced. There was difficult
breathing and finally the respirations ceased
and no heart sounds were audible. Hot tow
els were applied and injections of strychnine
used but without success. Finally twenty
five minutes after the heart had stopped
DR. Green decided to apply direct compress
sion TO the organ. An opening was made
sufficient to admit the right hand.


The heart was found TO be quite immobile
and facid. The doctor began rhythmical
compression. with the right hand pressing
the hearts lower surface and the left hand
outside. The rate of compression was about
seventy a minute. For two minutes
this was done without appreciate effect.
Then the doctor grasped the apex of the
heart in his right hand and continued in
termittent compression. Soon a slight fut-
tering of the heart was noticed, the pupils
OF the eyes contracted and within few
seconds the heart began to beat forcibly
with more than normal vigor.


Meanwhile artificial respiration had been
continued all the time and within short
period after the restoration OF the pulse
spontaneous breathing asserted itself. grad
ually becoming regular. In ten minutes the
heart and lungs performed their functions
in a normal manner, though the patient had
not recovered consciousness and sensibility
indeed never returned. The patient devel-
oped spasms early the next morning and
the heart beats and respiration had been re-
established.

LONDON. Feb. 24.-The American
duchess Of Marlborough since her lat
est visit to sandringnam has been high
in Queen Alexandra's affectionate es-
teem.


The queen recently invited the
duchess, who was Miss Consuelo Van
derbilt of New York, over from Blen-
helm castle to drink tea en- tete-a-tete.
Although the death of the king Of
Denmark, Queen AIexandra's aged
father, was announced on the day set
for the visit, the duchess, receiving no
countermand, duly presented herself
at Windsor castle.


She was ushered into the boudoir,
where the queen had shut herself UP
from everybody since the morning. Her
majesty said most cordially that she
was expecting the duchess, kept her
chatting for an hour, kissed her ON
both cheeks when she was about to go
and said she would make her re-
turn private visit to Blenheim some
spring afternoon.


The duchess, who is passing few
days in Paris, had an agitating expert
ence before leaving. The dukes aunt,
Countess Howe, who has been con-
firmed invalid since she suffered a
paralytic stroke about two years ago,
has recently imagined herself well
enough to take house at Newmarket
and to attend all the race meetings
during the season.


The duchess. to whom the countess
is greatly attached, was summoned to
reason her away from the resolve. The
countess telephoned to her physician
and on his arrival excitedly bade him
to declare the true state of her health.


The doctor emphatically said that
the countess could not possibly endure
the fatigue that fashionables go
through at Newmarket.


Whereupon Countess Howe became
SO excited that in the presence of the
duchess and the doctor, she suffered
paralytic stroke, which caused
her death Friday.

Marvellous experiences of George
Whittell, the millionaire, and his son.
George whittell Jr.. In an automo-

adding one more chapter to the volume
Of ecord-breaking occurrences which

The Whittell residence at 1155 Cali

Jones, opposite the old Charles Crocker
mansion, and one of the show places
on Mob Hill, was in the path Of the
great sweep of fire which spread
swiftly toward the hill the morning of
April TO- Whittell hesitated to aban-
don his home. but as the flames roared
through Pine street, attacking the
block along Powell and then fought in
upon the Hopkins Institute Of Art, only
two blocks distant, the Whittells made
their last move to escape, only to find
that their way was almost blocked on
the eastward. Young Whittell planned
to go to his Alameda residence. taking
such of the most valued household be-
longings in his big touring car.
+ The machine was loaded with ef-
fects, and the young man took charge
determined TO fight his way to the
ferry.


With his father and F. A. Stearns
Of Oakland, young Whittell started
from the California-street residence.
Through Mob Hill he drove, reaching
the crest of the hill at Powell street. 1t
seemed beyond human possibility TO
drive the car down Powell street. the
steep hill, forbidding in its grade ordi-
nary conditions, was more dangerous
with the fre-swept blocks.


Down Powell street toward Market
the machine was started, travelling
rapidly under the steady hand of the
young man. until the first steep slope
to Pine street had been safely covered
Then the descent became less precipi-
tous. and the run was made through
Powell street amid ruin, debris, smoke
and fire.


Great masses of brick and stone and
tangles of wire covered the streets
Turning eastward on Market street
Whittell headed for the Ferry Depot
Along the wide street, now framed
with the wreckage and rubbish of the
ccntlagration, the occupants picked
their way slowly to the water front
After an hours labored manipulation
of the car the Whittells arrived at the
ferry. Their record breaking journey
through devastated city was accom-
plished and soon they were on the
ferry boat bound for Oakland.

rious disturbance occurred here on Sat-

abandoned cemetery behind the Ameri-

mistreated. A number of personal en-
counters resulted, and one officer. draw

rived on the scene with the promise
that the mems demands would be grant
ed, whereupon the gathering quickly
dispersed and returned to quarters.


During the demonstration the public
held aloof, and neither the police nor
the military interfered. During the
interval there was much agitation at
the Yildiz Kiosk. The Sultan, who
was greatly disturbed, repeatedly is
sued fresh instructions to his Minis
tiers. Such occurrences have been fire.
quent in the provinces. but disorders
hitherto have seldom been seen in the
capital.

The four-oared barge Dolphin, the
property of the boating club of the
same name, was wrecked yesterday
morning off Green street dock. The five
occupants of the boat R. Keenan,
Horace Perazzi, Charles Farrell, Adam
Schuppert and John Peat-had to leap
into the water and swim for their lives
They were rescued Immediately by
passing craft. At the time of the acc1-
dent they were passing down the bay,
just abreast of Green street, when the
boat was suddenly struck by a big
wave, which swamped the frail craft
They leaped into the water, and, all
being expert swimmers, struck out for
the barge John Wieland, which was
close by, and were soon hauled on
board that boat In the mean time the
Dolphin had turned turtle As the
barge lay bottom up she was hit by a
succession of heavy seas with such
force that she was torn in two.

NEW YORK, Nov. 29.-The childish
fear of Harold and Alice Martin,
who live with their parents in the
outlying Glendale section of Long
Island City, kept an old man, Carl Ham
mond, in dark icehouse for more than
week. And yet to their childish super
stitions is due the mans s release yester-
day from his terrible Imprisonment.


Not that Harold and Alice are respon-
sible for the mistake that cost the man
much suffering and nearly caused his
death. But they heard his cries for as
sistance, growing fainter each time they
returned, and did not know their mean


ing.


Harold. an imaginative child of 8,
thought there was a Thunder man" in
the building, and told his sister so.
Gradually the possible tenants of the
fearsome structure became, in his mind,
"Thunder-man, Thunder-dog. and q
Thunder-cat," and although his sister
Alice. year older, rdiculed his imagin-
ings, she fled, as he did when the feeble
cries of the man imprisoned answered
their timfa rappings on the door.


Treasuring their secret, admitting to
1t not even their parents, the noises
made, as they supposed, by the "Thun-
der-man" and his companions, might
have failed one day to follow their timid
signaling to him had not the reasoning

breaking over the bow the customary

sliding down the ways the Music was
gliding down past San Pedro bay on
her trial trip, and was given salutes OF
welcome by other craft on the bay.

Fulton and Iverson, with their families
and friends. Also the owners, Messrs.
Napier, Wares and Suessmilch, with
their families and friends.

and Long Beach, beginning Sunday.

Philadelphia.-Bryn Mawr girls
turned out in force at ain. Wsdnes-
day to fight fire which threatened
to destroy the Low building, one of
the college group. The nerve displayed
lege doubtless saved the property.


Glasses were about to assemble in the
main building when the blowing of the
college fire whistle threw the students
into futter of excitement. The whis-
ties shrieking aroused all Bryn Mawr,
and the girls detailed to the fire squad
dropped their books and made rush
for the reel of hose that constitutes
the college fire department.


While score of more of students,
hair flying loose in the wind and skirts
held tightly, dragged the hose down the
steep slope leading to Low building,
the rest of the student body made a
short cut across the lawns to the scene
of the excitement. Smoke filed the
corridors and the girls, in true fireman
fashion, tied dainty. lace-edged hand
kerchiefs over their mouths before
plunging into the sitting Railways.


The girls bravely dragged their hose
into the midst of the commotion and
the signal was given for those above
to turn on the water. After a few
minutes play from the hose the blaze
was extinguished.


The damage is estimated at $1,000.
Much of this is due to water, as the
girls forgot to turn off the stream for
half an hour after the fire was out.

PORTLAND, Sept. 13.-In the states
of Oregon and Washington, which sup
ply the world with cascara sagrada,
practically no bark was gathered this
year.


The season for peeling has just come
to close, and the returns received
show that not to exceed two carloads
Were peeled in Oregon and only about
four carloads in Washington during the
summer months.


few years ago, when the excitement
in the cascara bark market was at its
height, the daily receipts at Portland
often exceeded that amount. The
quantity harvested was far in excess
of the demand and prices from that
time dropped sharply.


With the decline in value the produce
tion has fallen off, until now the drug
trade of the world is face to face with
a cascara famine.

designed to promote the development
of commercial interchange between
this country and Brazil.


Condensed milk. rubber seals. var

Ice boxes, scales, windmills and inks

most important commodity in the list.
and the duties on breadstuffs have long

Brazil and the United States.

leaders thus far have successfully prevented
a strike, urging the necessity for continu-
ing work until the signal is given from Mos
COW and ST. Petersburg.


At Yuzovka and Yekaterinodar, however,
without waiting for the general signal,
many factory and mine workers have
struck.

rinoslav have made representations to their
governments regarding the necessity of
protecting foreign subjects. three foreign
managers of mills having been attacked
during the last week. German manager
was shot with a revolver and killed while
leaving his factory, a Belgian manager
escaped death through the Intervention of
a policeman, whom the workmen shot dead,
and a French manager was compelled to
flee under menace of death.

BERKELEY, Oct. 22.-President

detachment of student fire fighters
made UP of college men, and after th1r-
ty minutes of strenuous toll succeeded
in extinguishing blaze that threat
ened the safety of the new mining
building and the college of mechanical
engineering this morning.


When the fire had been subdued and
danger was passed, President Wheeler
and his aides presented much bat
tered spectacle Coatless and hatless
and with hair awry and faces smeared
with dust, SCOT and torn by contact
with trees and underbrush, the col

men adyenturers. They had won their

dent Wheeler leading the way, fought

down the campus from the northeast
ern point, as did the blaze a year ago,

alarm was sounded.


President Wheeler ran from his Of

nal of danger and gathered up recruits

tachments of fire fighters and at every
point The flames were attacked. Wet
sacks and buckets were employed and
finally a line of hose was run out from
the college of mechanical engineering.

feet of the mining building. the smoke
and flames blackening the walls of
that noble pile.


The Berkeley Fire Department was
not called upon for help until the ex-
citement was almost over. The coll
legians had saved the day and Presi-
dent Wheeler Joined with Chief Ken
ney in congratulating the lads upon
their strenuous work.

BY Associated Press.


COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Feb. 13.-
The coffin containing the body of King
Christian was removed today from the
palace to the Christianborg church,
where it will lie in state until Feb. 10.


The crown prince and other members
of the royal family, the court officials
and army and navy officers followed
the hearse on foot through the crowd
lined streets. After a brief service at
the church the royal party returned to
the palace, leaving the body in charge
of guard of army and navy officers,
who will remain day and night station
ed at the head and foot of the cata-
falque


The public will be admitted to the
church at stated hours daily


Hours before the church was opened
the vicinity was densely thronged with
those desirous of paying their last re-
spects to the body of the old monarch.


The line from the church door was
fully mile long and constantly
lengthening when the doors were
opened to the public, and thousands
passed the bier during the subsequent
two hours. The German minister dur
ing the morning placed two enormous
floral tributes from Emperor William
at the foot of the catafalque

packed with over a thousand refugees who
have been brought across the bay to escape
the terrors of the San Francisco conf1agra-

last night at the station from long benches
provided by the children's relief committee,

frantic efforts to check his downward

into an open field and when friends
arrived few minutes later they
dragged his limp and senseless body
from the wreck. He was not seriously
hurt and quickly revived.

Berlin. Nov. 3.-The International Radio-Tele-
graph treaty was signed this afternoon. The
details contained in the semi-officiaI summary
OF the treaty agree with the synopsis IN the
dispatches Of November l.


The representatives OF all the powers signed
the document, but Great Britain Italy. Japan,
Mexico. Persia and Portugal did not join in the
special article containing one OF the United
States proposals. that intercommunication be
obligatory between ship. and ship. The British
delegates some days ago offered as a compro-
mise TO accept compulsory intercommunica-
ton between ship and ship upon matters per-
tanning 10 navigation alone. The United States
delegates declined 10 agree TO the compromise
affirming that they were willing to stand or
lail on the principle of free intercommunicati ton
They were supported by the great majority OF
the delegates who adhered by signature TO the
article to-day, only the six countries named
declining. Great Britain. Italy Japan, France
SPAN, Denmark, Persia, Portugal and Turkey
dld not sign the remuneration clause, thus ex-
cepting from the provisions Of the treaty such
stations as these governments might select All
the other powers agree 10 free ship to shore in
accommodation with all stations open 10 the
public. naval and military stations excepted.


The period for the ratification OF the treaty
ends July l, 1905 The next conference will
take place in 1911.
