WORCESTER, Mass, August 13.-For
the first time in the history of the National
Association of Amateur Oarsmen medals
and banners have been awarded to two
| crews for a championship race, and the
New York Athletic Club and Riverside


Boat Club Of Cambridge. Mass, together


hold the senior eght-oared championship.


The race, which was remarkable one in


many ways, was to have been rowed or


yesterday morning, but fear of police in


reference for violating the Sunday laws


caused the regatta officials to change the
original plan, and the race was declared of.
Two unsuccessful efforts were made to
determine the winner of the event, both of
which failed. The first race, in which the


New York Athletic Club. the Riverside Boat


Club of Cambridge, Mass, and the Argo-


naut Rowing Club of Toronto, Canada, par
ticipated, was the last event on the national


regatta program. The New York Athletic


Club crew finished first but owing to a


foul committed by the Argonauts the race


was declared of and the Canadians dis


qualified The second race which resulted


in dead heat, was replete with thrilling


incidents. and broke all rowing traditions


in the United States. The race was rowed


at 10 o'clock Saturday night. with the


New York Athletic Club and Riversides as
contestants. A searchlight was used to


illuminate the course on Lake .Quinsiga-
mond, and while the race was in progress
the referees launch struck a sunken buoy,
and became entangled in rope Edward
P. Reynolds of New York plunged into the
water from the launch with his clothes on
and got the launch free.
During the trip to the starting point the
New York Athletic Club shell ran down a
canoe and broke the outriggers. The boat
was taken back to the Lakeside boat house
and repaired. Meantime the Riverside crew
had been rounded up, and was waiting for
the New Workers. After considerable delay
the two crews were sent off. but before
half a dozen strokes had been made F. NJ.
Wheeler, No. Z, Of the New York crew
snapped his oar, and the boats were re-
called. Another oar was secured and once
more the boats were sent on their journey,
and were soon lost in the darkness. A yell
announced the fact that the imaginary
finish line had been crossed, but the judges
were not close enough to the contestants to
render decision.

IRUN, Spain, May 25.-King Alfonso
greeted his bride, Princess Edna OF
Battenberg as she entered Spain in
the early hours of the morning amid
an enthusiastic popular welcome and
the homage Of the Spanish ministry.


The special train bearing the Prin-
cess reached the frontier shortly after
sunrise. The morning mists still hung
over the river Bidassoa, separating
France from Spain, as the train reached
the center Of the bridge and the Span
ish fortresses belched n welcome sa
lutte OF twenty-one guns from the
heights of Pena de Aya, commanding
the frontier. At the same time regl-
ments of carbineers and Sicilian guards
were massed ON the foot ways Of the
pier and with trumpets and banners
kingdom, while the bands played al
ternately the British and Spanish ma
tional hymns.


In the meantime King Alfonso, in
the uniform of a field marshal and
surrounded by the ministers of the
crown, the court chamberlans and
the military and civil authorities
awaited the princess at the railroad
station, which was decorated with a
floral arch, carpeted with red velvet
and hung with the royal banners and
other insignia.


Premier Moret directed the governor
general to admit the public to the plat
form and to give the people every ia
cility to see their future queen.


The meeting of the king and the
princess although a ceremonious state
function, was none the less marked by
the unaffected joy and cordiality of the
young monarch. The king presented
his ministers, who officially welcomed
the bride to Spanish soil and she
graciousy acknowledged the official
salutations.


At 5:15 a. M. amid continued salvos
from the fort and the cheers of the
people the train left Irun for Madrid.
The peasantry lined the tracks and
packed the stations along the line, Civ
ing the young couple a continuous
ovation.

opera house, proved herself a heroine
of the most romantic type yesterday
afternoon when, by a desperate effort,
after having fallen from her carriage
she managed to stop the horses which
had become frightened and were run
ming away.


TO see Miss Glosz daintily tripping
before the footlights, to see her deli
cate features all smiles and dimples
and hear her sweet voice thrilling over
the audience and to see her small and
shapely hands, one would not think
that at a moments notice the soft curve
of the throat could be changed to rug
ged muscles, that the great blue eyes
could narrow and sparkle like fire. But
they did dyesterday.


Miss Glosz following the afternoon
rehearsal, started toward the telegraph
office at First and Spring street


The carriage stopped in front of the
telegraph office and Miss Glosz at
tempted to alight. She had not reached
the ground when the horses became
frightened and made leap to get away
and Miss Glosz was thrown to the
pavement.


The actress garments were ruined
but she managed to regain her footing
and caught the horses heads and held
them quiet until an officer went to her
assistance.


She then went to the theater and ap-
peared at a last rehearsal and danced
through her lines while the mud and
water trickled down her immaculate
skirts and Eddie Gallagher, with whom
she has several touching scenes in the
play to come, went through the love
scenes according to the long distance
fashion.

SEATTLE, Sept. 21.-The steamship
Harold Dollar, Captain Thwing, which
carried supplies to the whaling fleet in
the Arctic, reached port last night.
Thirty-o one men of the wrecked whaler
Alexander and fifteen sick men from
the other ships of the fleet were brought
down on the vessel She also brought
whalebone valued at $4,000 which
had been loaded on her from the diff
ferent ships.


The Dollar met the fleet at Point
Barrow and delivered the stores and
foodstuffs and coal The entire fleet,
with the exception of the whaler Jean
cite, is to return this season, unless
they are caught in the ice which was
reported to be fast closing in when the
Dollar left.


Twelve of the whalers are still in the
north. They are the Narwhal, Beluga,
Jeanette, Alexander (wrecked), Bay
liss, Karluk, Thraube, Thurman, Mon
terey. Belvedere, Bowhead and Olga.
The whalers state that the catch of the
entire feet amounts to fifty-two
whales


The men who return on the Dollar
tell stories of terrible suffering on the
different ships one of the principal
causes being the lack of food on the
different vessels. They also state that
charges have been preferred against a
number of the whaling captains, among
whom are Captain Bodfish, master OF
the Bayliss: Captain Newth, master of
the Jeanette, and Captain Elton. for
mer master of the Alexander and pres
ent master of the jeanette in the alb
sence Of Captain Newth, who, with Cap
tain Bodfsh, is under arrest.


The men also confirm the stories of
stealing of native girls from their
homes for immoral purposes and say
that full depositions regarding these
charges were taken before they left.
Charges OF brutality and of insufficient
feeding are made against Captain
Thurston and also Captain John Cook,
master of the Beluga.


The Dollar encountered the fleet at
Point Barrow. Her officers say that
the crew of the wrecked wha1er Alex
ander were living ashore in the whaling
station at which they had arrived only
a few days before. The fifteen sick
men had also been put ashore. Some
Of the men are scarcely able to walk
and are suffering from various diseases.
consumption being the most prevalent.


AS soon as the fleet had receive
their supplies and discharged part of
their whalebone into the hold of the
Dollar they started for the westward
whales. The feet left Herschel Island
as soon as the ice broke last summer.

The nursery's full of fairies:


They come, when you're asleep,
Between the slanting window blinds,
Into the room they creep,
When out of doors the star beams
At tag with shadows play, 49,, n,,.
When in the groves the ewes anu hympns
Await the break OF day.
I close my lashes almost tight,
And then the fairy hosts
Come stealing forth from dingy hooks,
Like multitudes of ghosts.
They gather on the walls so gay,
And nestle in the flowers
They're paper in the broad daylight,
But real in dusky hours)
They steal the honey from the bees
That fly from cup to cup
And sip and sip the luscious stuff
Until it's quite slipped up.
1 hear their voices whispering
Such strange, weird wonder tales
OF why the pansy eases hearts,
The Easter lily pales,
And how the lady slipper came
To be small size.
And why red roses always blush
Which nobody denies.
Then as the daylight in the east


Comes creeping through the gloom.
The fairies leave their games and feast,
And silence fills the room.
In broad daylight there is no sign
OF fairy folk or elf;
But that they surely have been there
I've proved 1t to myself.
About the walls and ceilings


Where they have danced and played
I've found a tiny little path


Their fairy feet have made.
They've trampled through the flowers fair
And over ferns and leaves.
And on the sky-blue ceiling, too.
Their dainty pathway weayes.
You need not tell me fairies are
Creations of my brain;
For II they came before at dawn,
They surely will again.

From the Honolulu Advertiser.


A very dark shadow has been felt to hang
over the future of the native Hawaiians.
1t comes from the early and obstinate de-
population which began with Cooks dis
covery in ITS The most reliable estimates
place the then population at not less than
$50, goo. At the arrival of the missionaries
in 1920 not more than $50, 900 remained, and
the multitude of abandoned village sites
gave the old missionaries an impression
that fully two-thirds of the people had
disappeared


The causes of that enormous mortality
We're not obscure. They were the introduce
ton among a long isolated nature race
wholly lacking the immunity enjoyed by
continental peoples, of new and yirulent
diseases. which swept them off. Chief
among those diseases was one which
Cooks ship brought and which speedily
infected the entire population. tuberculosis
contributed.


Added to these hostile influences were the
depopulating wars of Kamehameha. and the
destructive collection of sandalwood, while
whaleships converted every seaport into
public brothel.


Mitigating and remedial influences have
since then operated favorably under in
creasing moral culture and intelligence, but
the depopulatin Is not yet wholly checked.
Estimating from the later census figures,
there are now remaining less than 10000





10000 part Hawaiians. The total racial
dininution has been about one-half in the
past half century, although part-Hawaiians
have rapidly increased during that time.
The excess of deaths over births still re-
mains, with a great mortality among the
pure Hawaiian children


What are their prospects for the future?
We should answer measurably hopeful.
There is manifest Improvement. Especially
is this the case among the mixed breed,
who are rapidly gaining in numbers, due to
their superior energy and intelligence, and
to their wiser care of offspring. Under
present outlook, the mixed Hawaiians are
likely in a very few generations greatly to
exceed the pure native breed in numbers.
The prevailing language of both classes will
have become entirely English, due to the
vigorous teaching of English in the common
schools, where Portuguese and Asatic
youth alike with Hawaiian are learning
good United States" which viii displace
the outiandish tongues, as 1t does on our
continent


The future commingling of Hawaiian
blood with the other races will not be an
unwholesome one. The Hawaiian nature
is courageous and generous and peculiarly
receptive to new light. The Japanese race
ancient.y received very large infusion of
ceanate Oceanic blood which loosened up
their ancient Monaghan stiffness and made
them versatile and receptive We may thus
look forward to the future descendants, or
tue native Hawaifans with hopefulness and
pride. The future composite result VIII
make the coming Hawaiian civilization
bright one under the presiding power of
American institutions.

NEW WESTMINSTER, B. c., Sept.
27.-Mrs. w. ]. Kerr of this city, who
has been suffering for eight months
with a bronchial ailment that defied
the best efforts of doctors in this and
neighboring towns and which many of
her friends took to be a galloping con-
sumption, after violent parozysm of
coughing threw out a large molar tooth
that explained the whole trouble.


About eight months ago Mrs. Kerr
was put under the influence of chloro-
form in the office of a local dentist
while she had several teeth extracted,
and during the operation she must have
swallowed one of the loosened molars
without the knowledge of herself or the
dental surgeon. Shortly afterward she
experienced severe pains in the chest,
which instead of passing away con-
tinued to grow more excruciating.


Violent coughing fits racked her
frame several times every day and
throughout the entire night. while doc
tors and patent medicines alike failed
to bring any relief. Trips to the sea-
shore were equally unavailing and her
quick demise seemed assured till this
morning, when, after fit of coughing
more violent than its predecessors, the
tooth was discharged from her bron-
chial tubes. Relief from continuous
pains followed Immediately.

THE demand for hollow bricks and building


L blocks for house construction has induced
glass manufacturers to put hollow glass bricks
on the market, and they promise to be used ex-
tensively for novel and artistic effects.


The first glass bricks proved failure on &C
count of Their cost, but the hollow glass bricks
can be made at much less expense. They are
lighter and stronger than clay bricks, and are
such excellent non-conductors that walls built
of them are proof against dampness, sound,
heat, and cold. The bricks are sealed her
medically when hot, and are placed in walls
with colorless mortar made of special glass.
The bonding strength of the glass mortar is al
most great the bricks themselves. For
ornamental friezes, dadoes. string courses, and
facades they are of special value, and ADD
greatly to the artistic effects.


For those who might object to living in glass
houses through whose walls anyone could see,
it should be said that the hollow glass bricks
are made both translucent and opaque. Fur
thermore, the old adage that those who live
in glass houses should refrain from throwing
stones has no application to the modern glass
brick house, for the bricks are made so strong
that an ordinary stone thrown against wall
of them would rebound without cracking any
OF the masonry.

to erect the poles outside their establishments.

BY Associated Press.


SAN JUAN, P. r., Sept. 27.-The city
Of San Juan and the island of Porto
Rico experienced series of heavy
earthquake shocks today, beginning at
10:47 a. m.


The people were thrown into a condi-
tion of CONSERVATION and indescribable
alarm, but the resultant damage was
comparatively slight and there has
been no loss of life.


The first perceptible tremors brought
many people in alarm to the streets.
The tremors increased intensity
for twenty seconds and died for five
seconds.


Following this came the most severe
shocks, the earth shaking violently for
five seconds or more. Then all was
quiet. The first vibratory movements
were from east to west and were fol-
lowed by heavy motions, such as are
experienced on ships.


San Juan people were stunned and
when they realized that an earthquake
,wasnnen themGonsterra and alarn
prevailed throughout the city People
thought of the catastrophes of San
Francisco and Valparaiso. They fed
from their houses to the streets and
crowded the open squares.


Panic reigned and hysterical women
tainted.


Many began praying in the streets,
while large numbers rushed to the
churches. The government buildings
on the principal square in San Juan
were quickly emptied, everybody rush
ing frantically to the open, hunting for
places of safety.


Many clocks throughout the city
stopped at AZ minutes past ten. Wares
were shaken down from the shelves in
stores. Beds in the sleeping apart
mentS of the barracks were thrown
about in all directions.


The walls of the city hall, the infantry
barracks, the postoffice and the wo-
mems and children's hospital were
cracked in many places, but not badly
damaged.


The old artillery building near the
sea, now occupied by the quarter
masters office, was badly damaged.


Reports received here from other
points show that the shock was gem
eral and that 1t lasted for thirty Sec
onds everywhere. School houses and
churches in Huamaco, Gyamao and
Fajardo were slightly damaged.

While her friends hurried to intercept
her and break the news as gently as
possible, Mrs. Alice Eaton, the young
bride Of former Mayor Fred Eaton of
Los Angeles, boarded a train for the
north yesterday afternoon to join her
husband, all unconscious of the fact
that according to law she is not yet
Eaton's legal wife.


The much abused California divorce
law, providing that one year after the
signing of an interlocutory decree Of
divorce the final decree shall be issued,
is to blame for the most peculiar condi-
tlon of affairs which clouded the pretty
romance and wedding Of Eaton and the
former stenographer of the city clerk.


Eaton APPLIED for a license Saturday
and announced his intention of marry
ing Miss Alice Slosson.


Hurry to Justice office


The couple hurled to Justice Pierce's
Office and were married there. Then
Eaton left for the owens river valley
leaving his young wife with her
mother.


Yesterday morning the marriage
license clerks discovered that although
Eaton had been granted an interlocu-
tory decree of divorce three years ago
and under ordinary circumstances
would have been free to marry two
years ago, the final decree had not been
signed and therefore Eaton will have
to return to Los Angeles and have
Judge Smith sign his final decree.
Then he will have to take out a new
marriage license and the ceremony will
have to be repeated before Eaton and
Miss Slosson are legally married.


The young woman's friends heard Of
the unfortunate mistake early yester-
day and many of them tried to inter-
cept her and tell her of the state of
affairs They failed to find her, and
with her mother she boarded a car for
the north to join Eaton ana spend her
honeymoon in the Owens river valley.

Prior to the San Francisco trouble
Los Angeles automobile dealers had
more than they could attend to in the
way of supplying the demand for cars
and orders accumulated far beyond the
capabilities of the local houses.


The manufacturers were harassed
with applications from Pacific coast
branches and the output fell short of
the cry for more autos. Then came the
northern disturbances, and rather than
decreasing the demand for the horse
less wagons the disaster instanced in a
striking manner their real value.


The San Francisco supply has been
practically given over to governmental
service and private owners are In a
large measure forced to await the
pleasure of Uncle Sam until such time
as he can restore or make recompense
for the machines which were pressed
into service for the alleviation of the
stress attendant upon the earthquake
situation.


The northern part of the state which
depended upon San Francisco agencies,
is now looking southwark, and several
calls upon Los Angeles agents indicate
the fact that the auto has become an
indispensable factor of municipal well
fare.


Local dealers. however, will hardly
be able to respond to the demand from
the north, as the Los Angeles demand
more than equals the supply.


Shipments Diverted


Several shipments diverted from San
Francisco were received with acclaim
by local agents, who for the first time
in months were able to present well
filled salesrooms to prospective pur-
chasers. That was the situation
week ago, but the cars have been
gobbled up with the same degree of
persistency as characterized the south
ern trade during the past year.


Many a lesson has been learned in
connection with the San Francisco
calamity. The populace of the northern
metropolis now realizes the impractical
bility of erecting great buildings upon
mud soil. A thousand other municipal
lessons have been thrust home which
in the future are to cater to the welfare
Of Pacific coast cities, and far from the
least is that of the automobile, which
in the time of trouble proved godsend
to the harassed citizens as they fed
from the scene Of their ruined homes.

text:
Brant Rock Mass, Aug. 6-After crossing
four states and having landed once for break
fast DR. Julian p. Thomas and Roy knabenshue
ended the midnight balloon trip which began at
Port Morris, New York City, at Brant hoch'
Mass not far from the old home OF Daniei
Webster More than three hundred miles hao
been covered by the balloonists in little less
than fifteen hours From Port Morris to Brant
Rock In a straight line is somewhat over 20
miles, but the air currents, sending the balloon
first off to one side and then 70 the other. mate
rally increased the distance. The balloon was
cast loose at the East 13Sth street gas works at
SAP p. m. yesterday and landed at Brant Rock
at about 11:30 a. to-day.


When he landed, DR.. Thomas said that the bal
loon trip was the most successful that has been
made yet since the revival of interest in the
sport surprising any record made by any other
member of the Aero Club. The landing was
practically without incident the balloon being in
no wise injured, although Knabenshue received
a few cuts of no great consequence.


At nearly all points of its 300-mile trip the
balloon was seen from the cities and towns
along the Sound. Twice the balloon passed
within hailing distance OF yachts on the Sound,
and at Noank, one hundred miles this side of the
landing place. Knabenshue brought the balloon
down by means of the new windlass and the
anchor rope TO the ground. where some food and
water were procured, after which the voyage
was continued.


The trip over the Sound began about an hour
after the earth was left behind, when the bal
loon passed over City Island headed toward
Sands and NIatinnecock points, on the Long ISL
and shore. Above them was the August moon, hot
and angry looking, while the Sound stretched
out toward the Race and Plum Gut like a silver
mirror. Travelling fast as the light air.
the heat was as intense the sweltering
earth beneath them. Scores of yachts, off
toward Larchmont and as far along the shore as
Greenwich and Indian Harbor, could be seen.
their bodies and sails snow white in the moon
light.


Suddenly a low lying cloud bank appeared
along the Sound just below the balloon. The
horns and whistles OF the coastwise buoys and
light stations along shore drifted up to the two
men in indistinguishable medley of sound, so
that It was impossible even TO guess where they
were.


Somewhere off Bridgeport. the fog horn Of a
yacht heard with startling distinctness i'm
medately beneath them Knabenshue brought
the balloon down close over the craft and near
ly frightened the watch to death by hailing
them from above From them he learned his
exact position, and the balloon rose again above
the gradually thinning fog bank.


About o'clock the fog had lifted enough for
the party to see the dark outline of the shore
gradually lifting through the haze as they ap-
preached. AS they swept inshore DR.. Thomas
let the anchor trail until It caught: then. work
ing the windlass to which the line had been
made fast, the two aerOnauts pulled the balloon
down 20 the ground landing in the garden patch
OF Tilton Eldredge, Of NOank. The aerOnauts
had breakfast with Mr. Eldredge, and after
taking some water aboard UP with the anchor
and away again. The SUMS heat expanded the
ha1
the loss sustained by the descent. and the highest
altitude OF the whole voyage was reached soon
arter leaving Noank The wind still held from
the southwest. and the balloon gradually left
the Sound behind. soaring over the hills and
meadows of Rhode Island. At Warwick the
balloon was dropped near enough TO the earth
TO allow the passengers to ascertain their where
aboutS once more After passing this point the
balloon kept on over Narragansett Bay and be-
yond into Massachusetts,. travelling at about ten
miles an hour. Hills rivers meadows and bay
stretched fiat as the book Of a musical comedy
below the party@ The manufacturing cities of
Southeastern New England were noticeable only
through the smoky haze that overlay them, the
big factories fattening out indistinguishably as
the balloon passed over them Only as they
were raised distantly on the horizon did the
buildings look anything like what a normally
built structure should.


Finally Massachusetts, Bay was sighted, green
and blue in the sun, high up. ALMOST TO
the edge of the shore the two men allowed the
balloon to drift, and not until a ducking was
almost inevitable did they make their final land
ing. Dumping along as the basket hit the ground
and the gas retained it's buOyancy, the balloon
finally came to stop in the meadow belonging
10 George III. Thomas, at Brant Rock on the
Brant Rock side Of the Green Harbor River,
near the old Duxburgh turnpike The open
water of Massachusetts Bay was scarcely three
hundred yards away


Brant Rock is one of a group Of popular sum-
mer places in Plymouth County. The balloon
was seen approaching a long time before it
landed and almost as soon as the aeronauts had
jumped out of the car the cottagers and hotel
guests from Marshfield, Duxbury. Green Harbor
Scituate and other South Shore resorts arrived.
After packing up the balloon DR.. Thomas and
Knabenshue went to Boston. where the former
telephoned to Mrs Thomas. He will return
home tomorrow morning.

BY Associated Press.


PHILADELPHIA, Feb. 20.-The
spring municipal elections were held
throughout Pennsylvania today. Ideal
weather prevailed and a heavy vote
was cast in many localities.


Philadelphia elected two magis-
trates, seventeen select and thirteen
common councilmen, twelve school
directors in each of the forty-three
wards, constables and division election
officers.


Outside of seven small disturbances
in wards where there were spirited
contests, there was very little disorder
There were, however. numerous arrests
for Illegal voting. Little interest was
displayed in the contest for magis-
trates, as the majority and minority
parties were each entitled to one
magistrate and each party named only
one candidate.


Great interest was taken in the cleo
ton of eouncilmen, notably in the Sec
ond and Fifteenth wards. Party
lines were wiped out in many in
stances. In some of the wards the city
party and Lincoln party, which swept
the city last November, were split and
were fighting each other, with the help
of factions from the old Republican
organizations or the Democrats.

NORFOLK, Va, November 3.-The bat


tleship Virginia was rammed this morning


in Hampton Roads by the Old Dominion


liner Monroe. Both vessels came afterward


to this port The Monroe, inward bound


from New York. landed her passengers at


her pier, while the battleship, following


shortly under her own steam, proceeded


rapidly to the Norfolk navy yard.


The Virginia sailed from Old Point about


8 O'clock bound for Norfolk Shortly af-


terward the Monroe came in. following the


battleship through Hampton Roads. OFF


Sewells Point the Virginia slowed down,


apparently, and the Monroe Immediately


rang down.


Steering Gear Didn't Work.
The Virginia's steering gear seemed to
become deranged and she sheered ont of
her course. The Monroe could not stop nor
could she change her course in time, so
she came on, and. striking the battleship
on the afterpart Of her armor belt, raked
her starboar quarter. One set Of the bat
tleship's davits were turned inboard, and
1t seemed to witnesses that boat was car
ried away, while two Of the battleships
six-inch and one Of her three-inch after


guns were raked and probably materially
damaged.


Monroe Worse Damaged.
The Monroe, with bad twist Of her steel
Prov. seems to have been the worst dam
aged, and her damages may prove more Sc
rious than they now appear
A survey will have to be made to deter
| mine the full damages to each vessel.
There were many immigrants aboard the
Monroe. and when the ships crashed the
women set up a loud outcry. The fearful
were, however. soon Gained.

Fire of unknown origin last night
destroyed the old Rosedale school build
ing, Wentworth avenue and Forty
third street, and for nearly an hour
threatened to consume the new brick
building adjoining.


The Old building was of frame con-
struction and when the flames were
once fairly started the fremen could
do little to stop them. The fire started
at 10 O'Clock. Persons living in the
neighborhood saw the blaze in the win
dows and Immediately turned in an
alarm, which was promptly answered,
altho the run was an unusually long
one.


When the firemen had run their lines
to the building, the flames had spread
to all the four rooms and the fighting
had to be done entirely on the outside.
A part of the force was detailed to save
the brick structure, and this was done
only after a hard fight. Shortly after
the fight was begun the high wooden
walls toppled into the basement, turn
ing what was left Of the school into
furnace. After an hours work the
flames were extinguished.

New London, Conn. = Harvard's

Coming after years of defeat, the vic
tory was particularly sweet to the
crimson. 1t was a great Yale crew
that Harvard defeated, "a crew that
had broken all records in practice and
went to the stalleboat favorite. Har-
wards Joy is unconfined


Harvard won, but Yale rowed a race
that will live long in the annals of
college sports. Not only from the
start, but until the last sixteenth of a
mile did the shells cease to lap each
other. The men in the rival boats
could see each other for more than
three miles and half, as first one cox
swain and then the other called upon
his crew. Harvard really got the lead
when the killing pace proved too much
for the Yale men. In the final spurt
Boulton and Noyes were done, their
oars literally slipping away from them.


Harvard won the race by less than
two lengths and half. Her time was
23.02; Yales, 23.11.


While the crews had the tide with
them, they had a brisk Quartering
wind which made fast time impossible.
The record for the course is 20:10,
made by Yale in 1883.

BIDDEFORD. Me-, April 19.-The hen
which withstood the flames. smoke and
water during the Trull hospital fire in
Biddeford and calmly sat on her nest
until the excitement of that eventful
day was over has been rewarded for
her faithfulness by Matching one chick,


In the same fire the surgeons finished
an operation in which life was al
stake while the building was burning
over them and firemen were working
to keep the flames back until they had
finished.


That the surgeons were not without
rivals in heroisn was discovered after
the fire was out and the cellar full OF
water. The firenen, wading in the
hospital basement, found a box float
ing upon the bounding MAN," and in
it Biddy and the thirteen eggs upon
which she had been placed the week
before.


She had remained as steadfastly at
her post as had the life-savers on the
floor above. No setting hen ever
showed greater determination to Per-
petuate her race than this Biddy when
the firemen tried to pull her off her
floating nest.


The eggs had been chilled in the al
most ice-cold water which had soaked
up through the straw nest, and there
was slight hope Of any Matching. But a
hen that would set through fire and
water the hospital folks declared
should not be martyr to the practi-
cability OF a cruel world, so the box
was put up high and filled with new
straw and Biddy was left to do what
she could with the wet eggs.


The hospital people speculated two
weeks ago on the outcome. IF they
hatch the chicks will have web feet, "
declared the chicken fancier who owned
the hen. He missed his guessh for the
one resulting chick is perfectly formed
"a little black ball of fuzz--and its legs
are not icicles.

The thunderous detonations to which
the terrified city yoiistened all that dread
full Friday night meant the salvation
of 100000 people. A million dollars
worth of property, noble residences
and worthless shacks, were blown to
drifting dust, but that destruction
broke the back of the fire and sent the
raging flames over their own charred
path.


The whole east side of Van Ness ave-
nue. from Golden Gate to Greenwich

most of the structures stood untouched
by spark or cinder.


Not one charge failed Not one build
ing stood upon it's foundation. Not one
unlit torch was left pointing skyward
to carry the flames as through gigantic
chimneys in to the unburned district.


Unless some second malicious miracle
of nature reversed the direction of the
brisk wind the whole populous district
to the west, black with fleeing refugees
and unilluminated except by the dis
astrous glare from the burning water
front seemed safe by o'clock

Van Ness avenue is fiat as the earth
on the east side. Every pound of gun
cotton did it's work and though the
ruins burned it was but feebly.
From Golden Gate avenue north the
| fire swept across the wide street in but
one place. That was the Claus
Spreckels place on the corner of Cali
forna street. There the flames were
wrilhing up the walls before the three
dynamters reached it. Yet they made
their way to the foundations. carrying
their explosives, despite the furnace
like heat.


| oh IN 40 r11 cO
swiftly and the fuse lit in such hurry
that the explosion was not quite sue
cessfu from the trained viewpoint of
the gunners.


But though the walls still stood. il
was only an empty victory for the fire
as bare brick and smoking ruins are
poor food for flames.


Van Ness Was Last Chance


Captain MacBride's dynamiting
squad realized that stand was hope
less except on Van Ness avenue. They
could have forced their explosives fur
ther in the burning section, but not a
pound of gun cotton could be or was
wasted The ruined block that met the
wide thoroughfare formed a trench
through the clustered structures that
the conhagration, wild as it was, could
not leap.


| Engines pumping prllle tlllouSH VI
Mason from the bay completed the
little work that the gun cotton had left,
but for four days the haggard-eyed
6remen guarded the flickering ruins.
| The desolate waste straight through
the heart of the city is a mute witness
to the most heroic and effective work
of the whole calamity.


Three men did this, and when their
work was over and what stood of the
city rested quietly for the first time
they departed as modestly as they had
| come.


They were ordered to save San Fran
cisco and they obeyed orders.


Captain MacBride and his two gun
ners made history on that eventful

Celia Rosenschweig and her ffteen-year-
old boy Joseph arrived in the city last week
after a wearisome journey from their home
near Bielostok. Russia. At the outbreak
Of the Russo-Japanese war the head of the
family was drafted into the Russian army
and was killed in one of the first battles.
The woman determined to come to America
and started with a little money obtained
from relatives.


Mother and son started to walk to Ham,
burg. Their money soon gave out and they
| took to singing and playing in the villages
| to make their way. The mother had a
| tambourine and Joseph an accordion; be-
sides Celia possessed a fine voice. From
| village TO village they travelled, Joseph
| playing old Russian airs and his mother
| singing. The village folk enjoyed the treat
and Celia and Joseph, ere many weeks had
passed, found themselves in Hamburg with
enough money to pay their way across the
ocean.


They arrived here last week and put up
| with friends in Brooklyn. They had been
repeatedly invited to play for the cabin
| passengers Oh the great ship coming across
and had collected quite a oosey sum. They
had no doubt they would make their for
tunes in the streets Of New York. Every
morning the two started out and travelled
through the streets. singing and playing
Russian folk songs.


All went well until they struck the vicinity
Of Suffolk and Delaney streets yesterday
morning. Tn hundreds of refugees who were
on their way to work in the sweatshops and
factories Of the East Side stopped when they
heard the familiar airs of their native land,
and it was not long before the street was
blocked. The crowd grew to such proper
tons that q bunch Of cops thought a riot
had broken out. hustled to the scene and
took Celia and Joseph to the Delaney street
station house. ? The cops we're on the verge
OF charging mother and son with inoiting
crowds to riot when a Russian who had
followed the pair to the station house ex-
planned to the sergeant that they had been
merely playing and singing the old songs
Of their native land. Then charges OF
causing a crowd to collect were made and
the MINISTRIES we're taken to the Essex Mar
ket police court and arraigned before Magis-
trate Breen. DR.. Lebliner, the court inter-
prefer, explained the cause Of the crowd
collecting, and pleaded for leniency. The
Magistrate felt that the pair we're innocent
OF any w%rongdoing and discharged them.

spread. One car left the tracks near

SHERIDAN, Wyo., Oct 27.-Two
companies left Fort Mackenzie today
going north, and it is generally believed
that they have gone to intercept the
Ute Indians In case they attempt to
reach the Cheyenne agency before the
arrival of the cavalry from Fort
Meade.


Old timers here say that should the
Utes reach the Cheyenne they would
fire that band into revolt and a serious
war would result. The Cheyennes are
hard fighters and have given the gov
eminent much trouble.


The second detachment of cavalry
sent out from Fort Robinson left Gill
lette about midnight and unloaded this
morning at Kendrick, three miles from
Arvada. They had Instructions from
the department to "march close on the
heels of the Indians" but not to fire
unless absolutely necessary. They will
await the arrival of the troops from
Fort Meade before making a demon
stratiOn.


The Indians camped last night about
sixty miles northeast of Sheridan. Chief
Kannahph says they will not go back.
Beyond killing stock for food and rob-
bing an occasional sheep camp the In
dams are committing no depredations.

The Proclamation" edition of The
Herald issued yesterday represents one
Of the most pretentious efforts eve put
forth by Los Angeles newspaper. Its
instantaneous success, its pronounced
hit and the tremendous demand for
copies of it prove not only that it is
appreciated for its true value by its
many friends and admirers here at
he-ne, but that the need for such an
edition was pressing and that it fills
want which everyone interested in
Los Angeles felt most keenly.


That stories of earthquake destruc-
ton were sent all over the east by the
Hearst yellows, everyone knows. That
even though palpably false these Wild
eyed reports might have some adverse
effect, many feared. While no evil
dences of this have been discernible,
yet it was felt that an authoritative
showing of the absolute freedom of Los
Angeles from any deleterious effects
of the San Francisco disaster was both
desirable and timely.


The Herald undertook the task of
furnishing this refutation. 1t involved
much work, money and time. But the
task was bravely met, the work was
begun and The Herald of yesterday
was the concrete evidence of this labor
of love.


That this proclamation" edition was
just what Los Angeles wished, the rush
for it amply proved. Thousands and
thousands of extra copies above The
Heralds regular circulation and the
ordered-in-advance supply were print
ed, but they utterly failed to satisfy
the demand. Time after time it was
necessary to re-start the presses, and
the mechanical forces labored long
through the day, trying to catch up
with the incessant stream of pur-
chasers.


To those who obtained, read and
enjoyed this Proclamation" edition,
nothing more need be said. To those
who sent hundreds of copies to the east,
suggestion is equally superfiuous. To
others who perchance did neither, The
Herald has only this to say: Get, read
and ponder over this splendid showing
for Los Angeles, and do not fail to give
your friends elsewhere the same pleas
ure. By sending copies broadcast
throughout the lani, you are doing
good missionary work for Los Angeles.

LONDON, Dec. 22.-Dr. Green, surgeon OF
the Bristol Hospital for Children. describes
in the Lancet a remarkable case OF restora-
ton of heart action by means Of massage
after apparent death.


The patient, a boy OF o. suffered from a
complaint which necessitated an operation.
Chloroform was administered and the
operation was commenced. There was diff
flcult breathing and finally the respiration
ceased and no heart sounds were audible.
Hot towels were applied and injections Of
strychnine used, but without success.


Finally, twenty-five minutes after the
heart had stopped, DR.. Green decided to
apply direct compression to the organ.
An opening was made in the thorax SUI.
ficiently large to admit the right hand.
The heart was found to he quite immobils
and flaccid.


The doctor began rhythmioal compress
sion, with the right hand pressing the
hearts lower surface with the left hand
outside. The rate Of compression was about
seventy a minute. For two minutes this
was lone without appreciable effect.


Then the doctor grasped the apex OF the
heart in his right hand and continued inter.
mittent compression. soon a slight fiutter-
ing of the heart was noticed, the pupils of
the eyes contracted and within a few seconds
the heart began to beat forcibly with more
than normal vigor.


In the meantime artificial respiration
had been continued, and within a short
period after the restoration Of the pulse
spontaneous breathing asserted itself,
gradually becoming regular. In ten
minutes the heart and lungs performed
their functions In a normal manner, though
the patient did not recover consciousness
and s~ensibility indeed never returned.


The patient dcv Hoped spasms early
the next morning and began sinking. He
died twenty hours after the heart beats
and respiration had been reestablished.

SAN FRANCISCO, April 27.-Many of
San Francisco's homeless people camped
in the park squares and vacant lots were
awakened early this morning because the
water dripped through improvised tents.
which afforded poor protection against the
heavy rain that began to fall about /
o'clock and continued for several hours.
Drenched to the skin by the heavy DOWN

many persons were driven into nearby

Although the various camps were better

received and put up since the last storm
stiu there are thousands who are without

least distress and suffering was at the
Presidio where nearly all the refugees have

morning, and the difficulty of preparing
warm food added to the distress of the
homeless, especially floundering in the mud

paratively few tents have been issued to

and the drainage good. Where the rain

New London, Conn, Aug 5.-When the cr1liser
Denver, Captain Colwell. arrived here from New
port at noon to-day she brought of the
rescue of party aboard the battleship Names
launch, which was stranded on a ledge in New
port Harbor last night A boxing exhibition at
the training station ended about 10 O'Clock. and
the Alabarna's representative, who had 20
round bout with a Kearsarge man for the cham
pionship OF the feet was victorious. Attending
the bout were officers from various warships in
port. among them several from the battleships
Maine and Missouri, who started to return TO

bound for jamestown wharf

1O:I5 O'Clock IN heavy fog. and had reached

were futile The tide was fast receding. and
when it was found the launch was fast on the
rocks the regulation distress signal, five blasts
OF the whistle was sounded. at short intervals.
but passing launches and other steamers paid

cluded that they would be prisoners on the reef
all night when a whaleboat from the cruiser

mile away. In a snort space or time the snip

lights Captain ColweI having become anxious

women were transferred TO one of that cruis-
er's launches and taken TO their respective ships

say they should have received aid long before

while they were sounding their distress signals.

SOME GRASSHOPPER PEOPLE


on this particular Thanksgiving
1t is eminently proper to recall
the old story OF the "Arkansaw Trav-
eler," who asked his host why he did not
repair his leaking roof.


"w-a-a-1," said the Arkansan, "its
this away. stranger. You see, when It's
rainn' we can't go out and mend IT.,
and when les not rainin' Il don't need
mendin'" 4"


Thousands Of you who have settled
in Los Angeles during the past year
have been considerably disgruntled and
upset by the unexpected cold
snap Of the past week. You knew we
had crisp cool weather in the rainy
season. You were told in every PAM
phlet and circular issued by the cham
ber Of commerce that It was needful
that you bring along all your warm
clothing, underwear, overcoats and
gloves. Why? Because the weather in
the rainy season is chillier than In the
dry.


Well, the summer was beautiful,
wasn't It? You had glorious sunshine.
perpetual peace and comfort for seven
straight months. You enjoyed it all
beyond description. You reveled in the
flowers and birds and trees and the
everlasting green of the foliage.


Forgot about the cold weather, didn't
you? Sang all summer long, like a
grasshopper, and thought 1t would last
forever, didn't you?


Honest, now, how many times during
the last seven months has your good
wife reminded you to order a sack of
coal or half cord of wood? You won't
answer out loud of course, but she
knows the exact number of times. Didn't
pay any attention to her, did you? Just
worked and sang and drank in the
whole glorious summer, as the grass
hopper does.


But one day the splendid rain came;
blew in from the sea to lay the dust
and yellow the golden oranges. Snow
piled up on the mountains three feet
deep, and you could see it up there,
glittering in the sunlight. Looked beau
tiful and reminded you Of the old
home back east" Unfortunately 1t
didn't remind you Of that sack of coal
or half cord of wood.


And then, on another day, the wind
veered and came sweeping down the
grand canyons off the beautiful snow
capped mountains and the rain fell
again, and while the roses still bios
somed in your front yard the chills
crept up and down your spinal column.


Then what? Why. you hurried off to
the coal man and the wood man-25, 900
of you at the very least. And the coal
man and the wood man threw up his
hands and said: I'm sold out long
since. Why didn't you come here three
months ago?"


After that you rushed off and bought
a gas heater and went home and salved
your conscience. But just as soon as
the $4,000 or $4,000 or more of you
doubled your demands for gas in a
single day it was more than any gas
company could successfully meet and
the big generators broke down.


Then you felt the keen winds from
off the snow-capped mountains sure
enough.


And what did you do then? Be hon.
est, now. You "cussed' the climate
didn't you? Oh, yes, you're sorry
enough today, as you sit in the recov-
cred warmth and again gather the
roses. But you said ugly words about
the finest climate on earth. And then
you swore at the wood man and the
coal man and heaped torrents of wordy
abuse on the gas company, which had
broken down it's generators trying to
help you out.


On this Thanksgiving morning con-
slider these things calmly now and &C
knowledge all to yourselves that you
can put your finger on the man who is
to blame for your temporary discom-
fort of several days ago. Think of the
deep SHOWS back east, the terrific bliz-
yards that are sweeping the country
the intense cold that will grow worse
in the east as the season advances
and then thank God you live in a coun.
try where a little sack of coal or hall
a cord of wood will keep you comfort
able amid the few days of rare colo
weather that only makes the grass
grow greener and the roses little
redder and more beautiful than before

WASHINGTON, Sept 6,-The navy
department has decided to concentrate
all the battleships in the navy at the
home stations and to replace those on
the Asiatic station with armored cruis-
ers.


In accordance with this policy the
battleships Ohio and Wisconsin, which
have been in Chinese waters for sew
eral months past, have started back
to the United States.


The Ohio sailed from Che Foo yes
terday for Hampton roads. She will
stop at Cavite and then cross the In
dian ocean and proceed through the
Suez canal and the Mediterranean.


Her place as flagship has been taken
by the auxiliary cruiser Rainbow. When
the Ohio has been overhauled and re-
paired she will be added to the battle
ship division of the Atlantic fleet.


The Wisconsin is returning by the
Pacific route and will be added to the
Pacific fleet. She arrived at Kobe,
Japan, yesterday and from there will
sail for Honolulu, She is bound for
naval station in Puget Sound.


The armored cruisers West Virginia,
Colorado, Pennsylvania and Maryland
will take the places of the Ohio and the
Wisconsin. They will sail from New
York in few days and will follow the
Suez route.

lifeboat in which the remaining half

which brought the men here

At the intersection Of Wilde and Cen

internally injured. Seeker was taken
to the General Emergency hospital.

wagon became frenzied after the collis-
ion with the hack team and made am
effort to free itself from the shaft.


Sergeant Ditson and officer Roy AL
len, who happened to be in the vicinity
OF the runaway, rushed TO the en-
tangled teams and while Officer Allen
neld the delivery horse Sergeant Dltson
pulled the end OF the shaft from the
breast of the horse that was then lying
In deep pool OF blood. AS the rod was
taken out the animal dropped dead.


The driver OF the hack escaped injury
by leaping from his seat before the
collision with the delivery wagon.

Dodge are safe. Two men were lost on the
pile driver at Long Key; about forty men
were picked up and are safe.


There was heavy loss of life on the

this afternoon with bodies and will bring
details of the storm news


The steamer Miami will have news from
Long Key.


The steamer Biscayne arrived this morn
ing in good condition. She met the steamer
Virginia on her way after the bodies of
the men who were washed ashore from the
st. Lucie. The steamer Biscayne gave the
Virginia twenty-five men to assist in pick
ing up the dead. The Biscayne was at
Long Key after the storm and reports boat
No. gone to sea. The Virginia is expect
ed hourly with dead bodies, and all prep
arations are being made to care for the
-corpses and the injured. The launch En-
terprise and all other launches on Long
Key except the Elna are total wrecks.

embryo seamen will be given leave ashore

HALIFAX, y. =, Dec. 23-The steamer
Strathcona, running along the eastern
shore Of this province, was burned last
night as she was entering Port Duferin,
and her thirty-eight passengers had a very
close call for their lives.


1t was 0 O'Clock. and the Strathcona had
lust passed inside of Beaver Light when
6ames were discovered beneath the saloon.
The fire was spreading rapidly. Capt.
Abner Reid, who was in command, ordered
full speed ahead and directed the bow Of the
burning steamer to Smiley's Point, about
half u mile from the Port Duferin wharf T..
He also orde red the lifeboats made ready.


The flames were spreading with tre-
mendous rapidity and the ship presented a
terrific sight as she forged ahead at tho
top notch ~ her speed toward the shore,
where the captain had determined 10 beach
her. The engineers stuck to their posts In
the engine room till the flames broke
through and they We're driven out. When
they left full head Of steam was still on
and the engines in motion.


The man at the wheel acted with great
bravery. His work was all important, and
he stood by the wheel TO the last. The wheel
ropes were burned or and the man was
almost enveloped in flames, but he stood
at his post until the steamer was driven
upon the shore and she was beached on
Smiley's Point


The passengers were panicstricken. but
Capt. Reid was able to have his orders car
ried out, and he got everybody ashore.
Many of them were only half clad when
they landed and passengers and crew lost
everything. The captain was the last TO
leave the burning steamer.

NEW YORK, April 30.-A special to
the Times from Boston says:


After arranging with the Eastern
Yacht club all the details for the inter-
national yacht race between German
and American boats, Commander Heb
binghaus of the imperial German navy,
representing the kaiser, yesterday In
spected the course off Marblehead, over
which the German-AmerIcan races will
be sailed in September. He also visited
Marblehead and Manchester and saw
several of the boats building for the
elimination trials


Commander Hebbinghaus was the
guest of the regatta committee of the
Eastern Yacht club. After returning to
Boston Commander Hebbinghaus said
that the American designers had gone
to the limit allowed by the German
Sonderklasse rule, under which the
boats for the match are designed.


The boats have seen," he said, "are
big for the rule. The designers have
taken all they can get.'


Fourteen boats have been ordered for
the trials.


Commander Hebbinghaus said that
nine boats were being built in Germany
for the trials to be held in July at Kiel,
one of which was for the crown prince.
Three Of these would be sent to this
country to contest in the match which
will be held in September.

to release himself A crowd of men
soon hoisted the animal. and Lazoviteh


was taken out, suffering from bruises
and decorations about the face and


body. He was taken to the receiving
hospital. The driver of the wagon,
Jack Flary, jumped from his seat be-
fore the horse fell. and saved himself
from injury.


The runaway Of the transfer wagon
team started near the top or the hill on


First street, and flew past the central
police station like gust OF wind.

TACOMA, Wash, July 22.-Washing-
tons lumber traffic has increased so
rapidly that the Hill railroads are un-
able to move loaded cars across the
mountains and out of the state as fast
as they are assembled from the main
and branch lines radiating from Ia
coma.


Not until large number of engines
now building for the Northern Pacific
and Great Northern are delivered and
put into service next winter can these
railroads keep their yards free from
congested freight.


On side tracks between Tacoma and
Ellensburg, distance of one hundred
miles, three thousand carloads of east
bound freight, comprising lumber
chiefly, are now awaiting shipment.


The mills are getting cars almost as
fast as needed, but the motive power of
the railroads is insufficient to keep the
roads clear. Trains are kept moving
almost without interruption through
Stampede and Cascade tunnels. 1t is
doubtful If the congestion can be
avoided until Hills north bank rail-
road down the Columbia river is COM
pleted, giving another line across the
state.

acres of grain have been sown this

winds and cold snap which damaged

put the oranges in prime condition for
marketing for the balance of the sea-
son.

NEW YORK, Sept. PA vast throng
which rushed on the course today pre-
vented the completion of the elimina-
tion race to select five American racing
automobiles to take part in the race
for the Vanderbilt cup after three cars
had completed the race. Joseph Tracy,
who won the race, Herbert Leblon, sec
ond, and H. v. Harding, third. were
the only racers who were allowed to
cover the entire course.


They thus qualified their machines
for the cup races and the judges
selected machines driven by Herbert b,
Lyttle and Walter Christie as the other
two to represent American manufac-
turers in the big race.


When Tracy crossed the fnlsh line OIL
the 297-mile journey, after a nsational
race in which he mad one circuit of
the course at a. rate of a mile a minute,
including nine turns, the great crowd
of spectators which greeted him with
roar of cheers thronged down upon the
course and engaged in a scramble TO
see and congratulate the winner.


Leblon and Harding, who were on the
tenth and last lap, had to drive their
cars almost into the throng in order to
get across the finish line but the other
racers who were far behind were unable
to force their way through.


Perceiving that the action of the
crowd would prevent a fair finish of
the remaining two qualifierS, William
K. Vanderbilt, jr., the donor of the cup,
and the judges ordered the race stopped
and held a meeting to :-'ect the other
two cars to qualify.


Lyttle and Christie were chosen be-
cause they were in fourth and fifth
positions when the course was blocked.
Lawell was pressing Christie closely for
the fifth position.


Tracy's time for the entire course
was hours, q minutes and 40 seconds,
that Of Leblon 5 hours, 81 minutes and
25 seconds; Harding, hours, 25 minutes
and 80 seconds.


Course Dangerous


Notwithstanding that the course was
regarded as more dangerous than that
over which the cup race was run last
year and the drivers sent their power
full machines over it at a speed at
times as high as ninety miles an hour
and around sharp curves, only one OF
the racing cars was reported to have
been smashed, and from that the driver,
Mongini, and his mechanician escaped
without serious injury.


Twenty miles from the starting line
the car driven by Mongini burst a tire,
and turning out of the road crashed
into telegraph pole and was badly
damaged. Mongini was thrown out but
landed safely.


There were numerous minor accidents
to the machines, chiefly damage to the
tires, so that the racers were trailed
out at long intervals over the course
and many had not half completed the
distance when the winner finished.


Throughout the greatest part of the
race the contest for first place lay be-
tween Tracy, Leblon and Lyttle.
Lyttle led the others in elaspsed time
for the first two rounds. Leblon then

NEW YORK, April 9.-While Chris
tian churches last night, with sermon
and song, were celebrating Palm Sun
day and the entry of the Savior into
Jerusalem before his crucifixion, priests
of the Buddhist faith in a house at 62
West Seventy-first street, in strange
robes and with weird chanting, were
celebrating the birth of their savior,
Gautama Buddha, 2400 years ago. In
the little Buddhist temple there were
no hymns, no prayers nor other of the
religious forms of the Christian faith,
but the sermons preached by the Chris
tian clergymen and by the Buddhist
priests differed little 1t was the same
message of purity, peace and forgive
ness.


About 100 persons were present at the
Buddhist service. For the most part
they were women. At one end of the
large room a small altar had been ar
ranged, where incense burned. Every
where were flowers. They festooned
the altar, the walls. the chandeliers
Those in the little congregation were
admitted by card.


Back of the improvised altar was the
name of Buddha, inscribed on fine silk
Beneath this burned the incense. The
services began with the entrance of the
high priest and two others, who, stand
ing before the altar with clasped hands
and closed eyes intoned chant In
their own Language.


This being over addresses were made
by Swami Abekananda, head of the
Vedanta Society In New York, and by
other Buddhist priests.

WILKESBARRE, Pa, April 13.-Le-
high Valley freight locomotive No. 555
was wrecked by a most remarkable
series of accidents last night after run
ming away from Hazel Creek bridge to
Weatherly.


Near Hazel Creek bridge the loco
motive jumped the track on the heavy
down grade. Engineer Mcconnell and
his fireman leaped off to make an ex-
animation, and while they were doing
so the engine started down grade over
the ties, humping along at such speed
that the trainmen could not overtake
her.


The locomotives speed increased, and
half a mile down the grade at Wealth
erly crossing, where there are guide
rails and heavy planks, the engine took
the rails again and with accelerated
speed dashed through Weatherly, emit
ting redhot sparks from the wheels,
which were held by the set brakes.


The wild flight continued until tho
sharp curve at Black Creek junction
was reached and with last mad leap
No. 555 left the tracks there and
plunged into the creek at the very
place where a similar wreck occurred
a year ago.

CHICAGO, July 31-Four federal judges
on their vacations probably are responsible,
through their simultaneous absence from
the city, for the deportation today of Mrs
Czarne Feierstein and her eight-year -old
twins to Russia, whence they fled In terror
OF the riots less than year ago The
three had been admitted to the United
States on the perjured affidavit OF man
who claimed Mrs. Feiersten was his
mother. AS soon as the family passed at
Ellis Island he eloped with the eldest
daughter and disappeared. The mother was
traced to Chicago by the immigration au-
thorities and arrested


Probation officer Minnie Jacobs, who had
become interested In the case, undertook
to find federal judge who could stay the
summary deportation proceedings. local
society having indicated It's willingness to
give bonds guaranteeing that Mrs. Feier-
stein would not become a public charge
Court rooms and chambers In the federal
building were all closed and Miss Jacobs
spent yesterday in an unsuccessful hunt for
the absent four at their homes. An In
junction alone could stop the authorities.


She appealed for more time, but Immigra-
tion Inspector Schubert announced that he
would have to start for New York with the

BALLSTON, N. Y, July s.-The Sara
toga limited on the Delaware and Hud-
son Railroad. the finest and fastest
passenger train running between Sara
toga and New York, was wrecked in
this village early today. Although the
train was demolished, not passenger
was killed or injured.


The train left Saratoga at 7:40 o'clock
with twenty passengers and crew of
seven men. AT the north end of this
village the Schenectady electric rail-
way connects with the steam railway,
and when the limited approached at
the rate of fifty miles an hour the
switch tender made mistake and
opened the switch, thinking it was the
local train to be sidetracked.


The entire train leaped from the
track. The engine parted from the
train and landed In a ditch on its side.
Engineer Ed Crane and Fireman VIII
liam Flannery stayed at their posts and
were not injured. >The four palace cars
followed the track for few feet and
then overturned and went into the
ditch.


The fact that the engine parted from
the train and went to one side pre-
vented telescoping and probably saved
a score of lives


Engineer-Crane said that the signals
were set right for his train. 1T is be-
lieved that the switch was turned just

THE tunnels contemplated in New York at the pres
ent time will when completed form a vast under
ground network centering about the City Hall.
Future tunnels will honeycomb the island, so that
it will be possible to go to any portion of the city
without once coming into the open air. The speed
with which the will run, equaling and even
surprising the rate already attained the expert
mental roads in Europe, four hundred and fifty
miles in two hundred and ten minutes will allow
the people whose business carries them daily to
the city to live without inconvenience loss of
time fifty one hundred miles from the metropolis.


The completion of this underground system will
bring about another Transformation. The most
elementary of commercial axioms is that business
follows the traffic; that when the population of
the city will travel almost exclusively underground,
all the retail merchants will follow the lead of
institutions in New York and establish entrances
to their buildings directly from the subways Stores
of every imaginable kind will line these passages;
and on Monday mornings hundred years hence
the housewife will leave her home in the country
hundred miles away, travel to the city in hour,
finish her bargain hunting, take lunch, and return
without once coming to the surface from the time
she leaves her home until she gets back.


Not only will these tunnels be used for passenger
transportation, but many of them, like those in
Chicago, will be devoted exclusively to freight.
Pneumatic tubes, like those which carry the mails
from the post office to the railroad stations, will
be installed everywhere for the transportation of
merchandise. This complicated system will prac-
tically do away with all surface traffic, and

NEW YORK, December 5.-As they
turned the lock of the door in little cot
tage which they called home on the out
skirts of Westfield, N. j., Mrs. w. F. Wezel
and Mrs. Oscar Felter started for town yes
terday with light hearts. They said it was
blessing enough that their four children
were quartered snugly in the humble home,
where a wood fire cracked merrly against
the cold into which the mothers set forth to
their work.


Each was left a widow last summer and
each had two children. Before the deaths
of their husbands the women were friends
of long standing. They shared the sorrows
of their bereavement and decided to face
the future together. The problem of home
was solved when they took possession of the
cottage. II was only sixteen by twenty
feet in size. but they had patched it up for
the winter and made it cozy within.


Townspeople of Westfied who knew of the
brave struggle the two widows were max
ing gave them employment. While they
were away at work the children kept house.


Mrs Felters daughter, Louise, aged five,
was the oldest of the four. Next came little
Charles Felter, three; Samuel Wezel, three,
and baby Susie, four months old.


Each day, when possible, either Mrs


WeZel or Mrs. Felter hurried home at noon
to see how the children were getting on. 1t
CHANGED yesterday that both the widows
were working near enough to the cabin
home to visit it during their hours rest. All


was we'll save that the fire had died down
in the stove and the place was cold. The
mothers hustled about to see that the chill
dren did not suffer during the afternoon


and after filling the stove little store of
wood was placed on the hearth. Departing


they locked the door as was their custom.
1t was just getting dusk last night when
the nearest neighbors saw flames leaping
above the roof Of the cabin. Those first to
arrive pressed forward until they were
nearly suffocated by the heat and smoke
but the flames precluded all human posi-
bilty of succoring the children within the
structure.


Word had been sent to the Westfield fire.
men, who made all haste to the scene.
While the spectators were viewing help
lessly the destruction of the shanty two fig
ures were seen, staggering as il their
strength was spent, toward the illumination.
The crowd fell back as Mrs. WeZel and
Mrs. Felter approached. They had just left


the homes where they had been employed
for the day, and read the meaning of the
light on the outskirts of the town. Their
strength had been exhausted in their desper-
ate haste to reach the shanty and save their
children. They collapsed after reaching the
scene, and were well-nigh crazed with grief.
The firemen put out the flames, but not
until three of the children had been so
burned that identification was impossible.
Baby Susie was also dead. but the crib had
projected the body somewhat.

Olos6 Den1nd th6 limousine ID COM
fort is the perfected cape top. This
covering, which, with it's side curtains,
celluloid windows and glass wind shield,
affords almost as much protection from
the elements as the limousine. It has
the advantage of less weight and can
be folded away in pleasant weather,
thus reducing the wind resistance and
giving the tourist chance to get the
full freshness Of the sun and air.


It's a noticeable fact that where
last year even the best machines had
to be especially fitted to take the cape
top they are now fully ironed for it
30 that the purchaser may order the
hood and curtains from the maker or
may have set constructed to suit his
particular fancy.


Wood still leads in popular favor as
the body material for high priced cars,
as it is not subject to the unsightly
dents which disfgure a metal body
after a seasons running and are prac-
tically ineradicable. The lighter cars
are built almost entirely with alum
mum or sheet steel bodies, which COM
bine the advantages of cheapness and
light weight.


Springs are Easy.


Spring suspension has reached what
appears to be absolute perfection. Sew
eral makers are suspending the body
and chassis from separate sets Of
springs, thus relieving the passenger
from the vibration of the machinery.


Greater power in proportion to the
weight is another distinguishing char
acteristic Of the 1906 car. Where last
season seven horsepower was consid-
cred sufficient for runabout, ten horse
power is now considered the proper
thing, and light touring cars are being
increased from sixteen horsepower TO
twenty horsepower motors and con-
trolling gears are little changed from
last year, greater efficiency being the
aim of the makers rather than innova-
tions Of any sort.


The tire question, which last season
seemed to threaten the future Of the
motor car, is apparently solved. The
Improvement in springs has decreased
the strain upon the tire. Tire makers
are abandoning the machine process for
hand work and the better tires pro-
duced this way promise to eliminate
the bullying, bEstering and bursting
which made long trip last season a
gamble against "the innate perversity
of things.'


There is no distinctive 1906 type of
machine. Different makes in the same
class look much alike and the only way
to tell a new car is its greater perfec'
tion in detail and the improved lines
and more comfortable riding of the
body.

WASHINGTON, July 16.-Perfect
sanitation and clean linen are proving
fatal to the West Indian negroes em-
ployed on the Panama canal. Although
Colonel Gorgas and his assistants have
banished yellow fever and other tropi-
cal fevers which made the canal zone
one large burying ground for the
French canal builders, they have found
that sanitary precautions taken in the
quarters occupied by workmen make
the jamaican negroes especially sus-
ceptible to pneumonia and other throat
and lung troubles.


West Indians are not accustomed to
an abundance of fresh air and we'll
ventilated, clean quarters. Living for
generations in small huts where large
families crowd into rooms tightly
closed against the night air. the
negroes from Jamaica and other tropi-
cal islands have developed lungs with
cramped capacity and especially sus-
ceptible to changes of temperature.


The officers in charge have found
that the West Indian laborers cannot
be induced to eat sufficient wholesome
food to keep them In good health, even
when supplies are furnished TO them
at cost price and meals are made at
tractive at great expense to the Canal
Commission.


Chief Engineer Stevens of the Canal
Commission, Governor Magoon and
other men Identified with the work on
the isthmus have agreed that lack of
lung capacity and insufficient nourish-
ment, rather than laziness, are re-
sponsible for the inability of the West
Indians to perform an amount of work
equal to that done by white laborers
from Spain.

NEW YORK, December 31.-Far below

man recovered consciousness for mo-

man and his prisoner from the tunnel

air locks, where the heavy atmospheric
pressure under which the men work IN
the lower tunnel Is gradually reduced.

dening was sent to hospital and Lynch
to a police station

STOCKTON. Cal, Feb. 10.-Tono
Sablich and Guero Buvich, who have
been imprisoned in the App mine at
Quartz mountain by a cavern since
midnight last Monday, were rescued at
11:25 this morning, after having been
in the tunnel without food for period
of more than 100 hours. Fortunately
there was plenty of water at hand and
they did not suffer from thirst. They
were somewhat weak from lack of food
when rescued, but were otherwise in
good condition.


The fact that communication with
the rescue party was at all times pos
sible through the debris seemed to keep
up their spirits and their main suffer-
ing was from cold due to the water in
the tunnel The men were cheered
Justify when they were brought to the
surface after the rescue, and they have
been receiving congratulations and
shaking hands most of the time since.

from Cleveland, Ohio, to New York, ran
into an open switch at Guffey coal mines.
about fifteen miles east of Pittsburg, to-
night, killing the engineer. Harry Shep-
pard, and seriously injuring Charles Denny.
the fireman, and F. s. Farmer the bag
gage master.

bruised by being thrown from their seats,
but were not seriously hurt.


According to the officials of the Baltimore
and Ohio railroad in this city the wreck was
caused by some one opening the switch.
There was no reason. it is said, why the
switch should have been open, and the off,
Gals say some one who wanted to wreck
the train threw the switch.


That many lives were not sacrificed In
the wreck is remarkable. The train was
running at very fast speed. When the
open switch was reached the engine and
express were thrown from the tracks
on their side.


Fortunately the Pullman and day coaches
retained their upright positions. The cars,
however, were fearfully Jared and all the
passengers were thrown to the floor. The
wreck occurred at 1918 and most OF the
passengers were abed.

IN the French capital, married in redin bridal
gown OF red, with red VEIL red gloves red shoes, red

started fashion which may drive white satin and

Perhaps never before has revolutionary movement

white Society gasped when it was announced that

blossoms and this winter the holly berry has replaced

will surrender to the French fashion, and the makers
Of fashion the world declare that red has come
to stay and will supersede white entirely the color
for bridal gowns.

four hours has been responsible for much
uneasiness on the part of those employed
IN the navigation Of the Potomac river.
and incidentally for considerable discom-
fort to all who were out upon the streets.
The warm air meeting the colder earth and
water caused the formation of heavy fog
and steamboat masters report that they
were unable to see much beyond the bows
OF their vessels. Along the river fog sig
nails by moving vessels have sounded the
greater part Of the day, and the vessels
have been forced to move under half
speed to prevent accident. The Norfolk
and Washington steamer due here at Z
o'clock this morning, was detained by the
fog down river and did not arrive until
nearly IL o'clock. The fog bank extended
over almost the entire length Of the river.

were badly injured.


Great havoc was wrought TO Lock No. l.

A dispatch from New York SAYS: Nine
Emma Schell. a professional lion tanner.
FAMED almost as much for her beauty as for
her daring, stopped to wave greeting to
her cheering audience before she put her
mead within the jaws of a lioness at HUI
ber's Museum last evening and that second
of delay saved her life


The great rows Of teeth snapped together
and Nine Schell Is In Bellevue Hospital
Win both cheeks nearly bitten off by the
maddened beast and her beauty is so mar
red that she will never enter a lion cage
again.


Nine. Schells appearance has been a
drawing card at the Fourteenth Street MIL
scum for two weeks. Several times each
day she has entered the cage to compel the
lion and l1onesS to do the tricks she had
taught them. Her daring was considered
marvellous, for the two beasts she PLAYED
with are only half tanned, and the lioness
especially Is ferocious.


Five Hundred See Act.


Early last evening, before an audience of
five hundred persons. nearly all of them
women and children, Nine. Schell entered
the cage with nothing but a short whip to
protect her. AS she opened the door the
female sprang at her, but She cowed the
brute with whip lashes. closed the gate and
began to put the lions through their PAGES.


Though both growled and roared at times,
both obeyed the commands of the menacing
whip and Nine. Schell set her audience into
a whirlwind Of applause when she made
both beasts. in single file. walk over her
PROSTATE body. then leap back again to
the corner Of the cage, where they ODE
diently stood upon their hind legs


The climax comes in the finale, when the
lion tanner drives the lioness into the center
Of the stage, opens it's jaws with her hands
and thrusts her unprotected head inside.


Lioness Maddened at Climax


1t took minutes Of prodding by her as
sistant outside the den to force the angry
honess from her corner last night. Then
she sprang out with a great leap and
would have felled her mistress with a blow
of her massive paw If singing blow of
the whip had not subdued her. But even
as she raised herself sulkily upon her rear
legs, she snapped savagely at her tanner,
and the whip had to be used unsparingy
before she was again brought into submits
sion


Then Nine. Schell opened the huge mouth
with her hands ran her fingers along the
two rows of glistening teeth and bent her
head to thrust it between the menacing
Jaws.


She stopped to bow smiltngly at the eau-
dlence and wave her hand, as all perform
ers do before attempting a hazardous feat


The bow and the smile saved her life, for
at that instant the uoness, with a fearful
roar, thrust its paws down upon her Shout
der and buried its teeth in her left cheen.


The woman shrieked and staggered back;
the beast lunged. with open jaws. at her
head again and tore her other cheek.


Lion Attacks Lioness.


Then, as 1t was about to spring upon her
third time. she threw up her hands and
fell, unconscious. The audience Mortified
fed from the building.


Nine. Schell would have been torn to
pieces. but the lion. who had been growing
in his corner. sprang forward, and attacked
the frenZied lioness While they fought,
gnashing and clawdng at each other across
the cage, women in the audience tainted,
while even the men bofted for the street


moment later the tanners assistant re-
volver and prodd1ng pole On hand, had
thrown open the door and dashed in. He
fired a dozen shots at the raging Hons.
jabbed with the pole and succeeded in fore
ing them apart and into ddherent corners.


Then he carried the unconscious woman
outside and attaches OF the museum sum-
moned a Bellevue ambulance. Nine Schell
was carried to the hospital, still uncon-
scious Surgeons put twelve stitches in the
gaping wound in her right cheek and eigh-
teen In the torn flesh Of the other. They
said she would recover
