The car contained about fifteen pas
sengers and was running at a slow
speed through the dense fog, when not
fifty feet ahead the motorman, j. A.
Fitzpatrick, saw a pile of logs lying
on the track, and only by quick action
succeeded in bringing his car to a
standstill, but not before the. front
wheels of the car had passed over the
obstruction.


Six figures were noticed running
from the shadows near the death-trap
as the car was stopped, and the motor
man and conductor with number of
the passengers gave chase. Two of
the fugitives were captured after
long run, but the other four escaped.


Implcate Four Others


The car was one of the last to leave
the Fourth street station for Santa
Monica. and the prisoners were taken
aboard the car and carried to the
beach city last night. There they were
imprisoned and made the statement
that four other men had been asso-
ciated with them in the attempted car
wrecking, and promised to reveal ev-
erything If immunitv from punish
ment were promised them. Whether
this will be done in order to make a
capture of the other men has not yet
been decided upon.


1t is believed that the motive. for the
attempted car wrecking was either
robbery or vengeance. This same plan
of robbery was followed about a year
ago on the same line. The theory of
vengeance arises from the fact that
Sylvester Uquidez and James Garcia,
THE two men captured yesterday morn
ing, had at one time worked on the
section gang of the Los Angeles-Pa
cific road near Santa Monica, and,
owing to disorderly conduct, for which
they were fined in the Santa Monica
police court, had been discharged from
the employ of the railroad company.
tits said that they had nursed a griev-

ground in the west. and the brilliant heav-

In the Society of Friends the careful

physician tonight for treatment after a
battle with two giant "Maine hedge
hogs" which they had encountered in a
wood road while returning from work
this afternoon. The physician plucked

legs of each man, but no serious results
are expected, unless blood poisoning
sets in.

dusk, they picked up clubs and started
for the animals. The hedgehogs, as
they are called hereabout, jabbed their
needle-pointed quilts into the farmers
legs. The young men responded with

clubs, but the porcupines proved to
have the better weapon and carried the
day. Although one OF them was left
stretched on the ground, the other re-
treated triumphantly ana in good order,
master Of the situation, while the two
agricuturists limped home and out of
harms way as speedily as possible.

CHICAGO, Aug. 22.-Heat in Chicago
today was responsible for ten deaths
and twenty-nine prostrations, accord
ing to figures compiled by the police.


It is known however, that other
prostrations occurred which never were
reported and which swell the figures
given very considerably. BY IL o'clock
this morning the weather bureau ther-
-nometer registered 81 degrees and re-
manned at that point for four hours,
when the mercury climbed to 92 Later
in the day slight breeze sprang up
from the west, relieving the situation
somewhat, though the heat continued
oppressive.


Suffering was greatest in the poorer
districts of the west side In the Ghet-
10 tenement section men, women and
children struggled for breath and pur-
sued their usual avocations clothed just
sufficiently to escape arrest. Tonight
the landings of the fire escapes and
roofs are covered with exhausted hui
manity, seeking what relief can be
found in heat-tortured sleep.


All day long Chicago's sweat shops
were veritable hell holes. Here is was
no uncommon thing to see women and
girls. ard occasionally even men, faint
at their tasks, but when this happened
the others stopped only long enough to
dash q cup of water in the sufferers
face and then returned to their work


The parks were thronged with peo-
pfc and every available bit of shade
was sought out eagerly. Thermometers
on the streets in the business district
registered many degrees higher than
the official Instruments.


Tonight there is little let up in the
sitting heat and the official forecast for
tomorrow calls for a continued hot
wave.

Saturday night and had displayed con-

Two crowded excursion steamers were in
collision last night in New York harbor on
Staten Island. imperiling the lives of 800
persons, but neither in the crash itself nor
In the wild panic which followed was any
one seriously injured. The vessels were the
Perseus of the Iron Steamboat Company,
bound for Coney Island with 500 passengers
on board. and the Thomas Patten of the
Patten Line bound from Long Branch to
New York, carrying 1000 passengers.


The shrfll whistles of the colliding steam
ers soon brought assistance from beats
in the bay, and the frightened passengers
We're transferred quickly possible and
taken to the city. The Perseus and the
Patten interloGked and neither sank
Wrecking vessels were sent to their rescue


The lower harlbor was covered with a
dense fog at the time OF the collision and
the two vessels were running at reduced
speed. When directly of ST. George. Staren
Island the Thomas Patten crashed with
terrific force into the port side OF the Per-
seus. smashing the paddle wheel and box
and tearing away much of the joiner work
The Patterns bow and upper foredecks were
badly damaged.


The impact was so great that the vessels
remained fast together. No effort was made
by the Patten to break away, however. for
1t was felt that safety from sinking lay In
the vessels remaining interiocked.

Oakland. Cal, May 4-The aftermath Of the
earthquake and the fire has absorbed the atten-
ton Of every one in San Francisco and through
out the Pacific Coast. In Los Angeles, which is
five hundred miles away and which has always
regarded San Francisco as a rival, no one has
done any real business since the disaster Mer-
chants, professional men and others united to
raise relief funds and to devise means for
building the city by the Golden Gate; Los An
geles sent up several big relief trains, one being
a unique kitchen train Of fifteen cars, with chefs
and appliances for furnishing meals to several
thousand people. and the smaller cities Of
California and other states have been even more
generous than has Los Angeles. Marysville. which
is the leading city Of Yuba County, and which
received liberal aid from San Francisco twenty
five years ago when great food swept the city,
has actually contributed enough to represent
So for every man. woman and child In the town.
Santa Barbara and San Diego have also con-
tributed amounts that seem extraordinary when
the sizes of those places are considered. In
addition to aid from this coast gifts of money.
clothing and food have poured in from the East.


The relief work here has been handled with
rare executive ability. General Funston has
shown the same administrative capacity here in
handling the thousands Of refugees and in pre-
serving order in San Francisco that he displayed
in the Philippines Every one has united in
praising Funston's promptness in ordering out
the regulars half hour after the earthquake
and thus saving the big banks and business
houses from the !ootng which would have been
inevitable had only the police been left to cope
with the situation In relief work Funston has
also shown remarkable energy. He has cut red
tape wherever he has encountered 1t, and in this
he has been ably seconded by his officers. 1t
is safe to say that the uniform Of the regular
soldier has gained prestige on the whole coast
by the ability. good sense and selfsfontrol Of
Uncle Sans private soldiers as well as officers


Correspondents Of Eastern newspapers who
have come out here since the disaster have ex-
pressed their amazement over the cheerfulness
and pluck OF the San Franciscans in face of
their crushing losses On ferryboats and cars
and in all public places San Franciscans hailed
each other toked about their losses, cursed the
stupidity OF the militia that resulted in spread
ing the fire by black powder and dynamite, and
grew enthusiastic over the beautiful city which
would replace the well beloved town that had
gone up IN smoke. Instead of tears and lamen-
tations these strangers found the courage, en-
terprise and keen sense of humor that marked
the early argOnauts, who never knew when they
were defeated, and hence accomplished SEEM
ingly impossible things. The same miracle will
be seen In San Francisco. because OF the energy
and courage OF the San Franciscans Of the pres
ent day. Only the recently imported Eastern
man talks OF selling out and leaving the city.
All the old residents declare that they Will re-
build as speedily as possible, and meanwhile
they are keeping the wires hot ordering steel
and other material and In urging Eastern manu-
facturers to give them preference in their time
OF need. Amid such intense energy and such
buoyant enthusiasm there is no place for
/ lamentation.


The relief work IL now carefully organized
throughout the city. and all refugees are well
taken care Of. There are seven main supply
stations where food. bedding and clothing arc

PARIS, June S0.-Sisawath, king of
Cambodia, who has arrived here in
state, declares that the French women
wear too many clothes. His majesty
cannot find the same fault with his
wives and favorites and the women
of the royal corps of damsels which
fills his sumptuous residence here. The
government has rented the splendid
Hotel Brion on the Avenue Bois de
Boulogne for the Cambodian mon

Seated in the red and gold salon,
King Sisawath said to Commandant
Lannis of the Elysee palace: Your
women should wear no more than two
garments; one fitting close to the skin,
the other covering the first. Besides,
your women harness themselves so
tight that none of their motions are
free. At least they should have their
legs entirely free"


His majesty summoned several dane
ing girls and Illustrated his ideas of
feminine dress to Commandant Lam
mis-.


Sisawath is remarkably frank in ex-
pressing his opinion of France and her
people.


'The women squeeze their bodies so
tight that they have all sorts of nerve
diseases that were never heard of in
Cambodia," he continued.


Everybody here talks too much.
Everybody talks al the time; women,
children and men are shrieking at each
other all day long. Women interrupt
when their husbands are talking. Ser
wants without prostrating themselves
talk to their masters.


mo one has good manners. but the
most insolent are the men who make
pictures. Even my sacred dancers
they threaten with their diabolical pic
ture machines, which they hide in lit
tie black boxes"


His observant majesty also says that
the French do not pray often but he
admires their wonderful temple built
of fine white stone"


After the custom of Cambodia, Sisa-
wath is fully clad when he bathe5 in
the pink marble tub which his bath
room, lined with precious onyx, con-
tains. He sleeps in the same gorgeous
bed in which the czar reposed at Cam
piegne, but he angrily says is up-
comfortable and that he will use the
low, unpretentious couch he always

~FREELAND. Pa, Nov. 25.-Engine No. 434
of the Lehigh Valley road, hauling a train
of empty coa cars, plunged to-day through
an open bridge near Drifton Breaker and
fell thirty feet, leaving the train intact
on the track. The bridge had been under
going repairs. a fact that had been over
looked.


When James b. O'Donnell, the engineer,
saw the open bridge he reversed his levers
and applied the air brakes. Fireman
McGroarty jumped, but the engineer stuck
to his post.


In its descent the engine smashed a steam
pipe which carries power from the boiler
house to the Coke mines. The escaping
steam poured out over the engine, and it
was only when it had exhausted it's force
that the engineer was rescued from his
place in the cab. He was not seriously
hurt

MILLVILLE, N. J., Jan. 25,-Mid-
winter mosquitoes of mammoth size
with double appetities are breaking all
records by raiding many OF the towns
near here. Residents of Cumberland
and Ormond four miles east of this
city, complain that during the last two
evenings these pesky insects of the
genuine Jersey kind have made it very
uncomfortable for those who have gone
out of doors.

summer mosquito and have seemingly
double appetites. George Dixon, an
elderly farmer of Ormond, states that
he has never in his life seen larger
mosquitoes than those which invaded

VIENNA. December 31.-Two inventors
named Mach and Lagodzic have brought an
action for $500. which they allege they
have lost by reason Of the failure to pay
half a farthing. They protected at the
German patent Office a contrivance to pre-
vent accidents in working cranes. the year
ly payment being $35. This amount was
calculated by the Austrian postal service
and was duly sent by post office order.


The Berlin postal authorities, however,
declared that the amount received was a
farthing less than the sum due and sent
two notices to the inventors agent asking
for the balance. AS the notices were disre-
garded, the patent office declared the pat
ent lapsed. The inventors have now brought
their action against their agent for failing
to pay the extra farthing.

CHICAGO. ILL.,. October 18.-One man was
killed. several passengers were seriously in
jured and scores Of others had miraculous
escapes from death today, when fast pas
senger train on the Chicago and Eastern
Illinois railroad jumped the track after
striking a defective rail near Crete, ILL.,

at speed of forty miles an hour when

leaped into the ditch. Panic followed

trains speed. and were buried in showers
Of broken glass and splintered wood.


Several Of the passengers in the first coach
were reported to have been knocked uncon-

have been having hard time Of it since

These three counties run along the

Why should this really vast territory

Does that sound reasonable as an ex

Else why shouldn't Eldorado county

Just at the moment when the east
and the middle west had about decided
that they had evolved climate rival
ing that of Southern California, the
bottom dropped out of their thermom-
eter, the mercury fell below zero and
everything and everybody froze up,
good and hard and fast" Hence
forth until the first Of May, when the
cyclone season shall formally open, the
easterners will shiver and shake AMI
rustic for coal and wrestle with bursted
water pipes and suffer from pneumonia
and grippe and long for death in an
even tempered, fiery furnace.


They have yet one ray of hope and
promise. All the roads to Los Angeles
are still open-crowded, to be sure, but
always with room for one more. Here
we have no extremes Of heat or cold;
here it is always spring or summer;
here the fuel question is nearly elimin-
ated and the water pipes never freeze;
here is perpetual verdure, beauteous
sunshine and the unfailing gladness of
nature.


Isn't it strange that anybody will
persist in living in the rigorous eastern
and northern climates, when natures
most perfect work is calling to them
from the poppy fields and the orange
groves of Southern California?


But they are coming fast enough
so fast, in fact, that the people already
here are taxed to their utmost to pro-
vide for their reception. Blizzards and
storms and snowfelds and sunstrokes
are good advertisements for Southern
California. A few cyclones and tor
nadoes, thrown in for good measure,
will eventually uproot enough citizens
Of the east and transplant them TO
this country in numbers sufficient to
populate every available acre between
the Tehachapi pass and the Mexican
line. Let them all come and welcome.

NEW YORK, Feb. 20.-Over on Gov
ernor' island the army officers are
telling good story which has for its
hero their commander, Gen. Fred d.
Grant.


Two soldiers on the island were con-
stantly in trouble on account of their
hatred for each other, and every time
they met, which was almost daily,
there was a scrap. They were con-
stantly up before the colonel for disci-
pline, but the mild punishment he in
ficted was without result.


Finally the colonel lost patience and
put the matter UP to General Grant.
He studied the situation for a moment,
then sent for the sergeant-major and
said:


Just see that those two men, Crow
ley and Hitchins, clean all the bar
rack windows. Crowley TO do the out
side, while Hitchins attends to the in
side: and recollect, neither man is to
leave any window till the other has
finished"


The scheme was highly successful.
The enemies scowled thunderously,
even murderously, at each other for
five windows, but flesh and blood could
hold out no longer. At the sixth they
burst out laughing and have been the
best of chums ever since.

The gallant Seventh gets back from
service this morning.


Twelve companies Of infantry with
the signal corps and Troop ID cavalry,
under command Of Gen. Wankowski,
comprise the regiment that has recent
ly gained laurels in service that was
trying almost beyond belief.


The Seventh left Oakland yesterday
at noon and will arrive at the Arcade
station this morning at about O'clock
The soldier boys bring back to Los
Angeles with them the commentator
of those who saw the part they played
in restoring order in San Francisco
after the fire had brought about con-
ditions bordering close OH chaos.


Governor Pardee, Mayor Mott of
Oakland and all state; county and city
officials with whom they came in con-
tact unite in praising them. Col. Will
helm OF the regular army, together
with many other West Pointers, have
paid high tribute to the soldierly uuali-
ties that they displayed in coping with
conditions more trying perhaps than
warfare, and everyone in Oakland saw
them depart with genuine regret.


From the Arcade station the entire
command will march to the armory,
and their home coming will be very like
they had come from service in the
field, for they are travel worn and SER
vice weary after days on days of work
that was far from being light


The officers, from Gen. Wankowski
down, are proud of their command.
The service that they rendered was
valuable and effective to high degree.
Each man has done his duty and served
in such a manner as to reflect glory
upon Los Angeles, and the home COM
ing is in the nature of triumph, for
Los Angeles is proud of them and well
comes them back home with open
arms

Lady Jane Grey was the most learned
child of which history has any perfect rec
ord. Before she was nine years old she
wrote beautiful hand and was able to
play on many different musical instru-
ments. She could speak several languages,
both ancient. and modern, besides being
well grounded in philosophy.


When other children were playing she
would amuse herself by reading writings
of the philosophers in the original Greek


She led very lonely life when she was
child, as her mother and father were Of
ten away at court, leaving her to the care
of her governess and her sehoolmasters at
the gloomy family place called ERADICATE.
Perhaps that Is why she became so learned.


The big, square house was built on the
edge of a great forest surrounded by acres
of uninhabited land. There were very few
books and not any newspapers at the castle.
and Lady Grey had no playmates, as her
governess would not allow her to play with
the servants children, and there were no
others suitable for her companionship with
In miles. says Home Chat. Poor little thing!
She would have been happier with a little
more love and little less learning.

ANNAPOLIS. Md, August A.-Annapolis
is filled with midshipmen today, as the
feet bearing the midshipmen has returned
and is anchored in the Annapolis roads
The summer cruise has been under the
direction Of Capt. Colvocoresses. The feet,
consisting of the Cleveland, Des Moines.
Newark and Florida, dropped anchor inside
the harbor early this morning. and the
midshipmen were given leave at once.


The trains today and tomorrow will be
filled with departing midshipmen. as this
year they are given larger leave than
usual, and even those who live in far west
ern states will have a chance to visit their
homes.


The vessels composing the feet will leave
tomorrow for different stations. and Capt.
Colvocoresses has been detached to the
Naval Academy.

GADSBN, Ala, Feb. 11.-Bunkie
Richardson, a negro, charged with the
assault and murder of Mrs. Sarah
Smith here July Is last. was forcibly
taken from the Jail here at an early
hour this morning and hanged to a
bridge of the Louisville & Nashville
railroad across Coosa river. Twenty
four masked men went to the Jail,
overpowered the sheriff and jailer and
made short work of the prisoner.


Four negroes were charged with the
crime against Mrs. Smith, one of the
most flendish ever committed in the
state, two of whom have been legally
executed. The third, Will Johnson.
was recently convicted and sentenced
to death, but last week Governor
Jenks believing there was strong
doubt of the prisoners guilt, reprieved
the negro's sentence to life imprison-
lnent.


Richardson, the man lynched this
morning, had not been indicted, but
was in Jail awaiting the action of the
grand jury.


The coroner's jury which investigat-
ed the lynching returned a verdict
that Richardson was killed by parties
unknown.

As pretty college baseball game as
has ever delighted Southern California
diamond enthusiasts was witnessed
yesterday afternoon on the st. Vincent
campus when the Vincentian nine de-
feated the Highland Park team by
score of 3 to /.


AS had been predicted, the run get
ting did not amount to much because
of the compact fielding and strong box
work which thus far this season has
characterized the play of both aggre-
cations.


There was very little of the amateur
entering into yesterdays contest, and
throughout the game, which did not
last more than an hour and quarter,
some of the most brilliant fielding ever
brought off in the south occurred.


Both Phillips of St. Vincents and
Thaclxer for Occidental were in fine
form. and further demonstrated the
fact that they rank with the best col
lege twirlers yet developed from local
college diamond material.


Not until the fifth inning, when Al
Merrill, the Occidental catcher, walked,
did a Highlander succeed in reaching
first. Not until the seventh, when the
same player singled to center. did the
Occidentals find Phillips safely.


Phillips was given magnificent sup
mort, and had it not been for his two
errors in an endeavor to accept easy
bunts. the Highlanders would not have
come within hailing distance of the
plate.


'Thacker was also accorded the assist
ance which put spirit into pitcher
and one misplay by Beal at second was
the only error chalked in the Occidental
column.


Shaefer at third and Lamer at short
for the Saints played a wonderfully
fast game, and one that has not been
outclaSsed by any professional exhibit
tion vet witnessed in Los Angeles. Be
tween them they gathered in everything
that whizzed down the short field with
q cash and surety which had the Occi-
dentals out before their runners were
half way to the initial bag.


McCann and Campbell, at second and
first were invincible, and the latter
accepted seventeen chances in league
fashion A remarkable feature of the
exhibition was that the Vincentian out
fielders were not called upon for as
sistance during the game. Neither Tai
ty. Cunningham nor Grindell were cred
tied with a put out, and in but two in
stances did the ball leave the infield.


The Occidental team also accorded
their box man practically errorless sup
port, and the three runs of the Saints
were sent across the plate by oppor-
tune stick work and clever base run
ming.


Thacker struck out six of the Saints.
while Phillips had but three strike
outs to his credit. The Occidental
twirler allowed three men to walk,
while Phillips was worked for two
passes. The little Highlander pitched
even better ball yesterday than he did
against u. S. C. A disposition to put
them across high was noticeable in the
opening innings, but as Thacker settled
down the Saints gave up the idea of
walking and endeavored to baste them
out.


Snodgrass ard AL Merrill were terrors
for base stealers, and but one theft oc-
Cured during the afternoon. In one
instance Snodgrass whipped speedy
one to Mccain at second which caught
Merrill off the second sack by big
margin as the latter was calculating a
steal to third.

BURLINGTON. Iowa. July 9.-The
courts having ruled that woman who
wants baby of her own may have one,
and that the stork can be depended on
to pay a visit if invited, Mrs. Edward
Schmidt, a nurse of this city, today re-
ceived her share of the estate left by her
foster father, William Newbanks of
Knox county, Illinois. The woman
fought nearly twelve years in the courts
to obtain the property, for the will pro-
Vided that she should not come into her
Inheritance until she had been married
and had children. And Mrs. Schmidt
hasn't had any babies.


Newbanks died twelve years ago. His
adopted child, who was Harriet New
banks, brought suit for her share of the
estate. The case had dragged through
the courts since then. Miss Newbanks
was married here to Schmidt, fulfilling
part of the provisions of the will. But
the babies didn't come.


The case at last came before Judge
Rufus Robinson at Monmouth, ILL.,, who
decided that Mrs. Schmidt had fulfilled
the chief requirement OF the will by
getting married. He held that the re-
mainder of the contract might be left
safely TO the stork, and ordered the
money due Mrs. Schmidt paid over to
her.

Americans probably do not realize what
valuable possession they have. in the American
hen. They will easily understand, however.
if they will look over the annual statistics of
the Secretary of the Department of Agricul-
ture. That enthusiastic official reports that in
1905 the eggs of the United States were worth
more than the cotton or the wheat, more than
all the potatoes, the barley, the tobacco. the
sugar cane and the rice. The eggs are surpassed
in value only by the corn crop. But this is
not all. From another source comes a start
ling tribute to the value and the industry of
the American hen. Every three-months she
produces more wealth than the capital stock of
all the banks in the New York Clearing house,
while in two months she lays more value than
the annual production of all the gold mines of
the United States. More amazing still, she
could pay off the debt of the United States in
two years. If the American hen were ofthe
growing kind she might be pardoned for pro-
longed and lusty Dragging, but she is only
modest little cackler that attends to her bust
ness with rare industry and devotion.
headline: What the Hen is Worth.

LONDON. January 13.-There was a GER
tain amount Of animation on the stock ex-
change this week. The volume Of business
was fairly good and the tendency of prices
In all departments was upward Foremost
among the number of favorable influences
that operated on the markets was the great
improvement In the monetary situation. It
would not be justifable to say that the
money market has worked Itself into per-
manent ease, but for the time being, at
least, there Is an abundance of credits.


Money has been pouring into London dur
ing the last few days from Scotland and
the provinces, so that the bank reserves
has Increased f967 900. and funds have been
SO plenty that loan rates have shaded off
materially. The better situation in con-
tinental money centers also has helped Lon
don. and the evidence is that this better
feehng has been seen in purchases in this
market for Paris and Berlin accounts, the
good Ieellng on continental bourses being
due chiefly to the improved state of af-
Iairs IN Russia and the rather more cheer
ful outlook respecting the Moroccan ques-
ton.


1t is not possible, of course, to pre-
dict permanency for it, but the hope pre-
walls here that the European situation is
steadily growing better and the prevailing
conditions both monetary and political have
been dfstinctlvely promotive of investment
buying, SO that consos and other gilt-edged
securities have been in excellent demand.
Foreigners also have felt the effect of these
stimulating Influences, and responded with
a good upward movement in prices.


British rails for some occult reason have
not been dealt in heavily. but they close
with gains almost all along the line. Amer
lean railways have been active, especially
Atchison, Denver and Rio Grande, Mis-
souri,, Kansas and Texas and Southern Pa
cific.


Everything on the list is higher and
some gains are quite pronounced Even
mines have been more cheerful, and prices
are considerably improved.

. GENEVA, September 8.-Two girls named
Vachero. aged seventeen and nineteen
years, have just accomplished a daring
feat of smuggling.


They belong to family whose ancestors
have been smugglers for century. Their
hunting grounds are in the mountains
where the Swiss. Italian and Austrian from
tiers nearly touch at the Stelvio pass.


Many desperate fights with the customs
officials have taken place at this spot, until
the Vacheros have been almost wiped out.
There now remain of the family only the
father and mother and the two daughters,
who are the heroines of this latest exploit.


At present the father Is suffering from
a rife shot through the elbow, which he
describes as an accident" He was I'M
able to get large cargo of tobacco across
the Swiss frontier into Italy, and his
daughters determined to smuggle the con-
traband themselves.


They started. but near the summit Of
the pass were discovered by two customs
officials. While the elder girl proceeded on
the. journey the younger one kept the
officers at bay with rifle from a shell
tered position. The men replied. and the
fusilade continued until the sister with the
tobacco had got q good half hours start.
The younger sister then disappeared. and
returned home by making long detour
In the mountains, every path of which she
knows.

900. The roads doing the largest bust
ness with the government are the
Pennsylvania, the New York Central
the Lackawanna, the New Jersey Cen

Pennsylvania and the systems con-
meeting with it's main line get the bulk
OF immigrants because fully 20 per
cent of the immigrants settle in
western towns or cities. The Lacka-
wanna carries that portion which, by
natural trend, settles in coal mining
towns. The Baltimore & Ohio, with its
branch systems through the hard coal
territory, carries thousands into the
region. and for all the roads interested
the carrying OF the immigrant is a
profitable business.

"Hol for the beaches" was the cry
OF nearly half of Los Angeles yesterday
and before the sun was many hours
high street cars and trains were loaded
and the family horses were hitched to
the family carriage, to say nothing of
the hundreds of automobiles that car
ried the pleasure seekers to cool spots
within radius Of twenty miles of Los
Angeles.


Many who had contemplated spending
a quiet day at home with their families
changed their minds soon after Old Sol
drove chariot across the mountains and
shed the rays of an almost tropical sun
upon fair Los Angeles. Those who re-
mained in the city. however, did not
suffer from the heat, for a cool ocean
breeze was stirring most of the day and
drove away any chances for prickly
heat such as the people in the east were
compelled to endure.


Venice was popular yesterday and all
day the cars were crowded between
there and Los Angeles. Thousands of
people thronged the streets and pier of
the place, while the ocean breeze sub
dued the hot rays of the sun.


Long Beach and the other beaches
reached by the Pacific Electric probably
never afforded pleasure and comfort for
more people than yesterday.


An Umbrella Convention


The space for several feet back from
the ocean was so thoroughly covered
with umbrellas that very little sand
was perceptible. Those who donned
bathing suits and played in the water
from early morning until the sun began
slowly sinking numbered tens of thou
sands. Redondo and it's ever-present
bunch of moonstone searchers drew
thousands, as did Santa Monica.


The shady strand at Terminal island
proved to be an attractive place and
dozens of picnic parties ate their
lunches under the trees that border the
waters.


The first ain over the Salt Lake yes
terday morning - Terminal island was
well filled. mostly with people loaded
with fishing tackle who desired to spend
the day playing with the line Ind bob
ber. The officials were well pleased
with the additional service that was
inaugurated to this beach two weeks
ago.


In Launches and Livery


San Pedro and its many launches ap-
pealed to lose who wanted to sail on
old ocean.


Not everyone who sought pleasure,





went to the beaches. Early in the
morning there was a great demand for
turnouts at the Los Angeles liveries,
and hundreds went to the mountains to
spend the day in some shady canyon,
plucking flowers and resting or tramp
ing up the sides of the mountains where
the ocean breezes blow unchecked.


Los Angeles city parks furnished
shade for thousands. Early the parks
were well filled and the people read
their morning papers until noon. But
little time was spent over lunch and
dinner and the crowds strolleG about
the parks until the shades of evening
put an end to the reflection of the heat
from the pavement and brick and stone
buildings.


I'VE ought to be we'll satisfied with
this country of ours" said a well
dressed man as he calmly and comfort
ably puffed on his cigar in Central park
II had letter from friend yesterday
who lives in Chicago and he says that
he spent one day in a bathtub full of
water to escape suffering on account of
the heat. Los Angeles is good enough
for me-"

NEW YORK, July 1.-two crowded
excursion steamers were in collision TO-
night In New York harbor, off Staten
Island, imperiling the lives of 1900 per-
sons, but neither in the crash itself nor
In the wild panic which followed was
any one seriously injured.


The vessels were the Perseus of the
Iron Steamboat company, bound for
Coney Island with 800 passengers on
board, and the Thomas Patten of the
Patten line, bound from Long Branch.
carrying 1000 passengers.


The shrill whistles Of the colliding
steamers soon brought assistance from
boats in the vicinity. and the frightened
passengers were transferred as quickly
as possible and brought to this city.
The Perseus and the Patten interlocked
and neither sank. Wrecklng vessels
were sent to their rescue tonight.


Vessels Crash


Lowe harbor was covered with dense
fog at the time of the collision and
the vessels were running at reduced
speed. When directly off st. George,
Staten Island. the Thomas Patten
crashed with terrific force into the
port side of the Perseus, smashing the
paddle wheel and box and tearing away
much Of the joiner work.


The Patterns bow and upper fore
decks were badly damaged. The i'm
pact was so great that the vessels re-
NAMED fast together. No effort was
made hV thn p1ttan tO l.
1t was felt that safety from sinking lay
In the vessels remaining interlocked.
When the Patten suddenly doomed out
of the fog bank and 1t was seen that a
collision was unavoidable the passen-
gers on the two vessels became frantic
with fear. Just before the crash one
man on the Perseus jumped overheard.
He was quickly rescued, however.


Passengers Reassured


The crews of the two vessels were
summoned to quarters and then the
captains and officers went among the
passengers in an effort to restore quiet.
A hasty investigation showed that
neither vessel was in danger of going
down, and the passengers were assured
of the fact.


Meanwhile the whistles were calling
assistance, and while the passengers
We're rushing about the decks seeking
relatives and friends the excursion boat
Commodore and a Staten Island NUM-
cipal ferry boat ran alongside.


The transfer of passengers was quick
ly made and all were brought to the
city. During the panic many women
tainted and some were bruised but not
seriously.


One of the passengers who landed
from the Perseus declared that he had
seen two men jump overheard and he
thought both were drowned. There was
no confirmation of this, however.


Efforts were being made late to-
night to tow the disabled vessels to-
ward Brooklyn.

cold wave which has caused much sif-
fering in central Mexico and even on the
gulf coast has abated and the warmth of
the sun has been most welcome after three
days of clouds and north winds.


The police report that night before last
twelve members of the lower class perished
on the streets from cold and exposure, be-
ing poorly clad and most of them being
victims Of alcoholism. The cold produced
congestion of the lungs and the victims died
sitting in the doorways of business build
ings.


Gov. Landa had built fires In the streets
for poor people out at night. The poor have
suffered greatly during this remarkable
period of cold.

1RUN, Spain, May 25.-King Alfonso
greeted his bride, Princess Ena of Batten-
berg, as she entered Spain In early hours
of the morning amid an enthuastic popular
welcome and the homage of the Spanish
ministry.


The special train bearing the princess
reached the frontier shortly after sunrise.
River Bidassoa, separating France from
Spain, as the train reached the center Of
the bridge and the Spanish fortresses
belched a welcoming salute of twenty-one
guns from the heights of Pena de Aya,
commanding the frontier.


AT the same time regiments of carbineers
and an ancient Sicilian Guards were
massed on the footways of the pier, and
with trumpets and banners saluted the
brides entrance into the kingdom, while
the bands played alternately the British
and Spanish national hymns.


In the meantime King Alfonso, In the
uniform of field marshal and surrounded
by the ministers of the crown, the court
chamberlafns and the military and civil au-
thorties, awaited the princess at the little
railroad station, which was sumptuously
decorated with a floral arch, carpeted with
red velvet and hung with the royal ban
ners and other insignia. Scores of noble
ladies of San Sebastian, with their little
daughters daintily costumed in white, bore
bouquets and garlands for the princess
Premier Moret directed the governor-gen-
eral to admit the public to the platform and
TO give the people every facility to see their
future queen.

LONG BEACH, oct. 21.--Tomorrow
San Pedro will probably vote to annex
West Long Beach.


An election will be held In the 'harbor
city and in Terminal to determine
whether the latter, which was taken
into Long Beach year ago, shall now
be taken into San Pedro.


The probabilities are that Terminal
folk Will find themselves much annexed
and under the claims of two cities.


Ever since the election which deter
mined that Terminal should be annexed
to this city San Pedro has fought the
proposition at every turn.


Recently. after the fire at Terminal
island. San Pedro attempted to step
In and protect the claims of the squat
ters who had been ordered off their
former holdings


Long Beach then secured an injunc-
tion, cutting off this Interference.


San Pedro attorneys, at least Henry
Steiglitz, the city clerk, and City At
torney Goodrich, declare this intunc-
tiorf will not hinder the holding of the
contemplated election.


Attorney Goodrich, however, has adj
mitted that he thinks the election will
be without results, save to incur ad-
ditional expense to his city.


Local lawyers are wondering where
the authority for the election can come
from, since Judge Bordwell has up
held the validity of the former an
nexation.


However, the local authorities say
they will not interfere with the hold
ing of the election tomorrow. even to
the erection Of the booths in West
Long Beach.


They say that this city Is plainly
in the right and that San Pedro will
gain nothing by the election but, rath-
er, will lose.


Consequently Long Beach will not
trouble herself to interfere, one way
or another with the election.

sion.

cealed. All preparations are being

Railroad men are predicting the complete
annihiliation of jackrabbits along the Southern
Pacific line between Yuma and Tucson, and
also between Tucson and Ell Paso. The electric
headlight, they say, is doing the business. for
it seems to stupefy and frighten the cold, long:
cared creatures which sit on the track until
they are run down and killed.


Just how many thousand jackrabbits there
are along the Southern Pacific is problemat!c,
but the railroad men say that the ranks OF the
representatives of Kansas are rapidly being
thinned out Before the day of strong electric
headlights the jackrabbits would SIT along the
road and gaze at the trains as they passed by.
Now the rabbits sit on the track stoneblind
waiting death by the engine wheels.

Venice had a mardi-gras, a Coney

True Carnival Spirit

nthe Midway. When not doing some

scheduled. This helped trades people,

The confetti showers were so lavish

turn. There was no extortion, fact

ably.


Venice has never had such throngs

with unanimlty of opinion that it had
been profitable Fiesta day all -

LONDON. June 2.-From MANY
points of view the most interesting
American girls just now in London
are the Ogden-Mills twins who are
so closely related to the American am
bassadors wife. Though they cannot
be called beautiful, they are decidedly
good looking and having mastered the
secrets of chic dressing they thus ac-
centuate their charms.


Separately these two girls would not
attract any particular attention, but
together and invariably dressed alike.
from the tips of their toes to their
very Partisan hats, everyone stares at
them and everyone asks who they are


Ever since they were born Mrs. Og-
den Mills has insisted that they shall be
dressed alike to the minutest detail
Each of these girls has the same set
of friends and no one ever thinks of
giving present to one without also
presenting the same to the other. They
had birthday recently and their
friends had some trouble in duplicating
presents for these fair twins.


Mrs. Ogden Mills wished to procure
two necklets of the new stone, ultra
marine, for her daughters and had no
difficulty in finding one perfect gift
of the kind but in all London her jew
eler could not get it duplicated. The
important date was approaching and
the jeweler was at his wits end.


At last he explained to Mrs. Mills that
the only thing to be done was for him
to go straight to Paris and see what
he could find there. She accepted his
suggestion, paid all his expenses and
after a great search his eXertions We're
rewarded by acquiring the desired
necklet which, however, with the va
rious expenses, cost Mrs. Mills about
twice its real value.


The twins say that when they marry
their respective husbands will have to
live in the same establishment, as no
power will ever induce them to sepa-
rate from each other. Their maids
are also twin sisters and exceedingly
alike and they, too, are dressed exactly
the same


The Misses Ogden Mills are both ex-
perts in the art of motor driving and
among their recent birthday gifts were
two exquisitely appointed automobiles
painted and upholstered in white. Their
pets are always of the same family, for
instance, their special favorites, two
fox terriers, are brothers, while their
little Japanese spaniels are sisters.

DENVER, Colo, March 16.-Ouray,
Durango, Silverton, Leadville, Aspen
and other smaller mining camps have
been visited with snowslides during
the past two days. Hair-breadth es-

down the steep sides of the mountains

and grave fears are entertained for
scores of daring prospectors and miners
who are cut off from the outside world
in their lonely cabins far up In the hills.


One slide at Silverton struck the edge
of the town, doing considerable dam
age. The railroads in the San Juan
region are blockaded. The South Park
road is blocked by a slide near Lead
vile. The miners around Crested Butte
are completely cut off from transporta-
tion.

eraI storm of unprecedented severity
for this season throughout the east
ern and central portions of Colorado.

San Francisco, April 23.-The new San Fran
cisco that will rise from the ashes of the old
was to-day in its first stages of rebuilding. After
five days of confusion and almost superhuman
effort on the part Of citizens of CALIFORNIA;
metropolis, the great task of sheltering feeding
and otherwise caring for the homeless thou
sands has been performed, complete order has
been established and attention has been turned
to the future.


Through the great business quarter, where the
devastation by fire was the most complete, dan
gerous walls We're razed, buildings that had not
been disintegrated by fire were inspected with
a view to reoccupancy, and ground was cleared
for the immediate construction of buildings in
which to resume business at the earliest possi-
Bile time


Confidence has been restored. The statements
of insurance companies the measures taken by
the financial institutions the prompt and reas-
suring words which have reached the business
men of San Francisco from Eastern financial
centres, have all dispelled the feeling of uncer-
tainty.


The encouraging situation temporarily suf-
fered a setback early to-day because of a chill
ing rain which fell in the late hours of last
night and during the forenoon on the thousands
protected only by canvas coverings and even
less impervious shelters. While the rain caused
considerable suffering for the time being, con-
ditions were quickly improved by the prompt
action of every relief committee, as well as by
the voluntary acts of hOuseholders.


Homeless people were fed to-day i'll a sys-
tematic manner. On the waterfront, where the
boatloads of provisions docked there was an
endless procession of carts and drays carrying
food to the of stations established all
over the city and at the parks At these sta
tions food and drink. comprising bread, pre-
pared meats and canned goods, milk and linn
tied amount Of hot coffee, and even fruit, were
served to all those who applied. About fifteen
hundred tons of provisions are being moved daily
from the waterfront.


Large supplies of blankets tentings and other
material are reaching the supply stations rap
idly. Barracks have been completed at several
points, and in these many people have found
comfort and shelter against the inclemencies OF
the weather. The situation In the cOngested
camps such as Golden Gate Park and the vari-
GUS public squares in the city, has been consider
ably relieved by the departure of many people
for points on the other side of the bay While
the number OF people leaving the city is nothing
like the vast crowds which packed the ferry
building during the first two days following the
earthquake. the number was sufficiently large
to satisfy the relief committee that its task will
become less difficult from day to day


General health conditions are satisfactory.
While the number OF cases at the various hos
pitals has increased each day, sickness is mostly
due TO exposure and worry. The most encour-
aging feature is the absence of anything like
contagion or an epidemic of disease of any
nature, The somewhat unsatisfactory sanitary
arrangements in the various camps the lack of

some places there have been few cases OF such
diseases measles and chicken pox, but prob
ably not more than would develop under ordi-

Sheldon, Iowa, Dec. MANY farm
ers near here are forming what they
will call The Bird Friends society,"
Farmers have been studying the use of
various birds to their growing crops,
mostly against the crow, blackbird and
bluejay than formerly, for it has been
proven that these birds aid the farmer
more than they hurt him. James
O'Brien is president of the society.


The swallow, swift and nightingale
are the guardians of the atmosphere,
feeding on the wing and taking from
the air those forms Of insects that
might endanger the fruit trees.


Woodpeekers, chickadees and creep
ers are the guardians of the trunks
OF trees, eating the grubs that iniure
the bark of fruit or ornamental trees.


Blackbirds, thrushes, crows and larks
protect the soil, eating the worms and
insects that injure the corn, wheat and
oats. They scarcely partake of corn
except In the autumn.


The. snipe and woodcock are the
guardians Of the subsoil, reaching far
larve and insects that would soon at
tack the roots Of the growing crops.


The long prosecuted crow is really
the farmers friend, for he DESTROYS
more insects than the average bird and
rarely pulls up the corn, as alleged. He
has been known to have eaten 200
grasshoppers in single hour.


The pretty quail, whose life has been
spared bv the hunter only because of
the laws of several states, eats the
weedseeds which would otherwise scat
ter, and is also a good feeder on insect
life.


The grouse Of the west as well as
the east is prolific eater Of grubs
and grasshoppers and all forms Of in.
sects.

YUMA. Ariz., Dec. 9.-Once more the
entire Colorado River is flowing into

waters. The main line of the Southern
Pacific must again be moved to higher
ground unless the water can be

persons in the Salton Basin must lose

million acres of farming lands; the
Southern Pacific must build 200 miles
of new main line and irrigation about
Yuma must be abandoned. The Gov
eminent Laguna Dam irrigation project
may become an impossibility. At con-
servative estimate not less than $685.
100000 of present values are at stake
upon the success Of the efforts to close
the break.


What is known as the hind dam was
thrown across the new channel, and an
earth dixie was built up parallel to the
river for ten miles, mainly in Mexico.

Government dixie. Three days ago the
water found its way through both
bikes, flooding large areas. This was
thought TO be serious, but was not con-
sidered critical until last night, when
the water developed a distinct chan
mel. and this morning disclosed the
fact that the entire river had found
its way around the hind dam into the
channel from which II was recently
barred. The dam itself is uninjured.


When the water was turned into the
new channel last night the steamer
Searchlight on the Colorado. below the
break. was stranded two miles from the
water.

Pacific will Immediately order the con-
struction of fifty miles of road around

The Marchioness of Corsini, formerly
Princess Barberini, was killed last evening
by the overturnfng of an automobile in
which she was riding with her husband,
who is King Victor Emmanuels master of
horse. The marchioness, who was sixty
two years of age. was driving the automo-
bile, her husband, aged sixty-nine years,
sitting beside her. While crossing bridge
In the suburbs of Rome, seeing cart ap-
preaching, the marchioness essayed to turn
out to give the cart safe roadway. but ran
the automobile into the parapet of the
bridge with such violence that the parapet
gave way and the automobile was thrown
from the bridge into the ditch, fifteen feet
below, turning completely over as it fell
The marquis and the chauffeur escaped
without a scratch. but the marchioness was
crushed TO death.


The news of the accident was telephoued
to Rome, where ii came to the ears Of
Queen Helen. Her majesty Immediately
ordered her own automobile and FASTENED
to the scene of the tragedy, where she
found the marquis, almost crazed with
grief. beside the corpse OF his wife. The
queen took the marquis and the dead body
of the marchioness into her own automo-
bile and carried them TO the Quirinal. where
they still remain. It is believed the funeral
of the marchioness will take place from the
palace.

Pastor and people, knowing the

LONDON. May 26.-Word from Blan-
tyre. in British Central Africa. states that
the inhabitants of the little township of
Chiromo. on the Shire River, were recent
IN alarmed by cries of natives inhabiting
the neighboring villages


Eight lions had invaded the villages,
carried away one native and mauled an
other. The roaring of lions was heard in
Chiromo and five Europeans rushed out
with rifles and lamps. They found the
clothes of a native, torn and soaked in
blood, but nothing more


Next evening, shortly after sunset, the
lions entered the town itself. Natives
were taken off several verandas. mail
carriers clothed in the Kings uniform
were killed and eaten and a panic arose.
Natives deserted their villages and slept
on verandas, others Communicated
barses on the river and lay off in mid
stream, while yet others barred their
doors and windows. For several days nei-
ther native nor European ventured out sk
doors after sunset.

from San Francisco to Port Townsend.

SANTA ANA, May 26.--Acting on
orders delivered by the state or city
authorities, committee last night set
fire TO the Chinese settlement occupy
ing a half block here


The houses were mere shacks and the
financial loss is insignificant, while the
cleaning process does much to allay
public feeling since the discovery of a
leprous Chinese.


While eight men set fire to the shacks
citizens formed Gordon to see that
not an article which might carry con-
tagion was removed from the shacks.


The four houses and sheds and the
vegetable garden where the leper
worked were demolished, burned and
uprooted, reddening the sky and
bringing ranchers in from the outskirts
attracted by the glare.


Dogs, cats, rats and chickens were
quickly dispatched with clubs and
thrown back into the flames


Meanwhile the half dozen Chinese
were given new clothes and quarters
I'm tents, pitched in City Hall square,
where they can be watched IL white
patches should appear on their skin.


The leper came from Tustin, near
by city, about six weeks ago.


So quickly have the authorities acted
that all fears have been calmed, though
special vigilance will be exercised over
all Chinese or those who may have
been exposed to contagion.

A Pittsburg correspondent says that San
Francisco's earthquake shocks demonstrate
ed above everything else the utility of the
steel frame building In this country. When
San Francisco Is rebuilt the lesson will be
needed, and brick and stone will be rejected
in favor of the steel skeleton building
Many such buildings are In ruins, but they
have been destroyed by fire, not by the
shaking of the earth. While other build
ings were topping into the street the steel
frame buildings remained intact. They
swayed and swung on their foundations but
the boited steel beams and Orders hung to-
gether. The skeletons preserved their form,
although tested to the limit of fiexibility.
Only in one case was even the outside cas-
ing disturbed. Part of the rear wall OF one
building peeled off the steel frame and went
crashing into the street, but IT was only the
thin skin of the actual structure the frame
manned in place, and even the elevators
could have been operated had 1t not been
for the loss of the electric power


All the steel buildings were standing,
sound and stable, after the last of the
shocks, and they were In the best possible
condition until the flames swept westward
from the water front and engulfed them.
These buildings had been erected only after
the bitterest opposition by individuals who
looked upon them as not only certain and
absolute losses to their owners In the first

!. On the gate posts In front of the Brain
erd homestead two fat jack-o'-lanterns

In the flour trek a dime is hidden in a

Mrs. Brainerds sister was the gypsy who

in question was exceedingly liberal and
promised that he would not fracture
the law again.


Judge Mcdonald promptly assessed

being better acquainted with the citys
laws. Dixon deposited $l54 with the
court and will endeavor to raise the

When arrested last night Dixon had

consenting himself to. remain in Jail

San Francisco labor council last night, after
formally indorsing the democratic candidate
Theodore A. Bell, for governor, adopted the
following resolutions:


First, that the executive committee
should telegraph Samuel Gompers to use
his best endeavors with William R. Hearst
to have William H. Langdon, the candidate
of the Independence League for governor,
withdraw; second, that the executive COM
mittee of the council call upon the demo-
cratic campaign committee and have the
latter wire the democratic committee of New
York to use it's influence with Hearst to
have Langdon withdraw; third, that the
executive committee wire Hearst direct to
have Langdon withdraw.


The resolution indorsing Bell was adopted
after two hours debate, in which some Of
the members of the council stood for Lang
don and others for Austin Lewis, the social
list candidate for governor. The motion to
make Bells MISREPRESENTATION was
lost through opposition Of the socialists.

text:
Special to The Herald


DENVER, Feb. 4.-Fighting desper-
ately not only for themselves, but for
the lives and safety of over a hundred
passengers, Frank Barlow, engineer,
and William Brewington, fireman, bat
tied for half an hour Sunday night in
a swaying locomotive cab with a great
eagle.


The hand to-talon combat started
when the Rocky Mountain limited on
the Rock Island road was three miles
west of Agate, and the two men were
unable to subdue the ferocious bird un-
til the train pulled into Limon. 1t was
q running fight for twenty miles.


Frank Barlow, who lives in Denver
at South Ninth and West Colfax ave-
rue, has been connected with the Rock
Island for thirty-five years, and he says
that this is the first time that such an
adventure has ever been encountered
on a moving train In the history of
railroading.


Two big eagles have made their nest
near Agate for the past ten years and
they appeared fearless Of man or rush
ing trains. Sunday night the Rocky
passed Agate, Colo, when one of the
eagles raced with the train. The bird
became Infatuated and flew into the
open window Of the engine cab. The
other eagle followed, and although the
train was speeding across the prairies
at over fifty miles an hour, it circled
time and again over the cab scream
ing weirdly, while its mate engaged in
its terrible fight for life with the train
men.


The eagle struck Engineer Barlow a
terrific blow on the chest as it flew
down through the front window of the
cab and he fell from his seat.


The throttle was wide open and the
engines pounded out the miles, endang-
ering the lives of all on the train, while
Barlow and Fireman Brewington strug-
gled with the ferocious bird.


Fireman Yells for Help


Barlow started back to his levers,
when Brewington called out for help,
as he could not fight the bird off alone.
The roar of the train drowned their
cries, but John Snyder, the brakeman,
noticed that something was wrong and
went ahead. AS Snyder crept down
over the coal in the tender, the eagle
left Barlow and Brewington and at
tackled him savagely. Snyder carries
his left arm in a sling as a result. The
eagle fastened it's talons in his biceps
and, bracing itself against the sides of
the cab with its WINGS tore Viciously at
Snyder's arm.


By combined efforts the other two
men finally pulled the talons out of the
flesh, leaving very dangerous wound.


The eagle was finally beaten down,
but still fought fiercely, lying on the
floor and striking up into the air.


This dramatic battle was lighted only
by the Iurid flames shining through
the furnace door.


"The screams of the eagle, we three
men fighting and cursing like fiends,
with the ghostly light under the boiler
Pickering us with red, made that en-
CINE cab. rocking and reeling, seem like
a section of some strange hell" said
Barlow.


The eagle was bound with leather
thongs and brought to Denver, where
1t will be placed on exhibition in the
window of the Rock Island ticket Office.


1t is a magnificent bird, and measures
seven feet and eleven inches from tip
TO tip of it's wings.


1t is one Of the largest eagles ever
captured alive in the world.

ernor now stand between Mrs. lie Doux

fight to save the life of his client, the

The Southern Pacific passenger de-
pot at Long Beach, so long promised,
has had yet another setback.


The work of grading the lot at Second
street and Pacific avenue was begun
yesterday, but was later abandoned,
because George Newcomb, city building
inspector. refused to issue a permit for
the proposed structure.


The plans for the new depot call for
a building with wood studding, wire
coated and staff-covered, making
stucco building. Newcomb holds that
the plans must be changed to suit the
city ordinance. which provides that
within the fire limits such a building
cannot be put up.


The plans for the depot show a build
ing of mission style. with large waiting
rooms and commodious rooms also for
the roads agents. The present depot is
a rambling wooden shack, generally
considered to be one of the worst look
ing structures near the business dis
trict.


According to the plans, extensive
parking will be done around the new
structure.

Mrs. Ellen Ringold. colored. thirty-three
years Of age, Of 315 Sd street southeast
was seriously and possibly fatally burned
this afternoon about o'clock during fire
in her home, following the explosion of q
gasoline stove. The woman received painful
burns about the legs. arms and shoulders.
She was taken to Providence Hospital.
where the injuries were dressed. Her sister
received minor burns on the hands.


Mrs. Ringold was working over the gaso-
line stove in the kitchen shortly before 1
O'Clock. when the explosion occurred.


The flames spread to the cotton dress she
was wearing. The woman screamed for
help and her sister responded. The flames
were extinguished only after Mrs. Ringold
had been severely burned.


"She Will probably recover" a surgeon at
the hospital stated. but she will be con-
fined to the hospital for long time. Skin
grating may be necessary to save her
life."


The explosion of the gasoline also set
fire to the furniture and woodwork Of the
room In which the stove was located. A
telephone message was sent to No. 3 engine
company. which quickly responded and ex-
tinguished the blaze.

In no age Of the world nor in any

period during former years.

mined to make their permanent home
here.

westbound passenger business, but in
about two weeks the Shriners and their
friends will begin coming and then the
railroad men will have lively time.

the railroad employees when the

one, for the summer rates will go into
effect early and the tourists from Ne
vada and Arizona will be coming to

SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 4-when
the transport Logan arrived today
from Manila the police authorities,
who had been previously notified, took
off from the vessel number of men
who bore the reputation of desperate
characters The men were photo
graphed and exhibited to the various
police watchers.


When the Logan left Manila she car
ried sixty men who had been ordered
deported by the secret service officials
of that city. 1t is said that the policy
of the secret service men is to rid
Manila of her criminal and worthless
population and the transports are be-
ing used to take them back to America.
The deported men are all whites.


On several previous transports men
who had been accused and convicted
of serious crimes were landed in San
Francisco after the police had been
apprised of their arrival Among those
who arrived today were men who had
served terms for murder, robbery and
embezzlement. When the Logan ar
rived at Honolulu, where there was a
scarcity of sailors, thirteen of the de-
ported men who had been seamen,
were shipped voluntarily on the ship
Phelps. destined for Philadelphia.

exhibited the new arrivals they were
given their liberty.

CAMPTON, KY, Jan. 30.-A tele-
phone message was received from
Rogers, this county, this morning to
the effect that late last evening Willis
Hatton, the 7-year-old son of John Hat
ton, a prosperous farmer, had shot and
killed his mother because the latter
had spanked him for some small de-
reelection of duty.


After the mother had corrected the
child he turned to her and said: "I
will kill you for that" He then went
into another room, seized his fathers
revolver from a drawer, aimed at his
mother, and pulled the trigger. The
bullet struck Mrs. Hatton in the right
side above the hip, passing through
her body and out the left side, killing
her instantly.

PARIS, Dec. 16.-The serious dis
turbances that it was thought would
ensue on this, the first Sunday under
the law separating the church and
state were not realized. The services
in this city in particular passed off
quietly.


There was notable increase in
the size of the congregations and in
them were large numbers of men who
were determined forcibly to prevent
the interruption of masses by rowdies.


There were only a few cases where
rowdies entered the churches wearing
their hats, and they were promptly
elected and arrested.


Reports from the provinces show
that there was great excitement at
many places. Large professions
chanting psalms accompanied the
clergy to and from churches. Counter
demonstrations took place in several
cities, notably Perpignan and Amiens,
where the Catholics and free-thinkeTs
came into collision, necessitating in
reference by the police, who quickly
dispersed the crowds.


Several demonstrators were injured.

LONDON, May 21.-Captain Boyd
Alexander OF the Alexander Gosling
expedition reports from the Angu dis
trict on the river Welle, Congo Free
State, that he has secured a specimen
Of the okapki which the experition saw
alive. No white man ever before has
seen a living okapi The announce
ment greatly interests biologists.


The okapi was first described by Sir
Harry Johnston. who found a dead
one in the Semliki forest and drew a
picture Of the animal. The head is
described as being that Of a giraffe,
but there are no external horns. The
okapi Is about four and a half feet
high at the withers. The tail is rather
short and the neck short and thick.


The coloring of the animal Is It's
most extraordinary feature. Tho
cheeks and Jaws are yellowish white.
contrasting with dark colored neck.
The forehead and a line down to the
muzzle are a deep red chestnut and
the large broad ears are Of the same
tint, fringed with black. The neck,
shoulders and body range In tone from
sepia and jet black to red; the belly is
blackish and the tail chestnut, with
small black tuft. The hind quar-
ters and legs are either snow white
or pale cream, touched here and there
with orange and marked with purple
black horizontal stripes and blotches.

Ihe imperial Chinese commits: oners were
entertained this afternoon at Fort Myer by
Col Hatfield, commandant of the post,
with special cavalry and artillery drill
that had been got up for their benefit The
party left the Arlington Hotel in the early
afternoon and were driven over to Fort
Myer in carriages. There were about TWEEN
" IN the party, the commissioners being
accompanied by Sir LANG, the Chinese min
lister, and Mr.. Charles DENLY of the State
department. The commissioners had seen
some American army posts since coming
to this country, being entertained at Fort
sheridan on their way to. Washington but
this was the first time they had seen the
'Cossack drill and they were decidedly
enthusiastic over the personal intimacy
that seemed to exist between the men and
me horses. Col Hatfield and the commits
Sloners had met yesterday on the trim TO
Mount Vernon and they were thus in n
measure already acquainted with their
host They occupied the big box down at
the end of the riding hall, where so many
distinguished guests have been entertained
before them. and were presented to num-
Der of the officers of the post,


mere Is a question which attracted the
Ch1nese guests the more. the riding or the
driving exhibitions. The Chinese have sew
eral well-equipped horse batteries in the
service. but they are not trained to putting
up such fancy drill as the artillerymen
gave: and the exhibition was revelation.
The bareback drill, the vaulting over horses
on the run and the driving of barebacked
horses with the men standing on them were
all spectacular stunts that appealed both
10 the commissioners and their followers,
and they said that while the Chinese cav
airy did nothing of the sort, they realized
the value that such training must be both
to the men and horses


The two Commissioners. Viceroy Tuan Fang
and Mr.. Tai Hung Chi. will this evening
be the guests at dinner of Mr.. Charles
DENLY, who has been their guide and COM
panfon each day. during their stay in Wash
lngton. 1t will be small dinner, only the
two commissioners and their secretaries
Mr.. Woo and Mr. Use, being invited to
meet few guests, among them justice
Harlan of the Supreme Court.


The Post Office Department


Col Chun and Mr. Oyang King, the vice
consul at San Francisco, went through the
Post Office Department this morning. They
had been especially deputed to look up the
postal system, and they did it with char
acteristic thoroughness. They saw what
there was to see of interest in the post
office museum. but they were more inter-
ested in the system of the office and went
thoroughly into the workings of the rail-
way mail service. the local delivery, the
money order office and the special delivery
and inspectors divisions. China is a mem
Der of the information postal union, so
she knows pretty well in general way the
workings of the American system but this
was a chance to get the Information ut
close range from headquarters, and it was
not overlooked.


The visitors then went down to the Smith
sonian and the National Museum.


Government Printing Office.


The Chinese commissioners, accompanied
by the Chinese minister; Mr.. DENLY chief
clerk of the Department of State; the sec
rotary of the commission and three Chinese
military officers, visited the government
printing office at 10 O'Clock this forenoon.
They were accompanied through the great
est printery in the world by Mr.. Charles
A. Stillings, the public printer; Mr., Oscar
J. Ricketts,, foreman of printing, and Mr..
F. \. Collins, secretary to the public
printer.


The party first visited the big press room
and witnessed the work of the fat-bed
drum cylinders the fiat-bed tWo-revolution
cylinders, the presses with automatic feed
ers, the great rotary or web presses which
print the Congressional Record and the
speeches of senators and Representatives.
They were then shown the presses which
print the registration cards for the Post
Office Department, and the job press divl
sion with the up-to-date machinery there,
and the die stamping presses which pro-
duce the embossed stationery now SO gen.
orally used by Congress and the depart
ments.


Next the visitors were shown through the
divisions where the type is set by hand
with the racks for leads rules. slugs, ETC.
From there they were ushered into the di-
vision where linotype machines are used
and each of the visitors had his name set
on a linotype slug to be preserved as a
souvenir of his visit to Uncle Sans big
print shop. They were then shown the
workings of the monotype machines and
manifested much interest in the manipuia-
ton of the Lanston machines and the ope-
ration of the casters


Thence the party went through the bind
cry and showed great interest in the ruling
and sewing machines, the perforators and
numbering machines. At the conclusion of
the tour of the office the visitors expressed
great admiration at the wonders they had
seen. They were given very good insight |
into the workings of the printery through
their interpreters. The commissioners car
ried away with them other souvenirs-slugs, |
monotype matter and fancy designs exc
cuted on the perforating machines by the |
young lady operators. Mr.. Stillings had |
planned to have the commissioners take |
lunch at the office, but they had to hasten |
away to the military drill al Fort Myer


The commission will leave for New York |
tomorrow night.

CHICAGO, Aug. 24.-Although the
torridity was somewhat tempered today
seven deaths were reported from the
heat.


The most serious phase of the situa-
tion is the prospect of an immediate Ice
famine.


Many small dealers notified patrons
today that by tomorrow their supply
will be entirely exhausted.


Meat dealers have been in predica-
ment for several days, as the usual
supply Of ice has not been forthcom-
ing. The increased demand has
caused producers of artificial ice to cut
off their carload customers and small
dealers.


The vice president of the Knicker-
booker Ice company, the largest supply
house in the west, said today that if
the hot weather continues three days
longer the ice situation will be very
serious.
One peculiar feature of the record
breaking period has been the death of
horses. Fully 500 first-class animals
have perished within the last four days
and all horse hospitals are full to over
flowing with patients.


The temperature did not go above
7S today and dropped as low as 7S.

SANTA ROSA, April 26-The latest

injured and seven missing.


The entire business section of the
town was destroyed and many resi-

Twenty fires started. but the water

three hours the flames were under con-
troll, despite the fact that the engine
house was ruined.


Cut off by the disaster from COM

Santa Rosa knew nothing of the de-
arrival from there of a trainload of
nearly 1000 refugees, begging for help
that could not be given them. But
nearby towns came to the rescue and
and after period of starvation and
suffering aid was received.

The court house, the new Masonic
temple, the new library and the Odd
Fellows building went with the other
buildings, but larger and better struc-
lures will replace them.


1t is the intention of business men to
at once begin rebuilding. The Savings
Bank of Santa Rosa occupied $4,000
building It's new one, which will be
an office building, will cost $250000.


Con Shea, who lost five buildings
worth 100000, says that his five new
ones will be worth twice that sum.
The same spirit is manifested by all
who have been interviewed.


AS soon as the dead were buried.
business men began clearing passage
way through the streets and teams
were put to work hauling the rubbish
to waiting freight cars.

Manila.-Latest advices from Hong
Kong state that 5000 lives were lost
during the typhoon and that the dam
age to property, public and private
will amount to millions of dollars.


Twelve vessels were sunk, twenty
four were stranded, seven were dam
aged and one-half of the native craft
in port were sunk.


The shipping trade has been para
lyzed through lack of lighters.


Hong Kong-The typhoon which
swept this port destroying great
number of vessels and causing much
loss of life, was of a local nature. 1t
came suddenly and without warning.
The observatory had predicted moder-
ate winds. Half an hour after the gun
signal had been fired the storm was at
it's height 1t lasted two hours.


Most of the damage done was
wrought on the Kowloon peninsula.
The losses are estimated at several
million dollars. Oven one thousand
sampans and junks are missing from
Hong Kong alone. Wharves were swept
away and houses collapsed. The mill
tary barracks are in ruins.


The harbor is strewn with wreckage
thrown upon the shore. Hundreds OF
Chinese boatmen and their families
were saved by the bravery of the po
lice and civilians, but several thousand
of the Chinese water dwellers must
have perished, many within a short
distance of the shore. The losses in
lives and property among the Chinese
were appalling. To-day the police sta
tions of Kong Kong are surrounded by
Chinese identifying their dead. The
families of the Hong Kong boatmen
live night and day on the sampans
and thousands of these people are now
homeless.


Many valuable steel lighters have
been lost. Some of them were hurled
ashore. Channels will have to be dug
to permit some of the vessels ashore to
be refloated. The force of the wind
and waves was such that some vessels
were stranded almost high and dry.

More than pair of eyes, curious or sympathet-

blind professor rather striking figure, tall and
spare with the long gray beard his breast and the

There were many in the Auditorium that night

something of his honorable and pathetic history:
how he had hidden fair, generation ago, to be the

to win laurels here and how, even before he
had stepped American SOIL the blow had fallen
that wrecked his happiness and ended his career.
For his only child had been drowned in the harbor
of New York, and the father crazed with grief and
blaming himself for the accident, had raved for
weeks with fever and delirium, and had risen from
his bed in a New York hospital a shadow of his
former self, blind, ray.haired, and with only
fragment of his wonderful voice remaining.


There another phase of the story than this
one of which the world had heard little When Emil
Reinhardt had back to life after his long illness,
his thin trembling hands, cropping in the cruel dark,
had ever found two warm faithful ones waiting to
clasp them During the years that followed it was
his wife Elizabeth serene. cheerful, stronger and
Drawer than he. who managed their present and
planned their future; it she who encouraged,
strengthened, upheld, the broken man who was now
husband and child in one to her great love.


Gradually he had recovered somewhat from the
shock of his childs death and his sudden blind
ness but thing his wife had never been able to
persuade him to do-that to go back to the
Fatherland which he had left in all the joy and pride
of life. Drifting from city to city, they had at last
settled in Chicago, and there he had succeeded with
to furnish modest living; while his wife, born
Haas utter that she was, made the little fiat they
rented into home, simple but full of coziness and
comfort. They had made friends; not many, per-
haps but warm ones American customs and Ameri-
can speech had become familiar to them, and they
called America home; but still they were Germans

Warsaw. Dec. 16.-Reports received from
points throughout Russian Poland show what
results have followed the governments policy
of irnness This result was accomplished at a
terrible cost to the Polish people. the number
of victims being estimated at thousands Busi-
ness has become stagnant the trades and in
dustries are bankrupt and the masses are in a
state OF lamentable poverty


To-days reports from Czenstochowa. which is
about 10000. including many Jews. show that
seven so-called Terrorists have been tried by
drlImhead court-martial and executed in the last
two days.


In the arly part OF last week five Terrorists
were tried convicted and shot here, also
aszow and one at Lomza. These executions have
been going constantly through Poland.


Despite the depressing effect OF this martial
rule. the Poles are busily engaged In organizing
their forces for the next parliamentary elections
For the time being party differences have been
forgotten and the national spirit has brought
about merger of the three great Polish parties
Conservative. Progressive and Democratic.
These are selecting fusion candidates represent
ing Polish national ideals. The Polish
school system is also bringing out evidence of
national energy as the permission to establish
private schools with Polish teachers has already
resulted in the formation of eight hundred
schools, with an attendance Of seventy-five
thousand Polish children.


Altogether, despite the darkness of the pres
ent martial conditions, the situation has been
somewhat relieved by evidences of the in
domitable spirit of the Polish people.

body was picked up and taken to the
sidewalk and a physician was sum-

given to relatives.

Any connection that William Ward

murder of Mrs. William Algeria has
been proven a false theory, accord

the next few days, however, the police
say that they will have some startling
information to make public.


That Mrs. Algeria was murdered is
now a generally accepted conclusion
in police circles. The young woman
disappeared from her home, 413 Lake
Shore road, April 30, about o'clock
in the evening. She told her father
in-law that she was going out on the
back porch to get drink of water.
That was the last seen of her.


For the first few days the case was
looked upon by all concerned as a
suicide. But little heed was paid to
1t until Sunday night, when Algeria
made statements to the police that
led to the murder theory.


Make Discoveries


Immediately the police detailed two
detectives to work in conjunction with
Talamantes on the case. Yesterday it
became known that the men had made
some startling discoveries and it was
practically admitted that the case had
evolved into a murder.


So much secrecy is being thrown
about the work of the detectives that
1t strengthens the rumor that the case
is a murder and that the police have
made certain of this fact. Detective
Talamantes does not deny that the
case is a DrObahIe murder


Ward, the man who was connected
for time with the mysterious disap-
pearance, was employed by Algeria
for five years. He left the city about
the time Mrs. Algeria disappeared 1t
was because Algeria dismissed Ward
from his service that the police thought
that he might have been connected
with the case. 1t now appears that
Ward was in Santa Barbara two days
before the woman was spirited away
and had not been out of that city.

rooms to the front and stops to kiss his
mother. A quick trip is made to the

jections.

footwork in saving himself appears
wildly.

with his great strength.

mers for curing and preparing their
tobacco for the market; namely, sun
cured, air cured and flue cured. The
old and cheap way is called air cured;
the later discovery and improved way
is called fue cured. In fue-curing
the tobacco is taken from the field
and suspended over intensely hot
flues in houses especially built to re-
tain the heat, and there kept in the
proper temperature until this curing
process developes in the tobacco the
stimulating taste and fragrant aroma
found in Schnapps tobacco, just as
green coffee is made fragrant and
stimulating by the roasting process.
Only choice selections of this ripe,
juicy fue cured leaf, grown in the
famous Piedmont country, where the
best tobacco grows, are used in
Schnapps and other Reynolds brands
of high grade, flue cured tobaccos.

nor. Mrs. Largomarcino, in the midst

SAN FRANCISCO, March 22.-Su-
perior Judge Graham today granted a
divorce to Mrs. Henry E. Huntington
on the ground of desertion. No request
for alimony was made, and the attor-
neys refuse to state whether or not
there was any money settlement.


Mrs. Huntington appeared in court
accompanied by her brother, Edward
H. Prentice, and her attorney. Her
husband was represented by two at
torneys.


Mrs. Huntington took the stand and
stated that she and her husband had
not lived together for six years. She
also said that there was no community
property.


Her brother corroborated her state
ment about the time of desertion, and
Judge Graham tersely remarked:


"Take your decree"


The time occupied was not over
eight minutes.


Mrs. Huntington sailed for Japan on
the steamer Korea this afternoon.
